News.title: Family of 13-year-old hit-and-run victim heartbroken as killer set for release after just two years
News.content:
THE family of a 13-year-old boy killed by a hit-and-run drunk are devastated the driver could be freed from prison after just two years.

Kaylan Hippsley died in 2024 when he was hit by Harley Whiteman, 19, who then abused paramedics treating the teen.



He was jailed for six years, increased to nine after Kaylan’s family appealed.

But Whiteman, now in an open prison, has since had his sentence cut to just four years, so is to be freed in October under Labour’s early release scheme.



Kaylan’s family in the Rhondda, South Wales, urged PM Andy Burnham to keep him locked up.

His sister Chloe Williams said: “We as a family are calling on Andy Burnham to review our case and demand immediate action.

“The decision to move Kaylan’s killer to an open prison after barely two years goes against everything the Court of Appeal ruled.

“It feels like justice has been stolen from us.

“We will not accept this. We demand that he serves his full sentence behind closed doors. Kaylan deserves nothing less.”

And cousin Julie Craig said: “It beggar’s belief that after two years he’s allowed back into the community.



“It’s absolutely devastating.

“This just feels like a kick in the teeth.”

News.title: Cops seize three tons of cocaine worth over £200m at British port after drugs concealed in bananas sent from Colombia
News.content:
NEARLY three tons of cocaine with a street value of £232million was discovered in a container of bananas.

Border Force officers with sniffer dogs found the drugs in the consignment from Colombia.



The National Crime Agency was alerted and officers seized the dope at London ­Gateway Port in Essex on Friday.

They then watched as a man in a truck drove the shipment — minus the cocaine — to a warehouse, where a crime gang had “a massive panic” on finding the drugs missing.



The NCA raided the site near Buntingford, Herts, and eight Brits and one Dutchman were arrested.

A source said: “They must have thought they had been turned over by criminals but, worse than that, the NCA went steaming in.



“It’s the biggest seizure of cocaine in the last few years and this will cause serious grief in the criminal underworld.

“There could be massive fall-outs over the loss of the drugs.’’

The nine arrested, most in their 20s, have all been bailed ­pending enquiries.

NCA officers were still searching the warehouse on Monday.



The largest ever seizure of cocaine in the UK came in Southampton in 2024.

A total of 5.7 tons was found hidden in banana containers heading to Europe from Colombia.

News.title: Fuel prices have soared and what has Labour done about it? Sat back and raked in an extra £1BILLION in tax
News.content:
ANDY BURNHAM says he wants to “pull every single lever” to bring down the cost of living.

He’s off on a summer tour of the country, in what No10 calls “listening mode”, asking ordinary people how the Government can make their lives easier.



It’s a nice image — the Prime Minister, freshly back from holiday, rolling up his sleeves and heading out to the regions to hear from the public before he’s even properly unpacked his boxes in Downing Street.

I’d love to believe it. I really would.



But if these last few months have taught us anything, it’s that the political elite still seem completely disconnected from how the real world operates outside the M25 and the M60.

The latest figures from the RAC, released last week, tell their own story.



Petrol has climbed to around 161p a litre.

Diesel has surged to roughly 181p.

Filling a standard 55-litre family diesel car has breached the £100 mark once again.

Since the Iran conflict flared up, UK drivers have been forced to find an extra £5.5billion just to keep their tanks full for work.



Around 70 per cent of that has landed on diesel drivers — the tradespeople, the hauliers, the people who actually keep this country moving.

And what has the Government done about it?

It has sat back and let the Treasury quietly pocket close to £1billion in extra VAT.

As pump prices rise, so does the taxman’s take.

Ministers are, in effect, making money from the very crisis that is squeezing working families and pushing up the cost of everything else.



So while Mr Burnham talks about pulling every lever, the lever he really should be reaching for is the one sitting right in front of him at the pumps.

In his first week in the job, he announced a cut to VAT on household energy bills and a £2 cap on bus fares, both presented as “everyday fixes”.

Fine as far as they go — but they don’t go very far at all for the millions of people whose working lives simply cannot be organised around a bus timetable.

Like so many metropolitan leaders before him, Burnham seems to have a shaky grasp of how towns, villages and rural counties actually function.

For millions of people, driving isn’t a lifestyle choice.



It’s how they earn their living.

A nurse doing a 2am shift at a regional hospital doesn’t benefit from a bus fare freeze.

A care worker doing her rounds between elderly patients can’t plan her day around a patchy rural timetable.

A plumber, an electrician, a carpenter — none of them can lug their tools on to the number 42.

Farmers and hauliers, who keep the supermarket shelves stocked, certainly can’t move Britain’s goods by public transport.



These are the people generating the tax revenue that keeps the country running, and yet they’re the ones being squeezed hardest to pay for it.

Even if you wanted to swap the car for the bus, good luck.

One in five buses fails to run on time.

Average bus speeds in major cities have dropped by 23 per cent since 2010.

In London, the average bus now crawls along at 8.6mph during peak hours — slower than 50 years ago.



In Manchester and Birmingham, congested routes barely outpace a brisk walk.

Meanwhile, 15 per cent of the entire bus network outside London has vanished since the pandemic.

At the same time, Burnham is happy to take credit for a rail fare freeze that his predecessors actually announced, even as a season ticket from Crawley to London Bridge still costs £4,856 a year — around a fifth of a minimum-wage worker’s salary.



Bus caps and rail freezes make for tidy photo opportunities.

They give increasingly image-conscious politicians something shiny to stand next to.

But they mean very little to people whose jobs cannot be squeezed into a timetable dreamt up in a city-centre office.

Those people need help at the pumps, and they need it now.

The existing 5p fuel-duty cut, still in place thanks to The Sun’s Keep It Down campaign, predates this latest crisis and simply isn’t enough on its own.



Cutting VAT on household energy bills is welcome, but it won’t take a single penny off the cost of filling a van.

Other countries have already worked this out. Italy cut diesel taxes by 15p a litre.

Greece targeted reductions of up to 13p for hauliers and professional drivers.

Ireland slashed excise duty by 27p on diesel and 23p on petrol.

Even further afield, Thailand, the UAE, South Korea and Australia have all stepped in with targeted relief.



Britain, by contrast, has simply let the Treasury enjoy the windfall while treating drivers as an easy top-up to the public purse.

So here’s my message to Mr Burnham as he sets off on his listening tour: Actually listen.

Cut VAT from 20 to 15 per cent and you knock 7p off a litre of petrol and 8p off diesel overnight.

Pair that with a genuine duty cut and you’d finally be delivering something that matters to the people who keep this country moving, rather than another photo beside a bus.

Cheaper transport is great for those who can use it.



But Britain’s tradespeople, carers, farmers and hauliers have no alternative but to drive.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

They’re not a bottomless cash machine, and they’re certainly not the enemy.

It’s time to stop posing beside buses and start backing the workers who actually keep Britain moving.

News.title: Andy Burnham must find a way to keep PC Andrew Harper’s killers behind bars or face public’s fury
News.content:
Find a way

ANDY Burnham has apparently been told by hand-wringing civil servants that it’s “not possible” to block the early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers.

They need to be told to try harder.



There are a few hundred inmates serving time for manslaughter.

Burnham needs to order officials to find a way to bar those serving the longest sentences from being freed.



That would minimise the threat of any legal challenges from lags and ensure remorseless thugs Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole stayed behind bars.

As the petition to keep Bowers and Cole locked up ticks up towards one million, the public’s demand is crystal-clear.

They expect Burnham to meet the hopes HE raised in the first place.

The Prime Minister must realise he has the power to overrule Government officials and lawyers all too often stuck in their comforting bubble of State uselessness and a lack of accountability.

With a massive majority behind him, this issue boils down to a question of sheer will.

Push boat out

HOW much longer must Brits put up with migrants and people-smugglers making a mockery of our open borders?



Yesterday’s raid on UK waters by a mega-dinghy carrying a record 230 illegal asylum-seekers opened up a new front in the small boats crisis.

It’s clear that far from the gangs being smashed, the criminals are running rings around French cops.

Their new tactic of packing as many as possible on a single craft — enough yesterday to fill a Boeing Dreamliner jet plane — could soon make 1,000 arrivals a daily occurrence.

It’s not just the sheer numbers. The cost is becoming astronomical, too.

In 2023, the Home Office estimated each migrant costs taxpayers £106,000 minimum over four years in free housing, healthcare and other benefits.



That means yesterday’s mega dinghy could cost nearly £25MILLION.

That’s a staggeringly high price to pay while Burnham & Co leave Britain without any kind of plan.

Betting slip

FOR a bloke who claims to love sport and champion working-class culture, Andy Burnham seems surprisingly keen to demonise anyone who likes a flutter.

The Prime Minister says he will boost our High Streets by making it harder to open vape shops and . . . bookmakers.

But bookies are not anti-social enterprises. They provide good jobs and help keep sports like racing and rugby league afloat.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

In any event, it’s hard not to conclude Burnham’s plan is purely performative.

Thanks to Labour’s tax raids on gambling, what’s actually happening is hundreds of betting shops are closing.

News.title: Brit tourist, 66, dies in horror parasailing accident while on holiday with husband in Benidorm
News.content:
HOLS TRAGEDY Brit tourist, 66, dies in horror parasailing accident while on holiday with husband in Benidorm

A BRITISH tourist has died in a horror parasailing accident in Benidorm while on holiday with her husband.

The 66-year-old crashed onto rocks after a powerful gust of wind caused the line tethering her parachute to the boat to snap.



The woman went into cardiac arrest, but desperate efforts to revive her she was pronounced dead at the scene.

It was not immediately clear whether the unnamed holidaymaker’s husband was injured in the ordeal.



He is believed to have suffered broken ribs and was reportedly “walking wounded” following the horror crash.

The tragedy unfolded in Benidorm’s Rincon de Loix are at around 6pm on Monday after a sudden change in weather conditions.



Prior to the incident, a red flag was raised, warning holidaymakers at the famous Costa Blanca resort.

Witnesses described chaotic scenes as the parasail spiralled out of control.

After the line snapped, the couple hurtled towards jagged rocks as they were left at the mercy of the wind.

One witness said: “It was clear they were going to crash.”



A police investigation has been launched and remains ongoing.

This comes after a 16-year-old British cheerleader was killed in a horror boat accident while holidaying with her family.

Abbie Lainton, from Swindon, died “in a terrible accident” off the coast of a Caribbean island that also left her two siblings injured.

Abbie died after she was badly burnt when a tourist boat carrying around 35 people suddenly ignited and blew up off the coast of the Dominican Republic.

She was rushed to intensive care but died three days later.



Her siblings remain in hospital.

Authorities said 24 people were injured with 11 taken to hospital for treatment for burns.

Gisell Segovia and her husband Navin Torres, 35, were on the boat when it blew up and saw Abbie badly injured after the explosion.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Navin told The Sun how he was with the Brit teen as she fought for her life, calling Abbie “a warrior” who “did not go out without a fight”.

Authorities have not yet revealed the cause of the fire but have launched an investigation.

News.title: PC Andrew Harper’s colleague says Government is ‘spitting in the face of police’ over killers’ early release
News.content:
ONE of the first cops on the scene after PC Andrew Harper was dragged to his death has accused the Government of “spitting in the faces of police officers”.

Retired dog-handler Chris Bushnell spoke out as Downing Street ruled out an exemption that would stop PC Harper’s killers getting early release.



No 10’s rejection means that two of the officer’s three smirking killers, Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole, will be free within months — despite one of the biggest-ever public petitions demanding they be kept locked up.

Chris, 59, drove after the cold-blooded burglary gang that dragged 28-year-old newlywed Andrew to his death in August 2019.



He told the Old Bailey how the gang tried to ram his car with their Seat Toledo before fleeing the scene to their homes on traveller sites.

Chris spoke of the pain he still endures over his colleague’s death — and his anger that two of the killers are due to be freed.

He said: “When I first heard they could be let out early, I was shaking. It’s absolutely outrageous.

“I am angry with them, but I’m also angry with the Government. They’re spitting in the face of police officers.”

Chris said the prospect of early release will impact and demoralise many officers traumatised by losing a colleague in such a violent way.

He said: “This belittles them. It makes them feel worthless.”



Chris, who retired from Thames Valley Police in 2022, said he will “never forgive” Andrew’s killers for what they did.

He added: “To think these people could be out within weeks is appalling. The Government has to understand that this was the death of a police officer.

“Andy did his duty that night. The least they can do is show respect.”

Chris was working on a West Berkshire dog unit when Andrew was killed, and recalled having a cup of tea with him earlier in the day.



He said: “He was so friendly and always asked about the dog. He was an animal-lover, a nice lad.”

Late that night Chris was alerted on his police radio about a burglary gang that stole a £10,000 Honda quad bike from a house near Sulhamstead, Berkshire.

Unbeknown to Chris, Andrew had been lassoed round his ankles by a trailing rope from the teenage traveller gang’s car.

Andrew — due to go on honeymoon with wife Lissie after he finished his shift — was dragged more than a mile down a country lane.



Chris was waiting in a lay-by for the suspects’ vehicle when he saw it emerge from the darkness without its lights on.

He later fought back tears as he told the Old Bailey how he initially believed Andrew’s body was a deer carcass — before realising it was human as it accelerated away.

Chris pursued the vehicle and came to a fork in the road, telling jurors when he looked to the right he saw the Seat driving at him.

He said: “Without warning it was coming straight towards me.

“I then reared to the left. I took the view that they had deliberately chosen to drive straight at me.”



Chris gave chase after the vehicle until an inspector instructed him over the radio to stop.

In the meantime, Andrew’s patrol partner radioed: “My crewmate is gone. I don’t know where he is.”

Minutes later Chris received the devastating news that his colleague had been killed.

He said: “I’ve seen people die before. I’ve seen suicides. This was beyond brutal. It was awful.”

Chris was left “numb and in disbelief”.



He received counselling and support from the Police Federation, and revisits the scene of Andrew’s death every year.

He said: “I will never get over it.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A petition organised by PC Harper’s Police Federation branch — demanding his killers are kept behind bars — was set to hit 900,000 signatures on Monday evening.

Aileen O’Connor, chair of the branch, said: “The public are speaking loudly and clearly. The silence from the Government is deafening. What they’re doing is indefensible.”

News.title: Special Concorde flights, 500k flocking to Cornwall & biggest ever power surge… How UK stopped for 1999 total eclipse
News.content:
CROWDED on to rooftops, ships, hillsides and bridges, millions of us were awestruck as we witnessed 1999’s total solar eclipse.

The date was August 11, and it was the first time this country had experienced the celestial spectacle for 72 years.



No one wanted to miss it. Like the audience at a 3D movie, they wore special glasses to protect their eyes so they could gaze to the heavens as the moon covered the sun.

Factories closed, roads were clogged by traffic jams and trials at the Old Bailey in London were even briefly paused so that judges, lawyers, and jurors could watch day turn to night in the first full eclipse visible in the UK since June 29, 1927.



Tomorrow, the nation will once again have the chance to witness this incredible phenomenon when 90 to 95 per cent of the sun is hidden from view in a dramatic partial eclipse.

These cosmic coincidences happen because the sun is about 400 times larger than the moon, and about 400 times further away from Earth, making them appear almost the same size in our sky.

This allows us to witness wonders such as a breathtaking total solar eclipse, where the moon can perfectly cover the sun.​

So be sure you do not miss out on tomorrow’s marvel because the next full one is not due until September 23, 2090.

Dr Cyrielle Opitom, a member of the Royal Astronomical Society council, tells The Sun: “If the moon had been just a little bit further away from us there would never be a total eclipse.”

The moon passes just above or below the sun every month.



Normally, when this happens, the moon is not visible because it is obscured by the solar glare.

But during an eclipse, the moon passes directly between Earth and the sun.

In another stroke of random good fortune, Cornwall should again be the best place to view the phenomena.



In 1999, the “path of totality” — meaning the point at which there is a 100 per cent eclipse — passed between Penzance and Falmouth on the peninsula of England.

This time, around 95 per cent of the sun will be blotted out above Cornwall just after 7pm tomorrow.

Edinburgh and London will both see a 91 per cent eclipse, while it will be 93 per cent in Belfast and 92 per cent in Newcastle.

Anyone wishing to enjoy a “totality” tomorrow needs to head elsewhere in Europe.

The most western point of Iceland, a tiny part of Portugal and a large chunk of northern Spain are in its path.



To celebrate, Bjork is headlining a rave near Iceland’s capital, Reykjavik, and there are seven festivals in Spain.

Other fanatics will be out in the Atlantic on specially chartered ships to catch the historic moment.

A solar eclipse does happen once every 18 months somewhere on Earth and there are obsessives who try to witness as many as possible, though not all are as dramatic as tomorrow’s.



Dr Opitom, who saw a full one on the horizon from an observatory in Chile in 2019, says: “It is absolutely spectacular.”

Back in 1999, two Concordes were sent up by British Airways so that 200 passengers paying £1,500 per seat had the best chance of getting a clear view of the event from the air.

On the ground, a total eclipse lasts for around two minutes, but due to the supersonic craft travelling at twice the speed of sound, they got to enjoy it for some six minutes.

The number of people on the tiny Channel island of Alderney swelled fivefold, from 2,000 to 10,000, because it was one of the best spots to see the incredible sight.

Around 250,000 extra tourists headed for Devon and Cornwall 27 years ago, and there were traffic jams on the way to Land’s End, one of the first places in Europe to go fully dark at 11.11am.



As the eclipse started, the birds went quiet and ducks tucked their heads in their wing feathers, believing it was night-time.

Once it was over, the air was filled with a “dawn chorus” as they woke up again.

The temperature also dropped, but the South West was largely cloudy so onlookers only caught glimpses of the total eclipse.

There were some parts of the British Isles where the skies were clear enough to fully enjoy the eerie moment, particularly the North East of England.



Tomorrow, there is far more chance of the clouds parting as the heatwave continues.

Most of Britain should be sunny until the moon begins to obscure the rays just after 6pm.

Whether it is cloudy or not, one rule always applies — never look at the sun with the naked eye.

Even with the moon covering most of the giant fireball, it can still blind onlookers.



Wearing regular sunglasses is no protection at all and only eclipse glasses bearing the ISO 12312-2 safety standard should be used.

Make sure they are bought from a trusted retailer because fake ones are being sold online.

Despite repeated warnings about the risk in 1999, hospitals across the country received hundreds of calls from people complaining about eye problems in the aftermath of the eclipse.

If you want to keep the party going this year, then there is a good reason to stay out beyond 6pm.



That is because there is the added bonus of the Perseid meteor shower.

With the moon in its new moon phase, and its light diminished, during the Perseid’s peak it should be much more visible over the UK.

Keep your eyes peeled between midnight tomorrow and 5.30am on Thursday.

The eclipse will also be a far more relaxing occasion this time around.



In 1999, with the turn of the millennium just over four months away, there were a lot of predictions that the darkened skies heralded the end of the world.

Verses from the 16th century French astrologer Nostradamus had been interpreted to predict “fire from heaven” in that year.

Fashion designer Paco Rabanne had even warned that the MIR space station would plummet to Earth and that Paris would be destroyed.

As with all the millennium scare stories, no disasters befell anyone.

In fact, after the eclipse passed Britain on its way towards the Middle East and India, everyone returned to their desks to switch back on their computers and make themselves a cup of tea.



The power surge was the biggest the UK had ever experienced.

With a peak demand of 36,150 megawatts, it was even higher than when the nation tuned in to watch Prince Charles marry Lady Diana Spencer in 1981.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

And as the skies lightened there was one other lesson we learned from 1999.

Nothing can ever truly eclipse The Sun.

News.title: Residents of tiny Welsh community left ‘blindsided’ after migrant families are secretly moved into former village hall
News.content:
RESIDENTS of a tiny ­community say they have been blindsided by plans to house asylum seekers in their old village hall.

Locals were expecting the new homes to be put up for rent on the market but were shocked to discover the Home Office had already moved migrant families in.



Earlier this year, the Government promised to stop housing ­asylum seekers in newbuilds after The Sun revealed an entire street had been designated as migrant housing.

But out of the 15 new units in the North Wales ­village, 13 have been taken over by Clearsprings, the Government contractor run by asylum billionaire Graham King.



Gronant in Flintshire has a population of just 1,600, with residents fearing new arrivals will put pressure on stretched resources.

Kerrie Cox, 39, lives near the new asylum accommodation and said: “No-one was notified whatsoever.

“I was washing my car and a blacked out minibus arrived and seven people got out, five males and two females.

“We had been told the properties were to be leased out or sold with a promise of them going as social housing.

“Everyone is in shock. We have had the police here all day and night.

“We don’t normally have a police presence around here.



“I feel betrayed by the Government as a taxpayer.”

Julie Tuson, 65, said: “We want to know who is coming and vetted.

“If we want a better Britain, we all have to be involved. We were not told about it. I feel absolutely betrayed by the Government.”



Her partner Robert Bagshaw, 64, said: “They wouldn’t have a ­consultation beforehand because they would know the outcome. It’s definitely the wrong area.”

Laurie Gilmour, 29, said: “The feeling in the village is one of anger and uncertainty.

“It’s about not knowing who will be there. Who would want a load of random people moving into a village?

“It’s the wrong area. There’s nothing here.”

Keith Williams, 57, commented: “Our homeless people should get priority. You see ex-soldiers like myself on the street.”



Councillor Glyn Banks is seeking a meeting between the area’s Labour MP Becky Gittins, police and representatives of worried residents.

He told The Sun: “It’s just too big for a small village.”

Resident Joanne Gilmore has started a petition urging the council to reconsider.



She pointed to problems such as “limited access to healthcare, education and employment opportunities”.

Flintshire council said: “They are not illegal immigrants.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“They are individuals exercising their legal right to claim asylum and deserve to be treated with compassion and respect.”

A ­Government spokesman said: “The concerns of communities are central to our immigration reforms.”

News.title: Colombia earthquake LIVE: 132 confirmed dead with 570 injured in devastating 7.4 magnitude quake
News.content:
A 7.4 magnitude earthquake has struck San Jose del Palmar in Colombia, with the impact also causing major damage in the capital Bogota - 132 people have been confirmed as killed

The Colombian government has declared a national disaster after buildings were razed in a devastating 7.4 magnitude earthquake, with a total of 132 people now confirmed dead.

At least 132 people have died and a further 570 have been injured following Monday's monster quake, as per the Colombian Association of Capital Cities (CACC).

The city of Pereira has reported 60 deaths alone, a spokesperson for CACC said, adding that across the country a total of 86 buildings have collapsed and seven airports have suspended operations.

As per Bogotá radio station Blu Radio, 32 cities have been placed on red alert, meaning they are experiencing severe damage. Pediatric and neonatal sections of a hospital in Cali are understood to make up some of the buildings collapsed in the city of Cali.

Search and Rescue squads are now embroiled in a race against time to dig people out of the rubble. The government has declared a national disaster and deployed soldiers to the area to assist, and have recalled crews from neighbouring Venezeula following the devestation there, thanks to two powerful earthquakes mere weeks ago.

Witnesses felt the tremor, which had its epicentre in San Jose del Palmar, some 300 miles away on the border with Venezuela. The quake also was felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama, though minimal damage was reported there.

The earthquake occurred at a depth of around 115km, with the epicentre located in San José del Palmar; an underdeveloped area of western Colombia.

News.title: UK weather maps show heatwave to end with 7C chill and rain in 13 areas - full list
News.content:
UK weather maps show heatwave to end with 7C chill and rain in 13 areas - full list

UK weather maps show a shocking cold snap to hit the country after the fifth heatwave of the year as rain is forecast to fall in 13 areas starting from this weekend

View 4 Images Rain is set to hit the UK this week according to weather maps (Image: Getty)

Temperatures are expected to continue to sky rocket this week as a fifth heatwave is on the cards in the UK, however a sharp turn may hit at the weekend with temperatures plummeting to 7C in some areas.

‌



The cool conditions are also forecast to be accompanied by rainy spells across several areas of the UK, which is much needed as drought has been declared for almost three-quarters of England.

‌



On Thursday, forecasters have predicted that highs of 36C may be felt, however this could change come Saturday as August 15 is forecast lows of 7C.

‌



View 4 Images Rain is expected to hit the UK from Saturday (Image: Met Office )

The Met Office's forecast states: "Sunny spells and showers in the north on Saturday, with mainly dry weather in the south.

The following days are also likely to see further downpours as the weather outlet says: "Through Sunday and into the start of the following week, Atlantic frontal systems will probably approach or move across the UK, bringing some rain in places, perhaps heavy at times."

‌



Most of the rain is likely to fall in Scotland, especially in the Highlands as the weather maps show the area to be covered by downpours from 7am until 10pm.

The area is also predicted to sit at 7C for the majority of the day.

Elsewhere at 7am there is little chance of rain, but the outskirts of Essex may see a few scattered showers.

‌



Despite the chance of rain Essex is likely to remain much warmer than Scotland at around 15C, still a significant drop from a few days prior.

In the early morning areas in North Yorkshire will also have scattered rain.

View 4 Images By 1pm there will also be a small chance of showers in the north (Image: Met Office )

‌



As the day continues into the afternoon, Scotland will continue to be impacted the most by the wet conditions with downpours also striking the Scottish Borders by 1pm.

In the north, Cumbria is also likely to experience rain according to the weather maps. Alongside the wet conditions the area is also forecast to feel a 9C chill at this time.

By 4pm small spouts of rain will sneak into the Midlands as Derbyshire may see some light showers. There is also more rain expected in Cumbria.

‌



The maps show that Scotland will still be seeing the most of the rain, with the deepest precipitation falling in the Highlands.

As evening draws to a close at 10pm, the north may see some more rain, with the very outskirts of Liverpool and Blackpool forecast to be hit by drizzle.

View 4 Images The rain is expected to continue into the evening (Image: Met office )

News.title: Two charged after body of child found in Southend home
News.content:
Two charged after body of child found in Southend home

Sophie Dean, 31, and James Thorpe, 32, have been charged with preventing a lawful and decent burial of a dead body after officers found the body of a child after welfare concerns

View Image Police found the body of a child in a Southend home after welfare concerns (Image: Stephen Barnes/Getty Images)

Two people have been charged after the dead body of a child was discovered in a UK home.

The discovery was made after reports from social services regarding welfare concerns.

The body was found by police officers at an address in Kenway, Southend, on Thursday August 7.

A man and woman have been charged with preventing the lawful burial of a dead body following an investigation by detectives from Essex's Crime and Public Protection Command.

Sophie Dean, 31, of Coates House, Kenway, Southend and 32-year-old James Thorpe of Frobisher Way, Shoeburyness, have been charged with preventing a lawful and decent burial of a dead body between 3 July 2025 to 6 August 2026.

Thorpe has also been charged with obstruction of a constable in the execution of their duty.

The pair appeared at Southend-on-Sea Magistrates’ Court on Monday, August 10 and were remanded in custody to next appear at Basildon Crown Court on September 7.

The investigation into the child’s death will continue.

Article continues below

Essex Police are encouraging anyone with information that could assist them and who has not yet spoken to them to please come forward and do so, quoting investigation number 42/125225/26

News.title: Major pub chain giving away 20,000 free beers - how to claim
News.content:
Major pub chain giving away 20,000 free beers - how to claim

The offer was launched on Monday, August 10 and will see up to 20,000 free beers given away over the course of three weeks by the company - but there are conditions

View 3 Images The craft beer up for grabs has a 5.4% ABV (Image: Jam Press/BrewDog)

A craft beer pub chain is giving away thousands of free beers this summer.

‌



The offer by BrewDog was launched on Monday, August 10 and will see up to 20,000 free beers given away over the course of three weeks.

‌



BrewDog's popular Punk IPA will be given to customers who order a takeaway or groceries via Deliveroo.

‌



View 3 Images BrewDog Punk IPA is the product on promotion (Image: Getty)

Customers will also receive a separate voucher for a free pint to redeem at a BrewDog bar.

The pub was founded in Scotland in 2007, before being acquired by US beverage firm Tilray Brands in March this year.

‌



Brewdog's Punk IPA contains 5.4% ABV and a 440ml can costs £3.70 at Sainsbury's.

Those partaking in the offer must be over the age of 18 when making the order.

View 3 Images BrewDog is giving away free beers (Image: Klaus Vedfelt via Getty Images)

‌



They will also have to opt in to receive the offer. The promotion is only available in London.

It comes as BrewDog announced launched "Park IPA," a new campaign designed to make Punk IPA synonymous with one of London's most distinctive summer rituals - enjoying a cold beer in the park.

Lauren Carrol, Chief Operating Officer at BrewDog, said: "Summer in London is all about parks, pints and good company, and we want Punk IPA at the heart of it.

Article continues below

"For millions of Londoners, the park is where summer happens. Park IPA is our way of celebrating that culture and summer."

News.title: Woman who survived horror nightclub explosion says burns are 'best things in my life'
News.content:
Woman who survived horror nightclub explosion says burns are 'best things in my life'

Katya Komleva was out at a nightclub in Yekaterinburg, Russia, when people were told to leave the venue she ended up wading around in 90-degree water for 10 minutes trying to get to safety

View 5 Images Katya Komleva waded through 90C water for ten minutes to get to safety (Image: Katya Komleva / SWNS)

A woman who had eight toes amputated after boiling water "melted" her legs during a horror nightclub accident has said "getting my burns was one of the best things in my life".

‌



Katya Komleva, 35, was out at a nightclub in Yekaterinburg, Russia, when people were told to leave the venue. But when she stepped outside in bare legs and high heels, she ended up knee-deep in boiling water from a burst underground pipe.

‌



Katya ended up wading around in 90-degree water for 10 minutes trying to get to safety. By the time an ambulance arrived her skin was "melting" from her legs - leaving her muscles visible. Her family were told she might not survive at all. She spent two years in hospital and eventually proved doctors wrong by learning to walk again - although 30% of her body was left scarred, after the 2011 accident.

‌



View 5 Images Katya spent two years in hospital (Image: Jam Press/@katekomleva)

Brit tourist dies in horror parasailing accident on Benidorm holiday READ MORE :

Inside illicit relationship between prison officer pals and jailed gangster brothers READ MORE :

Katya quit her digital marketing CEO job, travelled the world, tried extreme sports, wrote a book and became a confidence coach - determined to make the most of life. She said if she went back in time, she wouldn't even change what happened - and refuses to wear prosthetics or have any treatment to reduce her scars because she doesn't want to hide them.

Katya, who now lives in Mexico City, Mexico, said: "I remember stepping into something wet and I felt this pain. You think you experience pain, but this was like another origin, it felt like something that could kill you.

‌



"When I had been rescued, I looked down at my legs and ankles and saw the skin literally melting. I spent two years of my life in hospital and I was told I'd never walk again. That was a future I prepared for."

View 5 Images When Katya was finally discharged two years later, life looked very different for her - but she was determined to see it as a chance to change her life. (Image: Katya Komleva / SWNS)

She added: "Looking back, getting my burns was one of the best things in my life. I felt like I was sleeping and I woke up, on a mental and spiritual level. If I had the offer to go back in time and avoid the accident, but remain the person I was, I would say no.

‌



"I'd go through the whole experience again to be where am now."

It transpired that an underground pipe filled with boiling water had exploded. Katya was given just a 50% chance of survival after the incident which saw her hospitalised for two years and changed her life for good.

Then a student, she had been out with friends at a nightclub when the DJ announced the club was closing for a 'technical reason'. She headed towards the doors and was the first to be let out, being warned she wouldn't be let back in again, she said.

‌



View 5 Images Katya has since gone travelling around the world, learnt to surf, quit her job as a marketing CEO and become a self-confidence coach and charity foundation founder. (Image: Katya Komleva / SWNS)

She said: "The floor was wet, but I had heels on so I didn't feel the temperature, and it was very foggy outside, but it is foggy sometimes in Russia. As soon as they shut the doors, the nightmare started. I stepped and felt this pain, but by then they had shut the doors and turned off the electricity.

"The fog was actually steam, I couldn't see my hand outstretched. I became so disorientated. My psychologist later explained that my brain just shut down, I was working on instinct, it forced me into fight or flight.

‌



"Instead of figuring out how to turn back I just kept moving forward into the water. I was just driven by the desire to survive and I knew I didn't have much time. I was walking in the water for between five and ten minutes I think, but it was impossible to say how much time passed.

Eventually, in a state of delirium, Katya spotted a figure in the distance and walked towards them in search of safety. She was rescued by a passing friend who happened to be driving by, and an ambulance turned up which she was taken into.

She said: "At that moment I knew I could die. I looked down at my legs and clearly understood that a person without anaesthesia should not see her body like that."

‌



She was taken to hospital where she spent two years recovering and learning to walk again after having amputations. In the early stages, she was too weak for surgery and caught sepsis twice due to the toxins that had got into her blood.

When Katya was finally discharged two years later, life looked very different for her - but she was determined to see it as a chance to change her life.

View 5 Images She has also written a book and become a yoga instructor. (Image: Katya Komleva / SWNS)

Article continues below

She said: "Now I feel like I have some super power, I was almost dying and now I feel I'm here for something. After two years in hospital and any absence of anything in my life, I wanted to believe life is worth living. It brought me the idea that I have a purpose, which is to help others, and it changed my perspective."

She said despite having other personal insecurities, her burns and eight and a half amputated toes have never been one of them - and has been comfortable showing off her scars. She said: "Some people will look at me because they find my body disgusting, others will find me attractive. Yeah, I lost my toes, but it's nothing. The best recipe is to stop suffering and start living."

News.title: UK's cheapest supermarket named — Aldi and Lidl are not included
News.content:
UK's cheapest supermarket named — Aldi and Lidl are not included

The cheapest supermarket is more than £100 cheaper than the most expensive if you exclude loyalty discounts.

View 3 Images The UK's cheapest supermarket has been named and it's the same one for the sixth month in a row (Image: Getty)

‌



The UK's cheapest supermarket for branded groceries has been named, taking the title for the sixth consecutive month. The latest research from consumer champion Which? reveals shoppers can pay more than double for identical products depending on where they shop and whether they use a loyalty card.

‌



Which? found price differences of up to 159% between the same everyday household items in major supermarkets in July. In an analysis of 224 popular branded groceries — including Heinz beans, Nescafé coffee and Mr Kipling cakes — Which? found Asda was once again the cheapest supermarket overall, with the list costing £769.80 on average throughout July.

‌



Aldi and Lidl are not included in this branded grocery analysis "because they do not stock a sufficiently wide range of branded products" but Which? said it "regularly finds Aldi and Lidl are the cheapest supermarkets overall in its monthly supermarket price comparisons".

Tesco using a Clubcard (£781.07), Morrisons with More (£799.24) and Sainsbury's with a Nectar card (£801.48) were the next-cheapest on average after Asda.

However, shoppers without loyalty cards faced significantly higher costs, Which? said, with Tesco (£873.66) and Sainsbury's (£881.88) both proving more expensive than Waitrose (£851.82) and Ocado (£821.29) on average, highlighting the stark impact loyalty pricing can have on the cost of branded groceries. Shopping at Sainsbury's without a Nectar card was the most expensive option overall, costing nearly 15% more than Asda.

‌



View 3 Images Which? analysed the price of 224 groceries from the most popular brands — and Asda came out the cheapest

Tesco and Sainsbury's both pointed out that 80% and 85% of sales respectively at their stores involved a loyalty card.

Listerine, Oral-B, Mr Kipling and Starbucks

When Which? looked at individual products, on average, Listerine Total Care Clean Mint Antibacterial Mouthwash (500ml) saw the biggest difference between the highest and lowest price. It was at its lowest price, on average, at Asda (£2.31) and was most expensive at Sainsbury's and Tesco without a loyalty card (£6) — a 159% difference.

‌



Which? said several branded products — including Oral-B Pro Expert Toothpaste, Starbucks Frappuccino Mocha Chocolate Flavoured Milk Iced Coffee and Mr Kipling Fruit Pie Selection — priced at around twice as much at the most expensive supermarket compared with the cheapest when priced without loyalty cards.

There were 155 products from Sainsbury’s on loyalty promotion through the month of the consumer champion’s analysis, 143 at Tesco and seven at Morrisons. None of the items in Which?'s analysis were subject to loyalty discounts at Waitrose. Asda and Ocado do not operate member-only pricing in the same way.

Which? said that while loyalty cards can unlock substantial savings, some shoppers remain unwilling or unable to participate due to concerns around data privacy or eligibility requirements.

‌



Natalie Hitchins, Which? head of home products and services said: "With many households still facing intense financial strain and bracing for predicted price hikes in the coming months, every penny counts and Asda is the most consistent for affordable branded goods.

"Our research has previously found that some branded items are so frequently on offer that shoppers should never actually pay full price for them. To avoid being caught out, consumers should try to look out for big price fluctuations, compare value across different products, and check rival retailers to ensure they are getting a genuine deal."

View 3 Images The products with the biggest price differences — loyalty card discounts may not be applied

‌



Loyalty card price considerations

Some of the products in the table above have lower prices when loyalty cards are applied. These are listed below:

Sainsbury's with Nectar (*)

Listerine Total Care Clean Mint Antibacterial Mouthwash 500ml: £4.97

Mr Kipling Fruit Pie Selection 6-pack: £2.06

Tilda Boil In Bag Basmati Rice 4 x 62.5g: £1.37

Colgate Plax Cool Mint Mouthwash 500ml: £3.77

L'Oreal Paris Elvive Bond Repair Shampoo 200ml: £9.65

Mr Kipling Mini Battenburgs 5-pack: £2.35

Nescafé Azera Americano Instant Coffee 90g: £6.09

Ryvita Thins Sea Salt and Cider Vinegar 125g: £1.96

Doritos Cool Original Tortilla Chips 180g: £1.50

Carex Original Antibacterial Hand Wash 250ml: £1.34

Quorn picnic eggs 140g: £1.72

‌



Tesco with Clubcard (**)

Listerine Total Care Clean Mint Antibacterial Mouthwash 500ml: £3.95

Mr Kipling Fruit Pie Selection 6-pack: £1.50

Colgate Plax Cool Mint Mouthwash 500ml: £3.85

L'Oreal Paris Elvive Bond Repair Shampoo 200ml: £7.97

Nescafé Azera Americano Instant Coffee 90g: £4.23

Ryvita Thins Sea Salt and Cider Vinegar 125g: £1.85

Doritos Cool Original Tortilla Chips 180g: £1.85

Mr Kipling Angel Cake Slices 8ea: £2.12

Carex Original Antibacterial Hand Wash 250ml: £1.15

How Which? worked out the cheapest supermarket

Which? analysed the price of 224 groceries from the most popular brands – including Chicago Town, Dove, Kellogg’s, Mr Kipling, Nescafé and Tilda – every day over the course of a month to work out the average cost per item. These are added up to get each supermarket's average total price.

‌



The list represents the most popular brands across a wide range of grocery categories based on industry data and is designed to produce a robust sample rather than to be representative of a typical shop.

Which? includes loyalty discounts separately in the table where they are available. The value of points, personalised discounts or other rewards are not included as these vary.

While Aldi and Lidl are regularly found to be the cheapest supermarkets overall in Which?'s monthly supermarket price analysis, they were not included in this branded grocery comparison because they do not stock a sufficiently wide range of branded products.

Article continues below

What the supermarkets said

Each supermarket included in the Which? price analysis was given the right to reply to specific examples. A Sainsbury's spokesperson said: "We have not been able to verify the calculations used by Which? as the group has not shared its full analysis. However, our customers know they can get great value by using a Nectar card when they shop with us, which is why 85% of our sales involve one. We remain focused on offering outstanding value on the products people buy most often, with more than 10,000 Nectar Price offers available every week on top of personalised Your Nectar Prices."

A spokesperson for Tesco said: “Clubcard prices unlock the best value at Tesco with thousands of deals in store and online each week. With more than 80% of sales at Tesco involving a Clubcard, most Tesco shoppers are already taking advantage of the great savings that Clubcard provides.”

News.title: Brit tourist dies in horror parasailing accident on Benidorm holiday
News.content:
Brit tourist dies in horror parasailing accident on Benidorm holiday

A 66-year-old British woman has sadly died after a parasailing activity went horribly wrong in Benidorm’s Rincon de Loix today - her husband is thought to have been injured in the tragedy

View 2 Images The tragic incident happened off the coast of Benidorm (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

A British tourist has reportedly died while on holiday with her husband in Benidorm.

‌



The 66-year-old woman, who has yet to be named, was parasailing at the popular holiday hotspot when tragedy struck. Despite the yellow flag weather conditions in place when the boat went out to sea, the couple went ahead with the activity.

‌



It has been reproted that when the woman was in the air she smashed onto rocks after a strong gust of wind caused the parasailing line tethering the parachute canopy to the towing boat to break.

‌



The woman went into cardiac arrest on impact with the rocks but efforts to revive her after she was taken to Benidorm Port proved unsuccessful and she was pronounced dead at the scene.

View 2 Images Benidorm draws in approximately five million visitors each year (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

‌



The tragedy happened around 6pm today in Benidorm’s Rincon de Loix area. One unconfirmed local report said paramedics who raced to the British woman’s aid managed to revive her briefly after she went into cardiac arrest following a fall “from a great height” onto the rocks before losing her fight for life.

Her husband is believed to have suffered injuries including broken ribs and was said to be "walking wounded" although police and hospital officials could not be reached late last night for comment. It is not yet clear what his nationality is.

Footage claiming to show the moments leading up to the tragedy was published online last night.

Article continues below

Witnesses recounting the moments leading up to the horror incident described moments of anguish as they saw the parasail spiral out of control following the line break and the couple head towards rocks as they were left at the mercy of the wind.

One told local press: "It was clear they were going to crash."

A police investigation into the incident has been launched and is ongoing.

News.title: Amber heat health alerts for almost all of England as next heatwave begins
News.content:
Amber heat-health alerts come into force across most of England on Tuesday as temperatures start to climb again at the start of the summer's latest predicted heatwave.

The UK's Health Security Agency (UKHSA) is warning that significant impacts are likely across social and health care, including a rise in deaths.

The amber alerts will be in place until Friday evening to cover high and even extreme temperatures expected through this week.

During the peak of the heatwave temperatures across England and Wales will widely be in the low to mid-30s Celsius.

Amber alerts are in place for all regions of England, aside from the North East, which has been given a less intense yellow alert for the same period.

It comes after drought officials declared 71.3% of England is now in drought.

News.title: Councils to get more powers to stop vape and betting shops, PM announces
News.content:
New vape shops will require planning permission and councils will get more powers to stop betting shops, under government plans aimed at improving high streets.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said town centres had been "hollowed out" by decades of decline and "for many people, the high streets they grew up with have become unrecognisable".

BBC News has exposed organised crime on high streets across the country, revealing shops selling illegal cigarettes and vapes, selling cannabis and cocaine, enabling illegal working and suspected money-laundering.

The Conservatives and Reform said the proposals would lead to "more empty" shops, without tax relief for other small businesses.

Burnham said the measures will give councils more power to control what businesses open in town centres.

The proposals come as the prime minister embarks on a tour of the UK, with Downing Street saying he will be in "listening mode" during his visits as he works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

The plans announced by the government include:

Changes to planning law which would mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open (England only)

Tightening the definition of a vape shop to prevent businesses avoiding the rules by describing themselves as a general convenience store or retailer (England only)

Scrapping a rule known as "aim to permit", which currently restricts councils' ability to refuse new betting shops and 24-hour slot machine shops (Great Britain-wide)

Requiring planning permission for new adult gaming centres, which offer 24-hour access to gambling machines (England only)

New powers to extend closure orders for mini-marts and vape shops found to be selling illegal tobacco or up to twelve months, something previously proposed by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer (England and Wales)

The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates that at least Â£1bn of criminal cash is laundered through high street stores in the UK each year through businesses connected to the sale of fake goods, tax evasion, illegal working and illegal drug supply.

Burnham said "the rise of vape shops, betting shops and rogue operators have replaced the shops, services, and community spaces that people are crying out for".

He added: "That's not on. I said we would improve Britain's high streets, and that's exactly what we are starting to do.

"We're putting communities back in control and giving local people a real say over what opens on their high street."

News.title: New Forest firefighting to continue overnight as cars abandoned
News.content:
A "devastating" wildfire in the New Forest, in Hampshire, is now under control, but firefighters say they will still be working into the night and for several days to come.

The wildfire began when a van caught fire on the A31 near Bratley Wood shortly after 17:20 BST on Sunday, forcing motorists to abandon more than 20 vehicles.

The area hit by the fire is protected heathland and home to a number of rare species, the New Forest National Park Authority said.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service on Monday evening asked the public to avoid the area, while National Highways said the A31 dual carriageway through the New Forest would remain closed until further notice.

Aerial footage of scorched vegetation showed how the fire funnelled outwards in a south-easterly direction as the wind fanned the flames.

Smoke from the blaze could be seen drifting across both sides of the Solent, prompting fire to urge people to keep doors and windows shut.

New Forest National Park Authority warned the impact on the forest ecosystem and rare species would be severe.

News.title: England set to eliminate hepatitis C
News.content:
Hepatitis C is spread through contact with blood infected with the virus, such as by sharing needles with someone who has it.

Donor blood is already screened for it.

It is a silent disease, meaning people often have no symptoms until much later.

Untreated, it can cause serious and potentially life-threatening liver damage.

NHS England says that since 2015, more than 100,000 people have been diagnosed and treated for hepatitis C, meaning the country is already meeting that target.

Another goal - a 65% reduction in hepatitis C-related mortality compared with 2015 levels - has yet to be met, but might be before the 2030 target date.

Around 50,200 adults are living with hepatitis C, figures for England in 2024 suggest.

Estimates indicate 84.6% of those living with hepatitis C have been diagnosed - just short of the 90% target.

The Hepatitis C Trust says England is "on the cusp" of one of the most significant public health achievements in our country's history.

Prof Frankie Swords, NHS national medical director, added: "England is now leading the world in the mission to eliminate this disease and on course to beat the WHO's 2030 target, but we are determined to keep up the momentum and finish the job.

"We are committed to finding and treating everyone who needs support and would urge those at greater risk to come forward by ordering a free and confidential home-testing kit online."

Adults born in Ukraine, Romania, Estonia, Latvia, Poland, Albania, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Czechia or Slovakia are particularly urged to test, as some may have been infected through medical or dental procedures before 1991.

People can order a free, confidential NHS home self-testing kit, external without needing to speak to a GP.

News.title: 'I started in my 20s and made £8,000': Why women are often better investors than men
News.content:
It can be "largely attributed to culture", according to Gillian Fleming, co-founder and managing director of UK-based Mint Ventures, a women-led angel investment firm.

"Men historically have been more likely to make family investment decisions, and women have also historically not owned the balance of wealth, but that is changing now," she says.

"Also, money and wealth creation is not a topic that women often discuss, and we would like to change that."

Teleri says she has noticed a shift of late. "Investing is definitely something that women are talking about more, which is always a good thing," she says. "That's the case with my friendship group."

When women do invest in stocks and shares, analysis by Fidelity International found that over three years its female personal investing customers recorded cumulative returns of 50%, compared with 47% for men. The analysis does not identify the reason for the difference, but why may it be the case?

One possible clue to women's slightly higher long-term returns lies in how often they buy and sell their investments, with Barclays data showing that women trade around half as frequently as men.

News.title: Perseid meteor shower reaches peak: When and where to catch a glimpse
News.content:
The best annual meteor shower has once again returned to our skies, and the Perseids dazzling display is set to peak on Wednesday night.

But skywatchers will be treated to not one, but two, impressive astronomical events within just a few hours of each other.

A deep partial solar eclipse will be also visible in the UK in the early evening before the Sun sets and the stars emerge. While the two events are unrelated, their timing makes for an exceptional night of stargazing.

Astronomer Dr Becky Smethurst said it was "the perfect cosmic coincidence of events".

Here is when to look up and where you will have the best views of the meteor shower.

News.title: The lonely Chinese men being conned by fake brides
News.content:
At 37, Wang Zhuang had almost given up hope of finding a wife, until he saw the glossy matchmaking adverts.

They promised he wouldn't have to waste years on building a relationship that had no future. They offered to introduce him to a demure, devoted woman.

"The matchmakers said that girls from Guizhou are frugal," Wang says. "They told me they are good at running a household, able to do housework, and their families are very poor, so after marrying into your family, they would settle down and live a life with you."

So Wang travelled to Guiyang, a city in the southwestern province of Guizhou, in the hope of finding his soulmate.

He thought he had, when he was matched with a woman who seemed to tick every box. They had only met a few times before they married.

Then, almost as quickly as his new life had begun, it was over.

"My whole family has been thrown into chaos," he says, shaking his head.

He is still picking up the pieces more than a year after he discovered that everything he had been told by his wife was a lie.

She was a former karaoke hostess who'd been married three times, had three children, a serious sexually transmitted disease and was deeply in debt. She had even lied about her age.

He is fighting for a divorce and cannot return home to his old life - at least until he can recoup some of his life savings, which he says he paid to the agency within hours of being introduced to several potential matches.

"My parents blame me. I have insomnia and anxiety. I can't focus on work."

News.title: Watch: What we know about Tupac murder suspect Duane 'Keffe D' Davis
News.content:
The only suspect ever charged for the drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996 is Duane "Keffe D" Davis. The 63-year-old former gang boss is due to stand trial in Las Vegas, where he is accused of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang.

He has pleaded not guilty.

The BBC's journalist Anoushka Mutanda-Dougherty explains what we know about the suspect.

Read more about the case here.

News.title: GB's Hunt comes of age with European 100m gold
News.content:
Amy Hunt had her coming of age moment as she stormed to 100m glory to claim her first senior international title and deliver Britain's first gold medal of the European Athletics Championships.

Hunt announced herself on the sport's global stage last year with world 200m silver in Tokyo - the first individual international medal of her senior career.

Having backed that up with Commonwealth 100m silver two weeks ago, the 24-year-old would not be denied gold this time in Birmingham.

"I have had such a string of silvers and I was starting to get a bit fed up with it, so I thought it was time for gold," Hunt, who won in 11 seconds flat, told BBC Sport.

"My parents gifted me these gold earrings to finally level up, because I wear all-silver jewellery.

"They said it was time for gold - they left me that note two nights ago - so it made me quite emotional.

"It was definitely time for me to come of age here."

It was Britain's second medal on the opening day of action after the hosts took silver in the mixed 4x400m relay.

Yemi Mary John held off Dutch athlete Myrte van der Schoot on the home straight to bring a British quartet also featuring Ben Jefferies, Charlotte Henrich and Toby Harries home in three minutes 10.47 seconds, behind winners Norway (3:09.62).

News.title: Treasury contributed to woman's death, inquest hears
News.content:
The death of a Treasury worker who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers was "materially contributed" to by her employers, an inquest has heard.

Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.

Surrey Coroner's Court heard the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy which would have made clear that if the allegations were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.

A spokesperson for the Treasury said it was "considering the findings carefully".

In a statement to the press, Moffat's family said they believed the Treasury failed in its duty of care.

"When she needed support, reassurance and fair treatment, she was left frightened, isolated and convinced her career and reputation had been destroyed," they added.

The inquest, in which a conclusion of suicide was recorded, heard that on 19 May Moffat went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.

She was told of allegations she had shared sensitive personal information about colleagues, obtained as part of her job.

Moffat, from London, denied this.

News.title: Cocaine worth £232m found in banana shipment
News.content:
Cocaine with a street value of Â£232m was discovered hidden in a large shipment of bananas from South America.

The 2.9-tonne (2,900kg) haul was smuggled into London Gateway Port in Thurrock, Essex, on Thursday.

The drugs were removed from the container and then delivered to an address near Buntingford, Hertfordshire, where Border Force officers swooped in.

They arrested nine men allegedly connected to the bust, who were later released on bail.

Border Force had been tipped off about the illegal consignment by the National Crime Agency.

News.title: No evidence of data breach after Chinese-made component found in Navy drones, MoD says
News.content:
The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said there is no evidence to suggest a systems or data breach after the Royal Navy's new sea drones were found to include a Chinese-made component.

During what the MoD called a "routine cyber vulnerability assessment" of the drones, the cameras were found to have sent a squark â also known as a heartbeat communication â to a Chinese IP address.

A squark can signal when the system is switched on, is functioning properly, but it can also carry location information.

"A thorough investigation found no evidence of MoD data or systems being accessed, compromised or transmitted externally," an MoD spokesperson said.

"Our assurance and testing processes are designed to identify and address potential vulnerabilities early, and we continue to undertake routine security activity across our systems and equipment," the MoD added.

This is embarrassing for the MoD which, like most Nato countries, has banned Chinese components from military equipment - not least over fears of spying.

The K3 Scout sea drones can remotely carry out surveillance, and according to their supplier, "support a wide range of mission profiles including maritime awareness, force protection, logistics and precision strike".

The supplier of the Royal Navy's 20 new K3 sea drones, Kraken, said it was given assurances about security. But a third party supplier of the drone camera still had Chinese-made components.

Kraken has said it is confident no sensitive information has been shared.

The story was first reported by The Telegraph., external

The security lapse has been addressed, but it is a reminder of the heavy dominance on Chinese supply chains.

Even the defence sector â which has taken measures to prevent espionage â still struggles to source materials, and technologies that are China free, or as cheap.

News.title: Vandals target playground before it has even opened
News.content:
A play area that cost more than Â£178,000 was vandalised days before it was due to open.

Knowsley Council leader Graham Morgan said he was "absolutely furious" that every piece of play equipment at the Finch Woods play park in Halewood, Knowsley had been spray painted with graffiti over the weekend.

Trees and safety surfacing were also damaged and rubbish was left strewn across the site, with the cost of the damage estimated to run into thousands of pounds.

Morgan condemned the "mindless vandalism", saying "it is the cost to the community that sickens me the most".

News.title: Antiques stolen in 16th Century manor house raid
News.content:
More than 20 antiques were stolen from a National Trust (NT) property during a break-in last month, it has been revealed.

The silver, pewter and brass items were taken from the 16th Century manor house at Baddesley Clinton in Warwickshire, on 30 July.

The most notable piece of the 25 taken was a Georgian silver salver engraved with the coat of arms of the Ferrers, the family who resided at the house for about five centuries, the NT said.

"We very much hope the objects will be returned, so they can be enjoyed by everyone," a spokesperson added.

News.title: MSP apologises for hurt caused by rape 'demonisation' comments
News.content:
A newly-elected MSP has apologised for the hurt caused by comments in which they talked of the "demonisation" of rape.

Scottish Green Party politician Q Manivannan has also faced criticism for suggesting rape is a "spectrum of things" during a podcast recorded before they were elected to the Scottish Parliament.

Earlier, the Scottish Rape Crisis Alliance (SRCA) - which represents four rape crisis centres - said there is "no hierarchy of rape" and warned the MSP not to minimise sexual violence.

In a statement, Manivannan said clips from the podcast had been "selectively edited" but said they were "sorry" for the upset, and insisted they would never seek to diminish a rape survivor's experience.

The comments, which were made during The Subjective Space podcast , externalrecorded last year, sparked fury after they re-emerged online at the weekend.

News.title: Owner of 250-year-old Grade II-listed windmill gave it colourful makeover without permission
News.content:
Dr Eiddwen Jones, 85, is the great-great-great-great-great-granddaughter of Thomas Jones, who she said was the first miller at Llynon mill in 1776.

He managed the property in the village of Llanddeusant, Anglesey, until he died in his nineties.

She said the windmill should be repainted in whitewash as it is a historical building, and traditionally "that's how the mills were".

The author, whose family moved from Anglesey to Flintshire 150 years ago, said she did not agree that the windmill was painted in the first place to celebrate the Eisteddfod.

She has visited the windmill several times throughout her life where Thomas Jones' name is painted inside, and said he "would have turned in his grave, I believe," if he had known about its new appearance.

Jones added that it looked "very impressive in its original colour" when driving towards it.

"It's been made fun of now rather than kept the fact that it was a historical building and that people have been working there for a couple of centuries," she said.

Holt said the mill can be hard to find for visitors, as it is not close to the A55 road.

But the new colours have sparked a lot of interest.

With winters especially proving difficult with fewer people coming, he added: "I have a duty to ensure the future of the mill for the next generation."

He apologised to the local authority, saying he "realises that they [the council] are only doing their job and I know that I have broken the rules".

But he added: "I'm struggling and the winter is hard, but painting the mill has attracted more visitors here and helped me pay the bills."

He is gathering the opinions of visitors to the mill this summer to make a case to the council.

Donald Trump’s executive order altering the federal guidance for childhood vaccines has been blasted as “dangerous” by the American Academy of Pediatrics and criticized by a Republican senator.

Trump’s called Monday’s order a “ historic step in our mission to make America healthy again” as he signed it in the Oval Office, while making unfounded claims about the non-existent link between vaccines and autism.

“My administration is recognizing gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases,” said Trump, who added that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine that has been used since 1971 would once again be broken up into three separate vaccines despite the lack of any such separate vaccines on the current market.

Despite Trump’s order, it is the states, not the federal government, that have the authority to require vaccinations for schoolchildren.

Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said that Trump’s announcement spread fear and confusion in an area where “there doesn’t need to be any of that.”

“Science about vaccines and their efficacy has not changed,” he said. “The distribution of viruses and other pathogens in our environment has not changed. Children in this country have not changed in the last 48 hours.”

Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said that Trump’s announcement spread fear and confusion ( Getty )

Sen. Bill Cassidy, the Republican chair of the Senate health committee who lost his reelection bid after Trump backed his opponent, also slammed the executive order in a social media post, saying vaccines are safe and do not cause autism.

“I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes,” he posted.

“Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism. Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe. Parents should listen to their child’s pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong.”

Trump also announced that vaccines for Covid-19, influenza and hepatitis B would no longer be recommended, despite warnings from health experts that not vaccinating against the liver disease could give rise to an epidemic of liver cancer in unvaccinated children infected with the virus.

“Parents can still choose to give their children all of the vaccinations if they wish. It's up to the parents. We're making recommendations that are strong, but it's up to the parents if they wish, and they will be covered by insurance,” he said.

Kush Desai, a Trump spokesperson, told The Associated Press that the president is “one of countless parents who have voiced questions and concerns about the combined MMR vaccine” and said the plan to develop single-disease vaccines would “give parents more options on timing and frequency for their children,” ultimately increasing vaccine uptake.

The Independent has reached out to the Department of Health and Human Services for comment.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

A record 51,000 migrants were arrested in July by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

To fulfill President Donald Trump’s massive deportation agenda, officers within the Department of Homeland Security have been pushed to reach high arrest quotas, with some reports stating as high as 3,000 per day.

A senior DHS official confirmed to The Independent that ICE made roughly 51,000 arrests in July, stating that the numbers beat June's record 43,000 arrests.

ICE was making an average of 1,645 daily arrests last month, multiple federal sources told Fox News, which first reported July’s record-breaking numbers.

open image in gallery U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has hit a new record with some 51,000 migrant arrests in July ( AFP via Getty Images )

“Every day, DHS is delivering on President Trump’s mandate from the American people to deport illegal aliens from our country,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement Friday.

“Just last week, ICE deported murderers, drug traffickers, and burglars. With deportations up, crime has gone down across the country. We will not stop deporting illegal aliens until we have made America safe again,” Mullin said.

But less than a third of migrants in detention as of early July have a criminal conviction, according to statistics reviewed by the nonprofit news site Stateline. The Independent has not verified the data.

open image in gallery Federal agents have targeted airports and used traffic stops to carry out President Trump’s massive deportation agenda ( AFP via Getty Images )

Federal agents are specifically targeting people with expired visas at airports and using traffic stops, a couple of which have turned deadly, to carry out Trump’s immigration crackdown.

An average of 20 to 40 migrants were arrested daily at airports in July, DHS told Stateline.

Federal agents have been making more arrests near gates and ticket counters at airports in San Francisco, Miami and Kansas City, Missouri, The Wall Street Journal reported last week.

The Trump administration received fierce pushback last month after ICE agents fatally shot a 52-year-old Mexican man, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, in Houston and a 25-year-old Colombian native, Joan Sebastian Guerrero, in Maine at traffic stops in less than a week.

DHS said an ICE officer fired his weapon at Guerrero because he feared for “public safety,” and Salgado Araujo was shot in “self-defense.”

open image in gallery The Trump administration received fierce pushback last month after ICE agents fatally shot two men at traffic stops in less than a week ( AFP via Getty Images )

Mullin ordered a pause in traffic stops after the deadly shooting, The Atlantic reported at the time. But Trump quickly reversed course.

“The men and women of ICE are doing a GREAT job, one that has to be done,” the president wrote on Truth Social in mid July. “We must be strong, tough, and smart, and we CANNOT give up one of I.C.E.’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools, THE TRAFFIC STOP!”

“Once we do, we are playing right into the criminal’s hands. The Radical Left Dumocrats would like to see this done, but it won’t happen on my watch,” he said.

ICE’s record-breaking arrest numbers this summer follow a slowdown in the weeks and months after the two fatal shootings of 37-year-old U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, according to the federal sources who spoke to Fox News.

A wave of protests followed the shootings, which the Trump administration claimed were in self-defense. The president’s border czar Tom Homan announced in February that hundreds of federal agents would be pulled from Minnesota amid public outcry.

Fox News’ sources said the record-breaking arrests are due to thousands of newly hired ICE agents and billions of dollars in new funding.
