‘’Poor remuneration: The salary of Nigerian Armed Forces personnel is too low, considering the current economic realities and inflation.

‘’Welfare: For instance, we are an army at war; our handling of casualties is paramount to how the rest working will be willing to continue and lay their lives for the country. There is also a need for robust welfare packages for all the members of the Armed Forces. There is also a need for serving personnel’s family welfare packages to be introduced. The COAS Loan Programme should be expanded and sustained.

‘’The AF NHIS package needs to be reviewed to include more critical health challenges rather than just malaria and typhoid. There is a need for a sustainable housing programme for the armed forces rather than isolated and disjointed packages.

‘’The issue of the Obasanjo car loan scheme needs to come back. I think the AFN needs a whole department dedicated to personnel welfare. I could elaborate on this if given the opportunity.

‘’Godfatherism: A system where you can hardly get anything without someone calling in on your behalf. There are officers who have been eight, nine years straight on operations. While we still have some officers who haven’t been to the North-East and will never be there.

‘’Pension upgrade: Col Adamu told me that his pension cannot buy his BP drugs. I feel sad when I saw CDS ordering ex-servicemen to be dispersed from their protest ground for improved pensions. We should remember that we shall all retire. Our ex-servicemen deserve better treatment. Charity begins at home; that is why I am starting from the armed forces.

‘’Removal of fuel subsidy: The government should have phased the removal and not the sudden removal, and the policy is anti-human. The primary purpose of government, as provided by the Constitution, is the welfare and security of the people… we have rather created more stealing avenues because governors now have more funds to steal.

‘’An average Nigerian is not asking for too much, just a bare minimum of being able to move from point A to B and also afford three square meals, good health, and the education of their children. The federal government should invest the subsidy money in a practical project that can reduce human suffering. The issue of Urban Mass Transit that started during the military regime should be revisited.

‘’Corruption: This must be given clear and serious attention because it is the mother of all crimes. Our education is in shambles. Those of us here in Abuja, how much do we pay for school fees, and how many officers/soldiers can afford school fees with their salaries?

‘’Budget padding: After padding a budget and awarding costs, they’re still not implemented. For example, you put one thousand naira for a water of 100 naira and still do not buy the water.

‘’These are people who got almost everything free, including education when growing up, but there is no free education anywhere today in Nigeria. They all turned their backs against the country. As a service personnel, how much of salary can you save that would buy you a house to live in ?

‘’Is it after using all your youthful years that you will start looking for money to survive after retirement?

‘’Some officers have served for over 15 years, and even a plot of land they don’t have. The policy of car loans was swept under the carpet. What happened to all these policies? An average officer or soldier is barely surviving, despite the huge sacrifices they are making on a daily basis to keep the country safe and secured. He concluded by asking for an opportunity to meet with the relevant authorities, apologise and commit themselves to pursuing lawful and peaceful means of addressing grievances.

World.title: Troops ambush Lakurawa terrorists in Kebbi, recover items
World.content:
Some recovered items

By Haruna Aliyu, Birnin Kebbi

Troops of Sector 2 Operation FANSAN YAMMA deployed for counter terrorism and anti-banditry operations in Kebbi State have said that they ambushed Lakurawa Terrorist Group (LTG) on transit to wreak havoc in Dandi Local Government Area of Kebbi State.

According to the Acting Director of Army Public Relations, Lieutenant Colonel Olayinka Osoba, the troops, acting on credible intelligence on the movement of Lakurawa terrorists who were on transit, swiftly mobilised and laid a tactical ambush for the terrorists.

The troops intercepted the terrorists at a known crossing point near Uguwan Hassan village.

He added that after making some contacts, the troops engaged the terrorists with superior firepower overwhelmed by the troops’ tactical response, the militants were forced to abandon their mission and retreat in disarray.

Osoba explained that during the encounter, troops recovered some items utilised by the terrorists for logistics and communication, including two motorcycles, mobile phones, T&T communication radios and one Nigerien ID Card belonging to one of the fleeing terrorists from Tilbiri Region of Niger Republic.

“The troops are currently dominating the general area with aggressive patrols and are in active pursuit of the fleeing terrorists to ensure the continued safety and security of the local populace,” he added.

The recent ambush is the latest in a series of counter terrorism gains of the military as they intensify crackdown on armed groups to liberate the northwest.

World.title: 14.5m children registered as Nigeria pushes for legal identity for every child
World.content:
… 6,000 wards now offer digital birth registration — NPC

… FG links birth registration with health, identity systems

By Chioma Obinna

As Nigeria joined other African countries to mark the 2026 Africa Civil Registration and Vital Statistics, CRVS, over 14.5 million Nigerian children have been registered under the country’s intensified birth registration drive even as the Federal Government moves to ensure that every child born in the country has a legal identity.



The National Population Commission, NPC, disclosed that digital birth registration services are now available in more than 6,000 of the country’s 8,809 wards, with registration increasingly linked to health facilities and community outreach programmes.



The 2026 commemoration, which marks the beginning of the new CRVS decade, 2026–2036, is focused on consolidating gains made under the African Programme on Accelerated Improvement of Civil Registration and Vital Statistics, APAI-CRVS, through integration, decentralisation and digitalisation.



The NPC Chairman, Dr Aminu Yusuf, said the commission’s priority was to ensure that no child was excluded from legal recognition because of where he or she was born.



He said: “Every registered birth strengthens the foundation for child protection and national development.



“Our priority is to ensure that every child, regardless of where they are born, is counted, protected and recognised before the law.”



Birth registration, stakeholders said, remains the first formal recognition of a child by the state and provides proof of identity required to access essential services, including healthcare, education and social protection.



It also provides governments with vital demographic data for planning and delivery of public services.

Nigeria’s CRVS system is being strengthened through collaboration among the NPC, National Identity Management Commission, NIMC, Association of Local Governments of Nigeria, ALGON, development partners and communities.



In states including Bayelsa, Gombe, Jigawa, Taraba, Kebbi, Niger and Zamfara, birth registration is increasingly being integrated with health facilities and community-based services to enable parents to register children closer to the point of birth.



Speaking, the Director-General of NIMC, Engr. Abisoye Coker-Odusote, said digital integration would make identity management more seamless from birth to adulthood.



According to Coker-Odusote, “integrated digital identity systems create a seamless pathway for individuals from birth through adulthood, while improving access to services and strengthening governance.”



UNICEF Representative in Nigeria, Wafaa Saeed Abdelatef, said birth registration should not be viewed merely as the issuance of a certificate but as a gateway to a child’s rights.



She said: “Birth registration is far more than a certificate. It is a gateway to protection, services, and opportunity.”



Abdelatef said UNICEF would continue to support the Nigerian government and other partners to strengthen integrated, decentralised and digitalised registration systems.



“As Africa enters a new decade of CRVS systems strengthening, Nigeria remains committed to expanding access to birth registration, improving vital statistics, and ensuring that every child has a legal identity from birth,” she added.



Also, ALGON National President, Hon. Bello Lawal, stressed the importance of decentralising registration services, particularly for children in rural and underserved communities.



He said: “Decentralisation is essential to ensuring that children in remote and underserved communities are not left behind.



“Bringing services closer to families increases access and encourages timely registration.”



Chairman of the House Committee on the National Population Commission, Hon. Okunjimi John Odimayo, said sustained political commitment was critical to building an effective CRVS system.



He noted that strong civil registration and vital statistics systems would support better planning, improved service delivery and stronger development outcomes.



Stakeholders also warned that millions of children across Africa remain without legal identity.



Current estimates indicate that only about half of children under five in sub-Saharan Africa are registered at birth, leaving the region with the largest share of unregistered children globally.

World.title: Nottingham Forest owner sues Crystal Palace over gun banner
World.content:
Marinakis

Nottingham Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis is suing Crystal Palace over a banner unfurled by the London club’s fans depicting him holding a gun to midfielder Morgan Gibbs-White’s head, according to reports on Monday.

Marinakis’ legal team lodged the defamation claim against Palace and “persons unknown” at the High Court in London on Monday, nearly a year on from the banner being displayed during the 1-1 Premier League clash between the two clubs at Selhurst Park.

Alongside the image, the banner read: “Mr Marinakis is not involved in blackmail, match-fixing, drug trafficking or corruption.”

The Greek shipping and media magnate has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to such allegations.

In November 2025, the Football Association charged Palace with failing to ensure that supporters did not behave in an improper, offensive, abusive or provocative way and later fined the club £50,000 ($67,000).

The game on August 24 last year took place amid heightened tensions after Forest had taken Palace’s place in the Europa League after the south London club were relegated to the Conference League for breaking UEFA’s multi-club ownership rules.

Marinakis, a 59-year-old Greek businessman, also owns Olympiacos in Greece and Rio Ave in Portugal.

AFP

World.title: The Judicial Facade: When The Grant Of Bail Becomes Its Own Denial
World.content:
Uche Diala

right of reply

A Reply to “The Advocate” of 4 August 2026

Onikepo Braithwaite’s column on the alleged illegal interception of the National Security Adviser’s telephone, and the bail conditions imposed on Malam Nasir El-Rufai, reads as measured legal commentary. Read against the law she herself cites, however, the author tragically fails herself. Ms. Braithwaite acknowledges every principle that should have led her to a different conclusion – that the alleged wiretapping offence is bailable, that bail conditions must not be excessive, that conditions amounting in substance to a refusal of bail are unlawful – and then declines to apply those principles to the facts in front of her. That is the central defect of the piece, and it is a profoundly tragic one.

An Admission That Was Never Established

Ms. Braithwaite’s argument stands on a single premise: that Mallam El-Rufai, in an Arise TV interview, admitted to the offence of wiretapping Mr. Ribadu’s phone. She writes that the unlawful interception occurred “by Malam El Rufai’s own admission,” and later concludes that whether he tapped the line “himself or through others, the law describes such a person as a principal offender.” That is a considerable distance to travel from an unquoted television remark. Nothing in the column tells the reader what El-Rufai actually said. The relevant portion of the Arise News interview is available on YouTube:

At roughly the 11:30–11:46 mark, El-Rufai’s own words were that someone had tapped Ribadu’s phone and reported to him that the NSA had ordered his detention. That is a claim about being surveilled, not a confession of surveilling. A public commentator may opt to read this differently, and a court is entitled to test it, but a commentator cannot simply supply the missing admission by assertion, and then build a felony, a national security escalation, and a justification for onerous bail conditions on top of it.

This matters because Nigerian law does recognise extra-judicial confessions in Sections 28 and 29 of the Evidence Act 2011, but the recognition of that category does not resolve the harder question at issue here. Whether a particular statement is a confession is not a label a reader attaches by impression. It is a question of construction, settled by examining the words actually used, their context, and whether they admit the specific elements of the offence charged, before any question of voluntariness or admissibility even arises. An ambiguous statement does not become a confession because a commentator characterises it as one. The Evidence Act supplies the framework for testing a statement’s evidential status; it does not authorise editorial substitution for that process. Tellingly, when the prosecution itself sought to rely on the same video in the wiretapping trial, two of its witnesses were unable, on cross-examination, to sustain the “admission” facade, which is to say that the construction Ms. Braithwaite offers as settled fact could not survive the very evidential scrutiny the law requires of it. If the state’s own witnesses could not make that leap under oath, a newspaper column cannot make it by inference.

Two Bail Regimes, Not One

A second problem is one of accuracy rather than advocacy. Ms. Braithwaite’s column actually describes two separate and materially different bail regimes, and the distinction matters more than her conclusion allows. In the wiretapping matter before the Federal High Court, Abuja, brought on the DSS’s petition, bail was fixed at N100 million with a single surety who must, among other things: hold Grade Level 17 or above in the federal civil service; reside in Maitama or Asokoro; deposit the original Certificate of Occupancy of landed property; produce three months of salary evidence authenticated by a bank manager; swear an affidavit of means; obtain a verification letter from his own department; and produce a tax clearance certificate. El-Rufai himself must produce a surety in the Kaduna State Traditional Council; surrender his international passport; and report to the DSS on a monthly basis. Ms. Braithwaite calls this set of conditions “reasonable enough.”

In the separate corruption matter before the Federal High Court in Kaduna, bail was fixed at N200 million with two sureties in landed property, and here too one of them must be attested by the Kaduna State Traditional Council, a body Ms. Braithwaite herself concedes operates under a State Government “not favourably disposed” to the defendant. Here, to her credit, she does not defend the condition; she calls it difficult and asks half-heartedly, without resolving it, whether it ought to be varied.

Conflating these two regimes, as casual commentary tends to do, obscures rather than clarifies, but it also obscures the single most telling fact in the whole affair: the Traditional Council attestation is not confined to the Kaduna matter. It appears, in near-identical form, in the DSS case before the Federal High Court in Abuja as well. Two different courts, in two different jurisdictions, hearing two different cases, have independently arrived at the same unusual and narrowly defeating condition, one that happens to route the defendant’s liberty through an institution controlled by a state government hostile to him.

That is not the kind of coincidence bail jurisprudence normally produces. Either the condition reflects a genuine, ordinary practice this reply has failed to locate elsewhere in Nigerian bail orders, or its recurrence across two courts points to collusion between two judges taking common instructions, or, at the very least, joined in a common cause to deny liberty to the accused. Ms. Braithwaite’s column, remarkably, treats the condition as a feature of the Kaduna case alone and never asks why it resurfaces in Abuja. That omission is itself worth noting. The Kaduna condition is the more indefensible one precisely because Ms. Braithwaite’s own facts alluded to it: a bail term cannot depend on the discretion of an institution controlled by a government adverse to the accused, because that converts a judicial safeguard into a political veto. Its repetition in a second, unrelated case only sharpens the point. That is not a close question, and the column’s decision to leave it as one is its clearest failure of nerve.

The FCT Conditions Fail the Test Braithwaite Herself Sets

The wiretapping case conditions deserve no easier a pass. Ms. Braithwaite is right that Grade Level 17 is a legitimate civil-service rank, that a recognisance is not a cash deposit, and that a surety need not own property specifically in Maitama or Asokoro. Taken singly, each condition can be defended. But Section 165(1) of the Administration of Criminal Justice Act 2015, which Ms. Braithwaite herself cites, asks a cumulative question: are the conditions, taken together, excessive? In Uduesegbe v FRN (2014) LPELR-23191(CA), the Court of Appeal treated exactly this kind of stacking as decisive, reducing a bond that on paper was merely large into one that in substance the court found unworkable, and holding that trial courts must be liberal, not exacting, in non-capital matters.

Here, a surety must simultaneously satisfy a civil-service grade level held by a small fraction of federal officers, a residence requirement confined to two of Abuja’s most exclusive districts, a landed-property deposit, bank-attested salary evidence, a sworn affidavit of means, departmental verification, current tax clearance, and attestation by a traditional institution in another state entirely, for an offence under Section 12 of the Cybercrimes Act carrying a maximum sentence of of two years. It is the accumulation, not any single term, that narrows the pool of willing and qualified sureties toward vanishing point. That is precisely the “excessive” that Section 165(1) prohibits, and Ms. Braithwaite’s column never runs its own cited authority against its own recited facts.

A Statutory Correction

One further point needs correcting, because precision matters in a debate about statutory bail rights. Section 162 of the ACJA governs offences punishable by more than three years’ imprisonment; it is Section 163 that governs the residual class of non-capital offences, including this one, where the offence carries a maximum of two years. The distinction is not academic. Section 163 leaves bail to the court’s discretion “unless there is a reason to the contrary,” but that discretion still sits inside the wider constraint that whatever conditions are set must not be excessive. Getting the section right does not weaken the underlying point; if anything, it sharpens it, because a discretionary provision offers no independent justification for excessive and exceptional conditions in a comparatively minor offence.

The Traditional Council Problem Deserves a Conclusion, Not a Question

The most serious defect in the Kaduna conditions is one Ms. Braithwaite states and then declines to resolve. If a certifying authority is institutionally controlled by a government hostile to the accused, asking “should the conditions be varied?” is not really a question, it is an answer in itself. A bail term whose satisfaction depends on the goodwill of the defendant’s political adversary is not a neutral administrative hurdle; it is a mechanism for indefinite detention while the order on its face still reads as a grant of bail. Nigerian appellate courts have already been here: in the Sambo Dasuki litigation, the Court of Appeal struck down a requirement that a civil servant serves as surety, precisely because status-linked surety conditions function as a bar to bail rather than a facilitation of it. The same logic applies with more force to a certifying body controlled by an adverse state government.

National Security Is a Charge to Be Proved, Not a Tone to Be Borrowed

Ms. Braithwaite is entitled to note that intercepting an NSA’s line is graver than an ordinary interception, given the office involved. But the gravity of an office is not evidence of harm. The column moves from the identity of the alleged victim to language evoking the Official Secrets Act and national security exposure, without identifying what classified information, if any, was obtained, disclosed, or compromised.

The trick works only by collapsing five distinct questions into one. The identity and status of the alleged victim is one question; it tells us who was affected, nothing more. The seriousness of unauthorised interception as a category of conduct is a second, separate question, answered by the legislature when it fixed the penalty under Section 12 of the Cybercrimes Act at two years. Whether national security information was, in fact, compromised, whether anything classified was obtained, used, or disclosed, is a third question, and an entirely evidential one: it requires proof of a fact, not an inference by a columnist. The statutory elements of the offence actually charged are a fourth question, fixed by the charge sheet, not by how alarming the surrounding facts can be made to sound. And whether any of the preceding four questions bears on pre-trial liberty is a fifth and final question, governed not by rhetoric but by Section 165(1) of the ACJA and the constitutional presumption of innocence.

Ms. Braithwaite’s column answers the first question and treats it as though it answers all five. It does not. The Official Secrets Act carries penalties of up to fourteen years precisely because it targets proven compromise of classified material, an offence with its own elements, its own burden of proof, and, notably, one with which El-Rufai has not been charged. Borrowing its gravity for an uncharged offence, to justify conditions imposed under a different statute entirely, is not legal reasoning; it is atmosphere doing the work that evidence is supposed to do. The offence charged under the Cybercrimes Act is the interception itself; escalating the register without escalating the evidence lets a two-year offence borrow the moral weight of a fourteen-year one, and a defendant should not be tried, even in the court of public opinion, on the vocabulary attached to the charge rather than the charge itself.

What Bail Is For

Ms. Braithwaite is correct that a grant of bail is not a verdict of innocence, and no serious commentator disputes that. But the proposition runs both ways: the absence of a finding of innocence does not license conditions designed, in their cumulative effect, to make liberty theoretical and unattainable. The presumption of innocence is not suspended because a defendant gave a controversial television interview, and it does not narrow according to how politically inconvenient the defendant happens to be. The test of bail is not whether each condition can be justified in isolation by a sympathetic reading. It is whether, taken together, an accused person granted bail can actually walk out of custody, or whether the order has become, as the Court of Appeal has put it in comparable cases, a refusal of bail wearing the language of a grant.

That is the question Ms. Braithwaite’s column raises and then leaves hanging. It is also the question this reply insists must be answered, and answered by the ordinary standards of the ACJA and the Constitution, for El-Rufai, and for any citizen who might one day find the state’s patience, and the vocabulary of national security, arrayed against them.

A court that grants bail with one hand and, with the other, assembles conditions calibrated to deny it has not exercised discretion. It has disguised a refusal as a grant. That is the judicial facade this title names, and it is worth stating without euphemism: bail obtained on paper but foreclosed in practice is not bail at all. It is detention that has simply changed its address, from the defendant’s cell to the surety’s impossible paperwork. The rule of law is not measured by the elegance of the order granting liberty; it is measured by whether the person the order names can actually walk free. Until that test is met, the case for El-Rufai’s continued confinement remains, on the law as it stands, unproven, and so, on its own terms, does Ms. Braithwaite’s sponsored diatribe.

•Dr. Uche Diala is a public affairs commentator and Director General of the El-Rufai Support Group Association, and writes from Abuja.

World.title: Building Institutional Firewalls: Why the 2026 GJF Democracy Dialogue Turns to Parties and the Judiciary
World.content:
By Wealth Dickson Ominabo





This week Tuesday August 11, 2026, the Goodluck Jonathan Foundation will assemble some of Africa’s most respected leaders and democratic stakeholders in Bauchi, Bauchi State, to chart the course for the continent’s democracy and governance. The Goodluck Jonathan Foundation Dialogue (GJF Dialogue), which enters its 5th edition this year, stands as a cornerstone of the Goodluck Jonathan Foundation’s programmes and a central expression of its vision for peace and prosperity on the continent.

The event will host President John Mahama of Ghana, former President Olusegun Obasanjo who is chairing the event, former President Goodluck Ebele Jonathan and Nigeria’s Vice President Kashim Shettima, with Governor Bala Mohammed hosting alongside constitutional experts and civil society voices drawn from across the continent.

This year’s theme is anchored on the big question that confronts Africa’s democratic and governance future: beyond elections, can political parties and the judiciary save African democracy?

It is worth asking, because the evidence of democratic recession is hard to miss and harder to explain away. East Africa has seen popular protests and rising resentment against governments. Southern Africa has watched public backlash grow against long-dominant liberation parties over economic stagnation. West Africa has gone further still, with several states falling to military rule after years of citizen frustration with civilian leaders and citizens wilfully ready to trade off their civic space for military doctorship on the promise of good governance. In countries where democracy exists, many citizens live in frustration and disenchantment. What links these regions is not geography. It is a widening gap between political promises and citizen lived realities and the fragility of state institutions to act as democratic safeguards and deliver accountability.

For decades, elections were treated as democracy’s proof of life. This assumption may not be tenable today. Elections have increasingly become a means for the capture of power rather than a genuine contest of ideas. Disputed results have repeatedly accounted for violence, deepened mistrust between citizens and the state, and acted as reverse gears in the very nation-building journeys they were meant to secure. This is the argument the Dialogue has spent five editions building toward, one question at a time.

The inaugural 2021 Dialogue, in Abuja, asked how democracy could hold a divided nation together at all. It was argued that post-colonial African states had remained detached from their citizens because inherited colonial institutions were never fundamentally transformed to serve them, an argument that hardened into the Foundation’s recurring case for African solutions to African problems.

The 2023 Yenagoa edition pushed further, exploring the democracy development nexus. The question then was whether democracy can survive at all if it fails to improve people’s lives. The conclusion was that democracy without development loses legitimacy, just as development without accountability tips into authoritarianism.

The 2024 Benin City edition turned to the human capital behind governance, arguing that Africa’s development crisis is, at root, a leadership recruitment crisis grounded in weak education systems. Last year, in Accra, under the theme “Why Democracies Die”, participants confronted the question directly. Their answer still stands as the clearest thesis the Dialogue has produced: democracies rarely die because elections stop happening. They die because institutions stop functioning.

Bauchi, home to Nigeria’s first prime minister, Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, carries that argument to its logical conclusion. This year’s keynote speaker, Professor Karuti Kanyinga, will narrow the Dialogue’s focus from the macro questions of unity, development and leadership that shaped earlier editions to the micro-dynamics of the two institutions that quietly decide whether democracy survives in the years between elections: political parties and the judiciary.

Political parties were never meant to be empty vehicles for winning power. At their best, they were the fulcrum of policy ideation, arguing out competing visions of society and putting them before citizens for judgement. They disciplined their own leaders, and where those leaders derailed, parties called them out and, on occasion, withdrew their mandate outright.

In the earliest wave of African democratisation, parties functioned almost as civic movements in their own right, mobilising citizens toward national freedom against colonial and dictatorial rule, a legacy still visible in movements like the African National Congress in South Africa and the independence-era coalitions of Kenya and Tanzania.

The judiciary carried a parallel weight. It stood as the conscience of society and the last line of defence when politics failed, the one institution expected to hold when every other check gave way.

Both have drifted from that role, and the drift has not been subtle. Many parties today are hollowed out, captured by narrow interests, existing almost purely to contest and hold power rather than to formulate policy or recruit competent leaders. Judiciaries across the continent face mounting political pressure, and public confidence in the courts is eroding nearly as fast as public confidence in the ballot box itself. Neither failure happened overnight, and neither will be reversed by another round of elections, however free or fair.

This is the question Bauchi puts squarely to the continent’s leaders: can these two institutions be rebuilt to do the work democracy requires, protecting the rule of law, equality, transparency and accountability, at a moment when citizens are no longer certain democracy can deliver any of it?

A major highlight of this year’s event is the Fireside Chat, bringing former heads of state and senior jurists who have managed the pressures of executive office into an open exchange with young leaders, scholars, and civic advocates. Rather than rehearsing set-piece speeches, these leaders will offer the candid, practical insights that rarely survive into official communiqués.

This is what distinguishes the GJF Democracy Dialogue from the usual governance talk shows. It does not settle for electoral commentary or another repetitive diagnosis of Africa’s ills. By placing those who have led African states, managed sub-regional crises, and protected constitutional orders in the same room as serving leaders and citizens, the summit elevates conversation into consensus-building and knowledge production. It centres citizen agency and focuses on the quiet periods between elections when democracy lives or dies. Africa’s democratic renewal will not be imported; it has to be forged internally. This is what the GJF Dialogues is doing: argument by argument and edition by edition, in rooms like the one about to open in Bauchi.

•Ominabo is the Communications Officer of the Goodluck Jonathan Foundation.

World.title: Inside inDrive’s Chief Wahala Officer Campaign and the Human Face of Reliability, Problem-solving
World.content:
In Lagos, “wahala” is part of everyday life, especially for commuters navigating traffic, delays and cancellations. inDrive turned this shared experience into its Chief Wahala Officer campaign, using humour and cultural relevance to humanise its brand while highlighting its commitment to reliability and problem-solving. Chiemelie Ezeobi writes

When inDrive advertised for a Chief Wahala Officer (CWO) earlier this year, the vacancy looked genuine enough to make many Nigerians pause. The role came with an unusual qualification: at least five years of surviving the realities of Lagos. Applicants needed composure under pressure, a strong understanding of “Lagos wahala” and the ability to navigate the unpredictability of everyday movement across the city.

It was not a conventional recruitment exercise. It was a marketing campaign. Yet, that was precisely why it succeeded. Rather than introducing another promotional slogan about affordability or convenience, the global ride-hailing and delivery platform built an entire campaign around an experience nearly every Lagos resident understands.

It acknowledged that daily transportation comes with delays, cancellations, traffic, surge pricing and countless unexpected obstacles. More importantly, it positioned the brand as a partner willing to confront those realities rather than pretend they do not exist.

The result was one of the more culturally grounded marketing campaigns seen in Nigeria’s mobility sector in recent times.

Turning Everyday Frustration into Brand Conversation

The campaign was built around a simple but powerful insight: Wahala is part of everyday Lagos life. Instead of avoiding conversations about customer frustrations, inDrive leaned directly into them.

The fictional Chief Wahala Officer became the human face of reliability, accountability, and problem-solving, representing a brand that understands the daily challenges commuters and delivery users face.

Whether it is a driver cancelling at the last minute, gridlocked traffic, delayed deliveries, urgent requests or fluctuating prices, the campaign acknowledged what customers already know. Rather than selling perfection, it offered reassurance that there is always a way through the chaos.

This honesty immediately differentiated the campaign from conventional advertising, where brands often focus exclusively on ideal experiences while ignoring the frustrations customers encounter.

A Marketing Strategy Rooted in Culture

Marketing campaigns succeed when they reflect the audience’s lived reality. The Chief Wahala Officer campaign did exactly that. “Wahala” is more than a Nigerian Pidgin word for trouble; it captures the shared experience of navigating uncertainty with resilience and humour. Every Lagosian has a personal wahala story. By adopting that language, inDrive avoided sounding like a foreign tech company trying to force relevance. Instead, it spoke in a voice that felt familiar, local and authentic. The campaign transformed an everyday expression into a strategic communications tool, allowing customers to immediately recognise themselves in the message. That cultural relevance made the campaign memorable long before any discussion of product features began.

Engagement Beyond Advertising

Perhaps the campaign’s biggest strength was its ability to turn audiences into participants rather than passive viewers. The vacancy announcement generated buzz across LinkedIn, Instagram and other social platforms. More than 450 Nigerians applied for the fictional executive role, sharing their own experiences and interpretations of Lagos wahala. In doing so, inDrive achieved something many brands struggle to accomplish. It generated organic conversations without relying solely on paid advertising. Every application, comment, repost and video became additional campaign content, extending its reach while reinforcing the central message. The recruitment process itself became entertainment; customer engagement and market research rolled into one.

The KieKie Factor

The campaign reached another level when actress and content creator Oluwabukunmi Adeaga-Ilori, popularly known as KieKie, was unveiled as the Chief Wahala Officer. The appointment made strategic sense beyond celebrity influence. KieKie’s public personality embodies humour, confidence and composure in chaotic situations, qualities that naturally aligned with the fictional role. Rather than simply endorsing the brand, she became the living representation of its promise to help users navigate everyday transportation challenges.

According to inDrive Nigeria’s Country Manager, Oladimeji Timothy, KieKie was selected because she represents ‘authenticity, humour and relatability’. The choice reinforced the campaign’s central message that understanding customers requires personalities people genuinely connect with.

Connecting Storytelling to Product Value

Many campaigns generate attention but fail to connect that attention to the product itself. The Chief Wahala Officer campaign avoided that trap. Every form of Wahala referenced throughout the campaign corresponded with an existing inDrive feature. Traffic congestion highlighted route flexibility. Ride cancellations drew attention to driver selection. Delivery delays are connected with courier options and tracking. Price uncertainty reflected the platform’s negotiated pricing model.

Ratings, real-time tracking, delivery support, and transparent user feedback all reinforced the campaign’s promise of giving customers greater control over their mobility experience. The storytelling, therefore, remained firmly connected to practical product benefits rather than existing purely as entertainment.

Why Acknowledging Challenges Matters

One of the campaign’s most significant lessons is that recognising customer frustration can itself strengthen brand loyalty. Too often, companies communicate only success while avoiding conversations about service challenges. Customers, however, already know those challenges exist.

By openly admitting that mobility in Lagos comes with unavoidable frustrations, inDrive established credibility before presenting its solutions. That approach made the campaign feel less like advertising and more like empathy. Customers are more likely to trust brands that acknowledge reality than those that promise flawless experiences.

The Chief Wahala Officer worked because the character never pretended that wahala would disappear. Instead, the campaign promised that customers would not have to face it alone.

Lessons for Modern Brand Communication

The Chief Wahala Officer campaign demonstrates that effective marketing is no longer about making the loudest claims. It is about creating the strongest connection. It showed that humour, local language and cultural understanding remain powerful communication tools when backed by genuine product value. The campaign also illustrated the importance of creating multiple engagement moments, from the initial job vacancy to the application process and finally the appointment of KieKie. One creative concept generated several newsworthy milestones across traditional and digital media. For communications professionals, the campaign offers a useful reminder that authentic storytelling often begins by listening to customers before speaking to them.

Ultimately, inDrive’s wager was straightforward. Rather than promising Lagosians a perfect mobility experience, it acknowledged the city’s everyday realities and offered something more believable: a platform that understands the challenges, speaks the language of its users, and strives to provide solutions whenever wahala appears.

In a crowded ride-hailing market where many brands promote similar features, that simple act of recognition may well have become the campaign’s greatest competitive advantage.

World.title: Security Forces Arrest Enugu Kidnap Suspects, Victims Released
World.content:
*Ransom, 4 AK-47 rifles, ammunition recovered

*Gov Mbah: You can’t get away with your crimes in Enugu

Security forces in Enugu State have successfully apprehended three perpetrators of the August 2, 2026 attack on St. Joseph’s Catholic Church, Inoyi-Affa, Udi LGA, Enugu State, and also recovered ransoms during the operations.

This was even as one of the kidnap suspects was neutralised in a gun duel during the joint operation of the Department of State Services (DSS), the Army, Police, Enugu State Forest Guard, and others, which also saw to the recovery of four AK-47 rifles, seven magazines and 133 rounds of ammunition from the hideouts of the kidnapping syndicate.

Fielding questions from newsmen during the parade of the criminals at the state headquarters of the DSS in Enugu Monday evening, Governor Peter Mbah, who was represented by the Secretary to the State Government, Prof. Chidiebere Onyia, added that the remaining two of the three victims of the August 2 attack, Seminarian Lawrence Igbo and Mr. Emmanuel Onwudi, had also regained their freedom.

Mbah also revealed that ransom deployed as a strategy was fully recovered, noting that security agents tracked down the criminals by deploying the state’s hi-tech security assets.

He hailed the DSS, Army, Police, Forest Guards and other security agencies in the state, adding that the victims had equally identified the apprehended criminals as their abductors.

The governor assured the people that his administration would continue to prioritise and invest in the security of their lives and properties.

“There was one fatality in this process. It was one of the criminals that died in the process of apprehending them. Usually, criminal elements will not want to be apprehended easily without a fight, but our people were ready, and we have one fatality, while the others are here now as you could see; and they will face the full wrath of the law.

“We made it very clear that if criminality becomes your venture, Enugu State is not the location to do that business; that we will pursue you, we will make sure we bring you to justice, and that was why we put the robust security architecture across the state, working in collaboration with the security forces to ensure that Enugu is uncomfortable for anybody that plans criminality, and you’re seeing that very clearly.

“We are intentional in investing in and organising our security architecture to prevent crime. But if there is a breach, you can run, but cannot hide for long. We must get you. You can’t commit these crimes in Enugu State and get away with it. No way,” he said.

He also warned locals who collude with the criminal elements or serve as their informants, vowing to come after them also.

“We will find you also, just as we have found these people, and we will prosecute you as part of this evil operation and this evil syndicate.

“Wherever you are, know that investigation is ongoing and that this government will track you down, and you will pay for your crimes in planning havoc on our citizens. So wherever you are, we are still coming for you,” he stressed.

He paid special tributes to the security forces for their cooperation and gallantry.

“We also want to very highly commend all the security agencies: the DSS, Nigerian Army, the Nigerian Police, the Enugu State Forest Guard, the military services, others for being very instrumental in some of the work that was done, and continue to do in Enugu State,” he concluded.

World.title: Why I’m Qualified to Govern Osun, ADC’s Najeem Salaam Speaks
World.content:
The Osun State governorship candidate of the African Democratic Congress, Najeem Salaam, has said his experience, exposure and development strategy qualify him to govern the state, promising to grow its economy and reduce its dependence on federal allocations.

Salaam stated this while appearing on Channels Television’s Politics Today, where he outlined some of his plans for the state if elected governor.

The former Speaker of the Osun State House of Assembly said his administration would focus on attracting investors, increasing the state’s internally generated revenue and using the additional resources to address critical sectors, including electricity and agriculture.

“I have a clear objective of what I will do. I will ensure investors come and we generate more money. For electricity, we will ensure that we give them 24/7 electricity. The economy and IGR will turn around,” he said.

On agriculture, Salaam said Osun had the potential to generate enough revenue to invest in the sector without continually relying on allocations from the Federal Government.

“For agriculture, we can generate money to improve it without waiting for federal allocation. I can fill in these gaps,” he said.

The ADC candidate said his strategy would be to make the state more financially independent by developing its own revenue-generating capacity and reducing its reliance on Abuja.

“So, the strategy is not depending on the Federal Government before we do things on our own,” Salaam added.

Salaam also spoke about his association with former Osun State Governor, Rauf Aregbesola, dismissing perceptions that he was merely operating as Aregbesola’s political representative.

“I am not Aregbesola’s man. Just because I know that people are myopic in their thinking, people think I do not know my worth,” he said.

The former lawmaker stressed that his political career predated his association with Aregbesola, noting that he had risen through the grassroots, local government and the Osun State House of Assembly, where he served as Speaker.

“I can stand on my own, and I have been here since grassroots — local government, House of Assembly, Speaker. I am not a dullard,” Salaam said.

He added that while he was proud of his association with Aregbesola, he remained an independent politician with his own agenda and vision for Osun State.

“I am proud to be with him and I am not regretting it. With my level of exposure, I have a clear objective of what I want to do with my ten-point agenda,” he said.

World.title: DSS Releases, Compensates Artisan Cleared of Links With Terrorists
World.content:
The Department of State Services (DSS) has released a Katsina-born carpenter, Mustapha Marwana, after investigations cleared him of allegations linking him to terrorist activities.

The release was ordered by the Director-General of the DSS, Oluwatosin Adeola Ajayi, following a thorough review of Marwana’s case by an investigation panel constituted by the agency.

According to a security source, the investigation established that Marwana was not a member of any terrorist organisation and had no operational links with the Ansaru terrorist group.

Marwana was arrested in connection with the abduction and killing of school pupils and teachers in Oriire Local Government Area of Oyo State.

He was subsequently subjected to detailed investigation to determine the extent, if any, of his involvement in the activities under investigation.

The source said the investigation found no evidence linking the carpenter to the membership, financing, logistics or operational activities of the terrorist group.

The DSS, according to the source, not only ordered Marwana’s immediate release but also compensated him for the period he spent in custody after being

cleared of the allegations.

“Following the review, investigators found no evidence linking the carpenter to membership, financing, logistics or operational activities of the terrorist group

“Consequently, the DSS DG ordered his immediate release and approved the payment of initial N3 million as compensation to assist him in meeting his immediate needs and restarting livelihood.

“Mustapha was subsequently released to his lawyer, Oghene Forgive, who received him following his discharge from custody,” stated the source.

Continuing, the source said Mustapha expressed appreciation to the DG for what he described as a compassionate and humane intervention.

“He prayed for Allah’s guidance and protection of the DSS leadership, stating that the gesture has given him an opportunity to rebuild his life,” the source stated.

Oghene Forgive, who received Mustapha upon his release also thanked the DG for his generosity and dedication to establishing Mustapha’s innocence.

The source added that the compensation was part of measures being adopted by the current DSS leadership to support persons cleared after investigations and facilitate their reintegration into society.

The source recalled the N20 million compensation the DSS DG handed a Sokoto-based businessman who was accidentally shot and injured in 2016, during a pre-dawn raid in Jos due to mistaken identity.

He also recalled the case of an Abuja-based businesswoman Chineze Ozoadibe the DG ordered her released and paid N10 million as compensation in October 2025 after reviewing her case.

According to the source, “since his appointment as DSS DG, Mr. Tosin Ajayi has been balancing national security responsibilities with respect for the rights and dignity of citizens, resulting in the payment of over N300 million as compensation.

“There are many more instances where DSS investigations have established innocence and have been followed by efforts to facilitate reintegration. These are the kind of measures through which the Service is strengthening public confidence and building trust,” the source said.

World.title: Efunkoya U-15 Table Tennis Tournament Opens with Two-day Clinic
World.content:
The Adegboyega Efunkoya Sports Foundation has announced the commencement of the 7th edition of the National U-15 Table Tennis Championships, beginning with a two-day clinic at the indoor hall of the National Stadium from August 11 to 12. The main tournament will follow from August 13 to 15, where new champions are expected to emerge.

Hundreds of young athletes will participate in the clinic, designed to sharpen their strokes, footwork, and tactical approaches while instilling discipline and innovation. The programme includes physical conditioning and modern training techniques, preparing players for the rigors of competition and offering them a platform to impress national selectors.

Chairman of the Foundation and former national team coach, Babatunde Obisanya, emphasized the importance of the clinic: “We are overwhelmed by the support we’ve received from stakeholders worldwide—former players in the diaspora, administrators, and enthusiasts who believe in our vision. Our mission is to continue the legacy of Dr. Adegboyega Efunkoya, ensuring that players combine sports with education. Each year we introduce new innovations, and this year will be no different. Beyond competition, we remain committed to supporting the education of players who excel.”

Since its inception, the championship has produced outstanding talents for Nigeria’s national teams. Notably, Matthew Kuti, discovered at the maiden edition, is now a key member of the senior squad and Africa’s reigning U-19 champion. Other alumni include Khadijat Musa and the Ayoola siblings—Umar, Usman, and Kabirat—who currently represent Nigeria at junior level.

The Adegboyega Efunkoya Sports Foundation remains dedicated to immortalizing Dr. Adegboyega Efunkoya, former chairman of the Nigerian Table Tennis Federation, whose vision transformed the sport in Nigeria. The Foundation continues to promote table tennis among junior players in primary and secondary schools, with the long-term goal of positioning Nigeria among the world’s top ten table tennis nations.

World.title: UEFA, CONCACAF, ASIA Confederations Accuse Infantino of Breaking Trust ‘Through Deception’
World.content:
FIFA and its President Gianni Infantino have been accused of breaking trust “through deception” in an open letter issued by UEFA, CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation.

The letter, signed by the presidents and general secretaries of the three regional governing bodies, said recent controversy over the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal was fundamentally about “the integrity of the game, and the integrity of those elected to lead it”.

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all FIFA competitions, including the World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

It was aborted after widespread criticism from several confederations, led by UEFA which has threatened a boycott of all FIFA competitions.

BBC Sport understands that there have been preliminary discussions between the three confederations over breakaway competitions – should Infantino remain in situ. However, substantive talks are yet to begin, according to others.

“When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned,” the letter read.

It added: “Leadership in football is not a possession. It is not about holding – or demanding – power to be held. It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it.”

While the statement did not name Infantino, sources have told BBC Sport that it should be seen as an opportunity for him to resign and leave his position with dignity.

It comes after FIFA issued a statement on Saturday evening which strongly criticised a “concerted and ongoing effort” to “undermine” the organisation and Infantino.

The three confederations – representing Europe, North America, Central America and the Caribbean, and Asia – criticised a statement released by FIFA after Infantino called management board members to a meeting in Rabat, Morocco last Wednesday.

The confederations cited Infantino shutting out FIFA Council Members and member associations from the meeting, instead summoning only FIFA-employed senior staff.

The open letter added that FIFA’s admission of mistakes made in the FFE process did not go far enough.

“It did not acknowledge that the proposal itself was inherently wrong,” the letter stated. “There remains no recognition that attempting to sell an interest in the FIFA World Cup was a profound failure of judgment.

“Not just a procedural misstep, but a fundamental breach of trust with the very institutions FIFA exists to serve.”

FIFA has committed to presenting a report to the next meeting of the FIFA Council, which is expected to take place in October.

But the three confederations said this failed to “recognise that proper governance in the face of such a profound lack of judgement would require that such a review be conducted by a fully independent third party”.

Their letter added: “There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness.”

It also underlined a legal warning made by UEFA that FIFA should not delete or destroy any documents related to the abandoned plans.

UEFA last week insisted that FIFA’s defence of Infantino “changes nothing” about a potential boycott of competitions.

The three confederations have considered possible breakaway competitions, but they have provided no detail on what they could look like or when they would begin.

Infantino still retains the support of South America, Africa, and indeed Mexico within CONCACAF. But is that enough? If UEFA and CONCACAF voted as a bloc (with a few exceptions) against him, it would only need around a third of the AFC to join them to win any vote.

World.title: Smiling Cameron Waldeck-Cooks speaks in resurfaced clip [video]
World.content:
Cameron Waldeck-Cooks is seen in an old clip about her student exchange experience in the US. Images via screenshot

An old clip of Cameron Waldeck-Cooks talking about an experience on a student exchange programme has resurfaced after her death, which has made headlines around the country. The St Stithians College learner is believed to have died in a murder-suicide involving her boyfriend, Ethan Coetzee, a former matriculant.

The teen couple’s bodies were discovered in a lodge near the Sabie game reserve in Mpumalanga a week ago.

CAMERON WALDECK-COOKS SEEN IN OLD CLIP

In a clip that has resurfaced on social media, Cameron Waldeck-Cooks is seen chatting about her experience on a student exchange programme to the US last year.



The blonde student spent time at the Holy Innocents’ Episcopal School in Atlanta.

In a video clip, an overjoyed Cameron stated that she felt “safe and welcomed” as an exchange student.

She shared that her favourite part of the trip was driving with her new friends, given that the legal driving age in the US is 16. She also enjoyed watching football matches and socialising with her peers.

“It feels like I’m in the movies”, she said.

Sadly, 17-year-old Cameron did not get to experience driving in South Africa.

In the comments section, South Africans expressed their sadness that Cameron’s life was “cut short”, particularly as she had a “bright future”. 

GONE TOO SOON

Both Cameron Waldeck-Cooks and Ethan Coetzee’s lives were tragically cut short in the double tragedy,

Cameron, a St. Stithians Girls College Grade 11 student, was working towards the Gold level of The President’s Award for Youth Empowerment, which is part of the Duke of Edinburgh’s International Award.

At the time of her death, her family said she had completed a five-day hiking expedition she hoped would help her achieve her goal.

She was also in the rowing and netball clubs and was described as a “natural leader” and a “big sister”.

Meanwhile, Ethan – who matriculated in 2025 – had been part of the first team rugby club, was a national champion in the equestrian sport of Eventing, and was a respected senior student at Penryn House.

WORKING WITH AUTHORITIES

Meanwhile, The President’s Award for Youth Empowerment has pledged to work with authorities in their investigation into Cameron Waldeck-Cooks’s death.

It shared in a statement on Monday, 10 August: “We are aware that the circumstances surrounding Cameron’s death are being investigated by the relevant authorities. The President’s Award will provide whatever assistance is appropriately required.

“The safety and well-being of every young person who participates in The President’s Award is of paramount importance to us.

World.title: ‘Faced a brutal battle’: Danny K’s wife praised over strength, bravery
World.content:
Lisa Koppel, the wife of Danny Koppel, fondly known as R&B singer Danny K, has been praised for her brave fight against an illness that took her life over the weekend.

The 41-year-old model-turned-lawyer, whose father is well-known mega-attorney Billy Gundelfinger, leaves behind her spouse and their three children.

DANNY K’S WIFE REMEMBERED FOR BRAVE FIGHT

In an emotional Instagram post, Lisa Koppel’s sister Justine Gundelfinger paid tribute to her sibling.



Justine – an actress – revealed that Lisa had passed on Women’s Day – on Sunday, 9 August. Lisa was remembered as a successful supermodel, lawyer and businesswoman.

She shared: “My magical Princess Angel Lillie [her nickname] had the purest and kindest heart. She was stunning, delicate, gentle and soft like a petal. Yet carried within her a strength beyond measure and the remarkable ability to endure even the greatest of storms. Her selfless, down-to-earth, gentle nature, witty sense of humour, brilliant mind, and unconditional love and devotion to her husband, Danny [K], their children, our family and her friends made her truly extraordinary.

Danny K and his wife Lisa Koppel.

Images via Facebook.

Images via Instagram

“She was very hardworking, caring, generous, altruistic and remarkably modest. She was utterly devoted to those she loved and had the incredible gift of making everyone around her feel valued and cared for. Her magnificent children, Jayden, Kyle and Chloe and her husband were the centre of her universe. The boundless love, strength, kindness, patience, and good values she gave them will live within them forever and remain among the greatest expressions of her legacy.



Justine revealed that Lisa Koppel had died after a brave battle with an illness.

She continued: “When Lisa faced the most brutal battle imaginable, she fought with such fortitude, powerful determination, extraordinary courage and phenomenal heroism. She was truly the bravest and strongest woman I have ever known. Her resilience was beyond comprehension. I will forever be in awe of the strength with which she faced even the greatest adversity.

“There is something deeply poignant about honouring Lisa on Women’s Day because to me, she embodied everything extraordinary about being a woman. We mourn her, but we also celebrate her beautiful life, her humour, her generous spirit, her incredible style, grace and elegance, her devotion to her family, and the immense love she gave so freely. 

“You are, and always will be, the woman I aspire to be. I love you beyond infinity”

SINGER’S BEST FRIEND AND SOULMATE

Danny K married Lisa Koppel (née Gundelfinger), whom he has described as his “best friend” and “soulmate,” in 2012 at the Lourensford Wine Estate in Somerset West, Western Cape.



The couple started dating in 2010, shortly after his engagement to ex, Lee-Ann Liebenberg, ended.

Coincidentally, Lee-Ann dated and is now married to businessman Nicky van der Walt, who dated Lisa around the same time as her own relationship with the singer.

Danny K told the Sunday Times in 2020: “It wasn’t an orchestrated swap. It is simply convenient because we both landed up with the people we were meant to be with.”



He continued: “When I look at my kids, and my life, I couldn’t imagine it any other way.”

South African singer Danny K is mourning the death of his wife, Lisa Koppel, with the family asking for privacy following her passing. Image: ChatGPT

South African singer Danny K is mourning the death of his wife, Lisa Koppel, with the family asking for privacy following her passing.

The news was confirmed on Monday by Danny K’s mother, Pam Koppel.

She indicated that the family would not be issuing a formal public statement and that the circumstances surrounding Lisa’s death would remain private.



RIP | Four school learners died this week – South Africa mourns

Deeply saddened by the passing of Lisa Gundelfinger, wife of Danny K.



Our heartfelt thoughts and condolences go out to Danny, their children, and the entire Gundelfinger and Koppel families during this incredibly difficult time.



May Lisa’s memory be a blessing, and may her… pic.twitter.com/fQp88isDuL — Yusuf Abramjee (@Abramjee) August 10, 2026

A life beyond the spotlight

Lisa, the daughter of prominent divorce attorney Billy Gundelfinger, began her career as a model before moving into the legal profession.

She was admitted as an advocate of the High Court in 2010 and went on to build a career in law.

Lisa and Danny K married in 2012 and shared three children.

While Danny K has enjoyed a long and successful career in the South African music industry, Lisa largely maintained a lower public profile, balancing her professional career with family life.



Family tragedy

Lisa’s death is another devastating loss for the Koppel family.

Danny K has previously spoken about the profound impact of losing his brother, Jarren, who died in a helicopter crash in 2003.

Danny K, a multiple South African Music Award winner, has remained one of South Africa’s best-known entertainers since rising to prominence in the early 2000s.

Poem

His father, Gavin Koppel, also appeared to reflect on grief in a poem titled My Promise, which he on Sunday, 9 August.

In the emotional poem, he wrote about turning pain into compassion and vowed: “I will use my pain to heal from this day forward.”

Although Gavin did not explicitly refer to Lisa or confirm her death, the post appeared as news of the family’s loss emerged.

Tributes and messages of condolence have since begun circulating as friends, colleagues and members of the public remember Lisa.

The family has asked for privacy as they mourn her death and support her three children through the difficult period.

World.title: Where pensioners can get private healthcare for free
World.content:
Getting healthcare is either an expensive process or a whole-day event.

Pensioners have a choice between sitting in long queues at a government clinic or paying R650 for a checkup at a local doctor.

That isn’t the case at one private healthcare provider, where pensioners can book an appointment for free.



Free Private Health Care

Clicks launched its Helping Hand Trust in 2011 in partnership with the Western Cape Department of Health (WCDH).

At the time, the initiative was intended to offer baby education, healthcare advice, and basic clinic services to young mothers.

Since then, it has spread nationwide. The service has also expanded.



Now, select Clicks pharmacies offer free basic clinic services on Wednesdays.

To qualify for the free service, pensioners must not have medical aid.

If they do, they will be charged through their medical aid.



Typically, the cost for this service ranges from R120 to R350 depending on the reason for the visit.

On Wednesdays, pensioners can visit a Clicks with a clinic and get a basic checkup for heart health or diabetes.

During these health screenings, the Clicks nurse will check cholesterol levels, measure blood pressure, conduct a glucose test, and offer healthcare advice.



Other free services offered by the retailer include HIV testing and counselling.

Select Clicks’ clinics also offer pap smears, breast exams, and non-invasive prostate screening, but these come at an additional cost.

Booking a Free Clinic Appointment

If your local Clicks has a clinic, you can wait in the queue from 08:00 to 17:00 on Wednesdays.



However, to skip the queue, you can book an appointment online by visiting the Clicks website.

When booking an appointment, you need to select the services with “Helping Hand” in the title.

It’s possible to make an appointment for up to four people. Confirmation will be sent via sms and email.



Pensioners can also book their Helping Hand appointment by dialling the retailer’s customer service line.

Affordable Private Healthcare for Pensioners

Pensioners who want affordable private healthcare through their medical aid can also use Clicks.

The retailer offers premium clinic services between Monday and Friday.



In addition to the heart health and diabetes screening, Clicks offers:

Flu vaccinations

Pneumonia vaccination

Vitamin injections

They also have a nurse-assisted virtual doctor consultation.

During these sessions, the doctor guides the consultation, and the nurse will assist.



Dischem offers similar services.

Dischem nurses provide basic clinic services, but they can also lead a virtual doctor appointment.

These consultations are roughly 45% cheaper than an in-person consultation at a local doctor.

World.title: 'Policemen are on the payroll of the gangsters' - Reiger Park community leader
World.content:
BOKSBURG - Reiger Park EMS Chaplain Eddy Walkerley has accused some police officers of colluding with gangs in the area.

Four people were killed in a shooting on Friday night in Reiger Park, East of Johannesburg.

Two Anti-Gang Unit officers are among those dead.

Walkerley claimed some officers are on gangsters' payroll and are protecting criminals.

"We know the gangsters, we know names. But there are people that know where they stay, there's people that know their faces.

“The people are living in fear, because should you go to the police, the local police, you will be the next target, no matter what.

“Our police are working with a lot of the gangsters. A lot of the policemen are on the payroll of the gangsters, and I'm not afraid to say it. I will say it and I'll even say it in their faces.

“I said it on Friday evening, whilst on the crime scene, I mentioned it, and I'm going to say it again, our police must get out of the pockets of gangsters."

World.title: UK radio broke rules in announcing king's death: watchdog
World.content:
LONDON - A community radio station breached the rules after accidentally announcing the death of King Charles III in a May broadcast, a UK watchdog said on Monday.

Radio Caroline, a former pirate radio that now mostly plays rock music, apologised in May after airing messages falsely announcing the monarch's death.

One of the messages had said "we have suspended our normal programmes until further notice as a mark of respect following the passing of His Majesty King Charles III".

The national anthem was then played, followed by around 16 minutes of silence before the regular programme resumed.

The presenter apologised 30 minutes after the messages were initially triggered, Ofcom said.

The regulator, which received two complaints about the broadcast, said the "very significant inaccuracy" and the "considerable length of time" taken to acknowledge the error breached two of its rules.

One requires news reports to be accurate and impartial.

The other requires significant mistakes to be acknowledged and corrected on air promptly.

Radio Caroline told Ofcom the error occurred when a member of staff accessed sound files pre-recorded in the event of the monarch's death while carrying out maintenance on the studio computer, as the programme was being streamed remotely.

The staff member played the files "out of curiosity", which stopped the stream from the presenter's remote location and broadcast the files on air.

The person then reportedly "panicked and left the premises" after realising what had happened, according to the Ofcom statement.

Radio Caroline said the remote presenter "would not realise that they had gone 'off air' unless they were monitoring their output via an internet monitor."

The presenter, believing they were still on air, was not actively monitoring their phone and did not immediately respond to calls from people at the station who had noticed the error, the report said.

The station said the person who played the files had been "reprimanded" and had "apologised".

It added the pre-recorded files had now been removed from the studio computer.

World.title: Reiger Park Shooting | Person of interest taken in for questioning
World.content:
BOKSBURG – An alleged gang member has been taken in for questioning in connection with the multiple murders that took place in Reiger Park on Friday.

Two police officers part of the Anti-Gang Unit were responding to the shooting of two civilians when they were ambushed.

Acting Police Minister Firoz told fellow officers, family members and the community at large that the state would deploy all the necessary resources needed to bring the culprits to book.

On Monday morning, two R5 rifles linked to the killings were recovered near Germiston.

In a media briefing held with Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi, Cachalia said a person of interest had been taken in.

“One person has been tken in for questioning. But he is not the only person of interest. These murders were not committed by one person,” he said.

He said the person of interest is a known gang member who is currently out on bail and facing six other charges.

Lesufi said “at least now we know who we are looking for.”

At the weekend, authorities visited the families of the slain officers. The funerals of the officers will be held on Saturday and Sunday, respectively.

Cachalia said he has not visited the families of the two civilians because investigations are still ongoing.

World.title: New German transport chief gets taste of train chaos
World.content:
BERLIN - Germany's new transport minister experienced firsthand Monday the problems plaguing the country's rail network, being forced to change train carriages during a trip after the air conditioning broke down.

Steffen Bilger was named to the post in a cabinet shuffle last month after his predecessor was sacked by Chancellor Friedrich Merz for insufficient progress on overhauling Germany's dilapidated infrastructure.

A key part of his role is turning around state-owned operator Deutsche Bahn and the rail network, which has faced mounting complaints in recent years due to dismal punctuality, breakdowns and poor service.

On a two-day trip, Bilger plans to gather information in northern Germany on train safety and station cleanliness.

But at the start of the journey, he had to change carriages in a train taking him from Berlin to Hamburg after the air conditioning stopped working, a transport ministry spokesman told AFP.

The breakdown, which came as Germany bakes in soaring summer temperatures, led to the carriage being closed off and forced passengers to find seats elsewhere on the train.

At the weekend, Bilger reportedly announced that bonus payments for Deutsche Bahn managers would be tied to targets set by the government, including on punctuality.

World.title: Bezos consortium nears deal to buy Liverpool stake: report
World.content:
LONDON - Amazon founder Jeff Bezos is part of a consortium nearing a deal to buy a one-third stake in Premier League club Liverpool, a report said Monday.

Sky News said Bezos was part of an investor group led by Amit Bhatia, the son-in-law of India steel billionaire Lakshmi Mittal, that also also includes Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin.

Liverpool owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG) confirmed the approach from Bhatia's group last month.

"An investment consortium led, managed, and represented by Amit Bhatia has expressed interest in making a strategic minority investment in Liverpool Football Club," an FSG spokesman told AFP.

Bhatia was until recently a shareholder in Championship club Queens Park Rangers.

The Sky report said the consortium was "closing in on a deal to buy a roughly one-third stake in Liverpool", with FSG preparing to make an announcement "as soon as this week".

Bezos, 62, is one of the world's richest men, with a fortune estimated by Forbes magazine at more than $280 billion, while Saverin's wealth is put at $33 billion.

Bezos has reportedly explored previous bids for the NFL's Seattle Seahawks and Washington Commanders, but decided against pursuing either deal.

Sky said the investment in Liverpool, part of an influx of American money into the Premier League, would reportedly value the 20-time English league champions at $6 billion.

FSG, which also owns the Boston Red Sox baseball team, bought Liverpool in 2010 for £300 million ($405 million).

It sold a minority stake in the club in 2023 to US private equity group Dynasty Equity.

Liverpool won the Premier League title in 2024/25 under Arne Slot but the Dutchman was sacked in May after a turbulent season.

World.title: MEC Maile calls on communities to help protect Gauteng schools
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Gauteng Education MEC Lebogang Maile has said protecting schools is a shared responsibility.

Maile briefed the media on plans to curb issues affecting Gauteng schools.

He said issues around bullying, gender-based violence and gangsterism have been of great concern.

The department has embarked on a campaign called - it takes a village to raise a child.

“Violence, gangsterism, bullying, substance abuse, gender-based violence, vandalism and criminal activity around schools were repeatedly raised. The program of action strengthened Safe Schools intervention and cooperation with SAPs, community policing forums, NGOs and communities.

“Work is also being driven on anti-bullying interventions and misconduct measures while school safety matters are being assigned to the responsible education support and curriculum functions.

“The purpose is to move from responding only after incidents occur to prevention, early intervention, clear escalation and coordinated action around high-risk schools. Communities themselves remain essential to the solution. Protecting a school cannot be left entirely to government.

“The communities must help identify criminal activity, protect public infrastructure, support learner discipline and refuse to normalize drug dealing, vandalism and violence around schools."

World.title: Wamboka: Kalonzo, Gachagua and Matiang'i should back Sifuna
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kabuchai Mp Majimbo kalasinga and his counterpart Jack Wamboka during a press briefing on Monday. [Juliet Omelo, Standard]

The political battle for the 2027 presidency has intensified, with leaders allied to the Linda Mwananchi movement urging opposition figures Kalonzo Musyoka, Rigathi Gachagua and Fred Matiang’i to abandon their presidential ambitions and back Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna.

Bumula MP Jack Wamboka made the call after a three-day political tour of Western Kenya by the Linda mwananchi brigade, saying the region had demonstrated growing grassroots support for Sifuna.

Wamboka said the tour was a major success, with close to 22 rallies held in three days. He added that the crowds reflected growing enthusiasm for Sifuna, particularly among young people, women, political aspirants and ordinary voters.

“We respect you, Kalonzo, Gachagua and Matiang’i. We know you have what it takes but in 2027, we ask you to stand with Sifuna,” Wamboka said.

He said the reception in Western Kenya showed that Sifuna’s campaign was gaining national attention.

The first time MP said Sifuna had focused on issues affecting Western Kenya, particularly the collapse of industries and the struggling sugar sector. He pointed to Mumias and Nzoia sugar factories, saying their decline had left farmers and workers suffering.

Wamboka accused National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula of failing to deliver development promises made to Bungoma residents citing unfinished roads and the stalled Bungoma stadium, saying several projects lacked adequate funding despite repeated commitments to voters during the campaigns.

He also questioned Wetang’ula’s political record, citing past controversies and accusing the Speaker of failing to live up to his promises adding that voters should judge leaders by what they deliver, not by speeches alone.

Kabuchai MP Majimbo Kalasinga said the tour had proved that Sifuna’s bid was gaining grassroots support.

“Edwin Sifuna is going for president, nothing else,” he said.

He said supporters contributed small amounts to the campaign, arguing that the movement was being funded by ordinary Kenyans rather than wealthy political backers. He said crowds turned up voluntarily.

Kalasinga also announced that Linda Mwananchi would hold a rally in Homa Bay on August 16 despite local warnings. He said Sifuna had a right to campaign anywhere in Kenya.

He called for peaceful competition and warned against attempts to block the rally or restrict political activity in the region emphasising that Kenya is for everyone, constitutionally, peacefully and equally.

They two vowed to fight for the Linda Mwananchi name.

The Wamboka-Kalasinga push adds momentum to Sifuna’s campaign and pressures opposition leaders to unite before the 2027 election.

World.title: High Court orders striking nurses back to work
World.content:
