Audio By Vocalize

Uasin Gishu County nurses strike over delayed payments and unfulfilled Collective Bargaining Agreement [Wycliff Kipsang, Standard]

Nurses across the 47 counties have been ordered to report back to work immediately or face legal action from the counties.

Justice Monica Mbaru of the Employment and Labour Court in Mombasa issued orders temporarily stopping the nationwide nurse strike that commenced on July 29, 2026, and ordered the Kenya National Union of Nurses and Midwives (KNUNM) to direct its members back to work.

Justice Mbaru said on Wednesday that any nurse absent from work without proper and lawful cause shall face disciplinary action.

This is after Mombasa County Government and its Public Service Board successfully enjoined the 46 county governments to make the order national.

“In the interim, the KNUNM (respondent) is hereby restrained from undertaking any industrial action relating to the strike notices dated July 21 and July 29 and shall direct all its members to resume duty forthwith and unconditionally to allow the court to address the claim herein on a priority basis,” said Justice Mbaru.

The judge ordered all county labour officers in the 47 counties to record attendance of nurses who report to work and compile a report in court on September 22, 2026.

“Any member of the KNUNM who will be noted by the County Labour Officer as absent from duty without lawful cause shall allow the counties to issue necessary notice to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken,” said Justice Mbaru.

In their petition certified urgent, Mombasa County claimed that the nurses strike has crippled services in public hospitals across all the 47 counties, thereby placing patients facing emergency and inpatient care at risk.

In Mombasa County, the nurses strike paralysed medical services at all medical facilities, including Coast General Hospital, Port Reitz Hospital, Likoni District Hospital and Shimo La Tewa GK Prison Hospital.

Mombasa County, through its Counsel Murtaza Tajbhai, said that the strike had turned from a labour disagreement to a matter of immense public interest.

Tajbhai said that the nurses’ union proceeded with the said strike despite the Mombasa Public Service Board inviting the KNUNM officials for talks to avert the said strike.

The union had raised concerns over the 2025-2029 Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA), implementation of the 2017 Return to Work Formula and pension terms for Universal Health Coverage staff care guidelines for nurses and the reinstatement of 46 nurses dismissed in Kisii County.

However, in their petition, Mombasa County said that the said grievances could not be addressed by each county individually.

Mombasa County Service Board Chief Executive Officer Fadhil Maamum told the court in his affidavit that most of the demands required consultation with national institutions like the Salaries and Remuneration Commission, while others cannot be implemented immediately given their significant financial implications.

He said that nurses under Mombasa County have no salary arrears and had met some of the union’s demands through negotiations.

Maamum said that while the nurses’ grievances can be resolved, the patients do not have the luxury of time.

“Nurses are designated essential service providers under the Labour Relations Act and the industrial action was unlawful because the statutory dispute resolution mechanism had not been exhausted," said Maamum.

He said the court's intervention will allow for negotiations and safeguard the constitutional right to healthcare.

However, the Union said that the strike was after failed action by the counties to meet their agreed grievances despite continued negotiations.

The nurses said they will not be reporting to work unless guided by the union.

World.title: Mukurweini MP John Kaguchia arraigned over alleged inciting remarks
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Mukurweini MP John Kaguchia arrives at the Milimani Law Courts in Nairobi on August 4, 2026. [Nancy Gitonga, Standard]

Mukurweini MP John Kaguchia was on Tuesday arraigned before the Milimani Law Courts over alleged inciting remarks made during a political rally in Kieni, Nyeri County.

Appearing before Senior Principal Magistrate Teresia Nyangena, Kaguchia was read the charge of offensive conduct by the court clerk but did not respond after his lawyers mounted a spirited constitutional challenge against the charges.

His legal team objected to the manner in which the charges had been framed, arguing they violated several constitutional safeguards and should not proceed.

The courtroom was packed to capacity as a battery of lawyers appeared for the legislator alongside political allies who turned up in solidarity.

Among those present were Nyeri Senator John Methu, Nyeri Woman Representative Jane Njeri Maina and several elected leaders who followed the proceedings from the public gallery.

The defence argued that the charge sheet failed to meet the constitutional threshold set under Article 50(2) which guarantees every accused person the right to be informed of the charge with sufficient detail to answer it.

The charge before you does not disclose an offence under the law and purely an attempt by the state to breach the freedom of expression and limiting the opposition.

Lead defence counsel Kiragu Wathuta and Ndegwa Njiru told the court that the MP's constitutional rights had been violated from the time of his arrest.

The lawyers narrated that on the night of August 2, Kaguchia had appeared on Inooro FM's Kiririmbi programme where public affairs were being discussed between 7 pm. and 9 pm.

According to the lawyer, after the programme ended, staff at the Royal Media Services station allegedly informed the MP that about 30 Subaru vehicles carrying hooded individuals had surrounded the premises looking for him.

"Because of the wave of abductions in this country, I advised him to remain within the Royal Media Services premises. At about 5 a.m., I found him having spent the night on the station's couches waiting for daylight," lawyer told the court.

He said that at around 9 a.m., a senior officer who identified himself as a regional DCI commander arrived with uniformed officers and informed the MP that he was under arrest despite there being no summons or warrant issued against him.

"When we inquired why no summons had been issued as is the normal procedure, the investigating officer told us they were acting on instructions from above," the lawuer submitted.

The lawyer further claimed officers initially indicated Kaguchia would be taken to Kilimani before driving him instead to DCI headquarters, where he said advocates were denied access to their client.

"They told us no counsel would be allowed into the DCI premises. Lawyers were locked out and denied an opportunity to consult with the accused," he said.

According to the defence, lawyers later moved to court and obtained orders from Kiambu High Court granting Kaguchia police bail of Sh100,000.

However, they alleged officers at Kamukunji Police Station refused to process the release despite the cash bail being available.

The lawyer told the court that the Officer Commanding Station allegedly declined to accept the money, saying he had received instructions that the legislator could not be released from the station and should instead deposit the cash bail at Central Police Station.

"The accused is not before this court because of any crime he committed. He is here to demonstrate to the country that it is now a crime to oppose the government," he argued.

Lawyer Wathuta also informed the court that Justice Gregory Mutai had on Tuesday morning in Milimani High Court Human Rights Petition No. E517 of 2026 granted the MP a bond of Sh500,000 and directed police to facilitate his access to legal counsel.

Lawyer Ndegwa Njiru argued that Kaguchia could not be required to plead before first receiving legal advice, citing Article 49(1)(c) of the Constitution, which guarantees every arrested person the right to communicate with and be represented by an advocate.

Njiru further challenged the jurisdiction of the Milimani court, arguing that the alleged offence was said to have occurred in Kieni, Nyeri County, and should therefore be prosecuted before a court with territorial jurisdiction over the alleged incident.

He also argued that the charge under Section 94(1) of the Penal Code was defective because it did not disclose who had allegedly been threatened, abused or insulted.

"The charge sheet merely refers to words allegedly uttered by the accused but fails to demonstrate that they were made in a public place or that they amounted to threatening, abusive or insulting words as required by law," Njiru submitted.

He also questioned the accuracy of the translated charge sheet, telling the court he understood Kikuyu and had noticed discrepancies between the original alleged utterances and the English translation.

Njiru argued that the translation distorted the alleged remarks, particularly the reference to the word "Kasongo", and maintained that the inconsistencies prejudiced the accused's ability to understand the charge.

He further submitted that the offence under Section 94 of the Penal Code is a misdemeanour punishable by a maximum sentence of six months imprisonment or a fine not exceeding Sh5,000.

Njiru argued that under Article 49(2) of the Constitution, Kaguchia ought not to have remained in custody for two nights over such an offence.

The defence also urged the court to order the release of the MP's Samsung A33 mobile phone, arguing that it had no connection to the alleged offence.

The hearing on the preliminary objections is still ongoing before Milimani Law Courts

World.title: Tension at Kamukunji Police Station as leaders demand Kaguchia's release
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Mukuruwe-ini MP John Kaguchia at Kamukunji Police Station in Nairobi on August 3, 2026. [Collins Oduor, Standard]

Tension is high at Kamukunji Police Station as opposition leaders led by Kipipiri MP Wanjiku Muhia and lawyers demand the immediate release of Mukurweini MP John Kaguchia, claiming police had failed to comply with a High Court order granting him police cash bail.

Kaguchia, who was arrested earlier on Monday over alleged electoral offences and incitement, remained in police custody hours after his lawyers said the court had ordered his release on Sh100,000 police bail.

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua in a post on his Facebook account said that the High Court had issued orders directing the Officer Commanding Station (OCS) at Kamukunji Police Station to release the legislator immediately upon payment of the bail.

Gachagua said that despite the court order having been served, the OCS had not acted and was instead awaiting instructions from his superiors. He warned the officer against disobeying a court order, saying that he could be held personally liable for contempt of court if the directive was ignored.

The former Deputy President further referenced the ongoing murder case involving the former OCS of Central Police Station, urging police officers to uphold the law and avoid carrying out unlawful instructions.

Several Members of Parliament from the Mt Kenya region have camped outside Kamukunji Police Station, insisting they would not leave until Kaguchia is released. The legislators accused police of delaying compliance with the court order and questioned why the MP was still being held despite the court's directive.

The lawmakers that claimed they had been redirected to Central Police Station while seeking information about Kaguchia's detention.

Kaguchia's arrest has sparked political debate, with opposition leaders accusing investigative agencies of selectively enforcing the law against government critics. They argue that other leaders who have previously made controversial public statements have not faced similar action.

World.title: CS sued in bid to kick out Railways boss, audit SGR contracts
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

A court battle is brewing over Kenya Railways operations and the corporation’s Managing Director Phillip Mainga's reign.

A petitioner is now seeking to push the KR boss out, claiming he is employed on permanent terms.

In the case against KR board, the Attorney General and Transport Cabinet Secretary, the complainant alleges that Mainga was appointed in 2018, noting that State corporations hire their bosses on short-term contracts.

Mainga has been named as an interested party.

“Under the prevailing governance principles applicable to the state corporations, the office of the Managing Director is not meant to be occupied indefinitely,” argues Wahome Mucunu, adding that Mainga’s tenure in office ought to have allegedly lapsed in 2024.

Mucunu claims that the corporation has been at the heart of numerous concerns over procurement and transparency.

He states that among the projects that have raised concerns are the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR project).

According to him, Transparency International this year in March this year allegedly indicated that SGR was a high-risk project, with a 4.9 out of 5 corruption risk score.

“The project has equally generated sustained public debate concerning transparency, accountability, value for money, public participation, procurement practices and debt sustainability. The Petitioner states that the people of Kenya, being the ultimate financiers of the project through taxation and public borrowing, possess a legitimate constitutional interest in the manner in which the project was conceived, procured, financed and implemented,” says Muchunu.

He further claims that Transparency International indicated that public institutions, among them KR, allegedly repeatedly failed to provide information requested by accountability actors and researchers. Muchunu alleged that the assessment concluded that the responses received were insufficient to facilitate effective public oversight.

“All material times relevant to this Petition, the first interested party, Mr. Phillip Mainga, has served as the Managing Director of Kenya Railways Corporation. The office of Managing Director constitutes the highest executive office within the Corporation and carries overall responsibility for the administration, management and operational control of the affairs of the Corporation,” he argues.

He also claims that many questions have been raised by members of the public, civil society organisations, governance experts and accountability institutions regarding the management of major projects undertaken by the corporation.

According to him, the answers given do not allegedly exude confidence as they are not allegedly fully addressed.

“Such concerns have centered on the adequacy of procurement procedures, transparency of contractual arrangements, disclosure of project costs and effectiveness of oversight mechanisms. The Petitioner states that these concerns have never been adequately addressed in a manner capable of restoring public confidence,” he continues.

In his case before Justice David Mburu, the petitioner urges the court to find that failure to disclose details about the SGR contract was a violation of the Constitution. He also seeks for a finding that Mainga ought to have left office by last year.

At the same time, he is urging the court to rule that the parastatal’s board had violated the Constitution and to compel it to find his successor.

Muchunu also wants to have the SGR project contracts audited.

World.title: Tiktoker Mauti changes plea, freed on bail in case involving Ruto's children
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

TikToker Hesbon Mauti was charged for posting a video threatening to kill and defile President William Ruto's children. [Nancy Gitonga, Standard]

TikToker Hesbon Mauti Thomas, accused of posting a video containing remarks threatening President William Ruto’s son George Ruto and daughter, has been released on a Sh5,000 cash bail after changing his plea to not guilty.

Mauti appeared before Milimani Principal Magistrate Geoffrey Onsarigo on Friday, July 31, 2026, where the charge of offensive conduct conducive to breaches of the peace was read afresh to him.

The accused, who had initially pleaded guilty to the charge on Thursday, changed his plea after his lawyer Cliff Ombeta applied for the matter to be reopened and for the charge to be read again.

The court allowed the application, after which Mauti denied the charge and pleaded not guilty.

According to the charge sheet, Mauti is accused of posting a video on June 25, 2026, through his TikTok account PROVIDENT@bonifaceaminga, containing remarks that prosecutors say were likely to cause a breach of the peace.

The charge sheet alleges that Mauti altered words in the video to make remarks targeting President Ruto’s son George Ruto and his daughter, while demanding that their parents be paid Sh2 million.

Mauti is charged with offensive conduct conducive to breaches of the peace contrary to Section 94(1) of the Penal Code, Chapter 63 of the Laws of Kenya.

After denying the charges, his defence team told the court that Mauti is a young man and a law student at Chuka University whose fees are paid by a church.

The lawyers further informed the court that Mauti is an orphan and has no parents to assist him in securing his release, asking the court to grant him a lenient cash bail.

“We are looking at the charges and when we look at it and the consequences that come from that, and if it goes on this particular way we know what the sentence is and what the consequences are. The court has got the right before passing the sentence to be able to reconsider when he changes his plea,” his lawyers told the court.

The defence also told the court that they had advised Mauti that the earlier position he had taken by pleading guilty carried serious consequences and offered to represent him in the matter.

The prosecution did not oppose his release on bail.

Magistrate Onsarigo granted Mauti a cash bail of Sh5,000 and directed him to provide one contact person.

The matter will be mentioned on August 18, 2026, for pre-trial directions.

World.title: Ruto calls for national dialogue to shape Kenya's vision
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Ruto said recent economic reforms had laid a stronger foundation for future growth. [File, Standard]

President William Ruto has invited Kenyans to take part in what he described as the country's most significant national conversation since the adoption of the 2010 Constitution, saying the discussions will help chart Kenya's next long-term development agenda.

Speaking on the country's development trajectory, the President said the conversation should move beyond partisan politics and election cycles to focus on a shared national vision.

"I invite every Kenyan to what I believe will become the most consequential national conversation since the adoption of our Constitution in 2010," Ruto said.

"A national conversation about Kenya's development. This conversation must rise above politics, transcend electoral cycles and unite us around a shared destiny."

The President acknowledged that while Vision 2030 had set an ambitious goal of transforming Kenya into an upper-middle-income country by 2030, the country remains off course to achieve that target.

"Vision 2030 set a target of Kenya becoming an upper-middle-income country by 2030. So far, we are off target. This is not a criticism of Vision 2030, nor is it a reason for disappointment; rather, it is an opportunity to learn from our successes proudly, reflect with honesty on where we have fallen short, and define together Kenya's next long-term vision," he said.

At the same time, Ruto announced that the government will formally launch a nationwide conversation on August 12 to develop Kenya's next long-term development blueprint as Vision 2030 nears its end.

"Accordingly, on Wednesday, August 12, 2026, we shall formally launch the National Conversation on Kenya's Future Beyond Vision 2030; the most consequential exercise in national reflection and public participation since the promulgation of our Constitution in 2010," he stated.

Ruto said recent economic reforms had laid a stronger foundation for future growth, citing improvements in key macroeconomic indicators.

"We have stabilized our currency, inflation has fallen, borrowing costs have declined, and investor confidence has returned," he said. "Last year Kenya attracted a record $3.2 billion in foreign direct investment, more than double the amount recorded in 2022."

He added that Kenya's improving investment climate had earned international recognition.

"The 2025 IMD World Competitiveness Ranking placed Kenya as the most competitive economy in Africa, reflecting the confidence our reforms have restored," Ruto said.

At the same time, Ruto also highlighted the establishment of the National Infrastructure Fund and the Sovereign Wealth Fund, saying the two institutions would help finance strategic investments while safeguarding the country's wealth for future generations.

According to Ruto, Kenya must now confront difficult questions about its development path to unlock its full potential.

"The question we must ask ourselves candidly and honestly is why other nations have fulfilled so much of their potential while we have repeatedly fallen short. What must we now do differently to ensure that the next chapter of Kenya's development story is fundamentally different from the last?" he posed.

He urged all Kenyans to help shape a new long-term national vision, saying the country's future depends on collective commitment rather than political divisions.

World.title: Lawyer seeks orders to suspend court boycott
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Advocate Adrian Kamotho argues that LSK's actions create the impression that court orders can be overturned through a boycott. [File, Standard]

A city lawyer has moved to the High Court seeking conservatory orders to suspend the Law Society of Kenya's (LSK) ongoing targeted boycott of judges and judicial officers.

In a petition filed under a certificate of urgency, Advocate Adrian Kamotho has sued LSK led by President Charles Kanjama, over its nationwide and targeted court boycott of Chief Justice Martha Koome, Deputy Chief Justice Philomena Mwilu and other judges, arguing that the action is unconstitutional, undermines judicial independence and denies litigants access to justice.

"The LSK's actions create the impression that lawful court orders can be overturned through a boycott, setting a dangerous precedent to the rule of law and thereby undermining the proper administration of justice," Kamotho states in the petition.

The lawyer has named the Judicial Service Commission (JSC), Chief Justice Martha Koome, Deputy Chief Justice Mwilu, several Supreme Court, High Court and Environment and Land Court judges, Court of Appeal Judge Sankale Ole Kantai, Kibera Chief Magistrate Stella Atambo and the Kenya Magistrates and Judges Association as interested parties in the case.

He is seeking orders to immediately suspend the implementation of the LSK's targeted boycott announced through statements and operational guidelines issued on July 17, July 20 and July 22, 2026, pending the hearing and determination of the petition.

"Pending the hearing and determination of this Petition, the court be pleased to issue a conservatory order restraining the LSK, whether by itself, its Council, officers, agents or any person acting under its authority, from implementing, enforcing or giving effect to the targeted boycott," Kamotho seeks.

According to the petition, the targeted boycott, which commenced on July 23, directs advocates not to participate in fresh hearings, part-heard matters or new applications before judges listed by the LSK.

East Africa Law Society president Ramadhan Abubakar Mukira addresses the media on the court boycott outside the Supreme Court of Kenya in Nairobi on July 22, 2026. [Benard Orwongo, Standard]

Lawyers are also required to seek adjournments, transfers or recusals of matters regardless of their clients' instructions.

"The Respondent has directed advocates not to participate in fresh hearings, part-heard matters or new applications before the listed judges and judicial officers," Kamotho states.

He adds: "Advocates appearing before the targeted judges and judicial officers have been directed to seek the transfer, recusal or adjournment of pending proceedings, irrespective of their clients' instructions, the circumstances of the individual case or the applicable legal principles."

Kamotho further claims the society has threatened disciplinary action against judges, judicial officers and advocates who decline to implement the boycott.

"The LSK has further directed that any judge, judicial officer or advocate who declines to facilitate the boycott be reported to it for 'appropriate action,' including possible complaints before the Judicial Service Commission and such further action as its Council may deem necessary," he says.

According to the petition, every day the boycott remains in force exposes court users to delayed justice and unnecessary hardship.

"Every day that the targeted boycott remains operative exposes litigants and court users to adjournments, disruption of part-heard proceedings, expiry of interim protection measures, prolonged detention, additional expense and denial or delay of access to justice," Kamotho argues.

He also faults the LSK for allegedly including the late Supreme Court Judge Mohammed Ibrahim in its list of judges affected by the boycott.

"The targeted list of judges includes Hon. Justice Mohammed Ibrahim (deceased), demonstrating unconscionable casualness on the part of the LSK and apparent failure to verify elementary material facts before imposing measures of such gravity," the petition states.

Kamotho contends that the boycott creates an unlawful mechanism for exerting pressure on judges outside the constitutional framework.

He argues that the dispute raises fundamental constitutional questions, including whether the LSK has the legal authority to organise an indefinite boycott, compel advocates to withhold legal services from clients and determine which judicial functions judges may perform.

He maintains that the boycott threatens litigants' constitutional rights to equality before the law, access to justice, legal representation and a fair hearing, particularly in urgent and criminal matters.

In his supporting affidavit, Kamotho says advocates have been placed in an impossible position by the LSK's directives.

"The directions therefore place advocates in an immediate and irreconcilable conflict between their lawful professional duties and the Respondent's threatened enforcement measures," he says.

He further says litigants are innocent parties caught in an institutional dispute.

"The practical burden of the boycott consequently falls upon litigants and court users who are strangers to the institutional dispute forming the alleged basis of the boycott," he states.

Kamotho insists the conservatory orders sought are intended only to preserve uninterrupted court operations and judicial independence pending determination of the constitutional petition, arguing that the public interest favours continued access to courts and legal representation rather than disruption of judicial proceedings.

The petition is pending directions and hearing.

World.title: Rather than capitulating to the US, Iran toughens its demands over the vital Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
The list of demands from Iran can’t have surprised the White House.

Hardliners have been repeating the mantra on a daily basis: the limited agreement in the works with Oman on the Strait of Hormuz is not the same as reopening the vital waterway in the way Washington wants.

For that, they say, “America must correct its behavior.”

Tehran has now spelled out what means, laying out a series of conditions that appear to go beyond the memorandum of understanding which was agreed in June but later suspended amid US strikes on Iran, Iranian retaliation across the Middle East and a resurgence of attacks on shipping.

On Saturday, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, a highly influential figure in the Revolutionary Guards, reeled off a maximalist set of demands.

That Iran is issuing such demands underlines the perception that Tehran believes it has the upper hand. CNN has reported on dwindling US munitions – something angrily denied by President Trump – and suggestions that his top general is looking for an “off-ramp” in the conflict.

It is also likely that Iran has taken notice of how many times Trump has threatened major strikes before not following through on the threat.

Zolghadr demanded the US lift its naval blockade and withdraw its military forces from around Iran.

The US must also pay damages caused to Iran by the wars this year and in June last year (which was principally conducted by Israel), he said. And the US must lift sanctions and release, unconditionally, Iranian assets frozen abroad.

A woman sifts through the rubble in her house in the Beryanak District after it was damaged by missile attacks two days before in US-Israeli strikes. Majid Saeedi/Getty Images

The implication of Zolghadr’s statement was that these conditions must be fulfilled before or in tandem with concessions on the strait, which would be at odds with the formula set out in the memorandum of understanding.

That held that sanctions would be fully removed once a final deal regarding Iran’s nuclear program was reached and envisaged a phased release of assets, in which the two sides “will mutually agree on the procedures related to the release of these funds.”

Iran’s apparent new strategy, though, is not without risk.

The fresh demands “narrows the options for the Trump administration,” according to the former Supreme Allied Commander of NATO, James Stavridis.

“Iran is overplaying its hand and it appears the hardliners are in control. The likelihood of a deal in the immediate term is declining,” Stavridis posted on X Sunday.

No US-Iran talks underway

The Trump administration has not responded to the latest Iranian conditions.

“What we’re really working through now is how you can actually set up a traffic scheme so that the ships that pass can pass through safely,” US Vice President JD Vance told Fox News on Saturday.

But the current situation smacks of stalemate.

Iranian officials, whether perceived as moderates or hardliners, are saying that renewed negotiations with the US are not in prospect.

“As long as the United States has not addressed its violations of the memorandum of understanding and remedied those breaches, we see no possibility of restarting negotiations,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday.

“We currently have no negotiations with America. Yes, there is an exchange of messages through intermediaries,” he added.

Araghchi referred to the more limited and temporary arrangement for Hormuz being negotiated with Oman, which borders its southern shoreline.

“I can say we are in the final stages, and the old routes that existed will be replaced with new routes,” he said, referring to how the thin traffic traveling through the strait is currently split between Iranian and Omani paths.

“This, of course, does not mean the opening of the Strait of Hormuz,” Araghchi told reporters in Tehran, which was “subject to the fulfillment of a series of other conditions.”

Other Iranian officials have indicated that an agreement with Oman would continue to give Iran considerable influence in the strait, which it did not enjoy before the war but which has become a red line as important as the nuclear issue for Tehran.

Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said last week the arrangement reflects a new strategy for exercising “effective sovereignty” over the strait, while stressing that Iran does not intend to routinely close the waterway in peacetime.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei cautioned last week that there could be a deal with Oman “provided that certain third parties do not obstruct the process” in a far from cryptic reference to the US.

Amidst the uncertainty – and sporadic attacks on ships passing through the Strait – traffic remains very limited. An average of about a dozen vessels a day have transited in the past week, according to shipping data.

That’s about one-tenth of the normal pre-war traffic.

Already into its sixth month, the conflict between the US and Iran shows no sign of resolution – but has instead evolved into an unpredictable cycle of escalation and pause.

World.title: Accused Thai school shooter had watched violent content online, police say
World.content:
Reuters —

The Thai teen behind a deadly school shooting outside Bangkok had an air gun confiscated by a teacher last year and had watched violent content online, police said on Sunday, as the government promised new safety protocols for schools.

As investigations continued into Friday’s rampage, where a 14-year-old boy allegedly shot dead his grandparents at home before killing another six people at his school before turning the gun on himself, police said the boy had used social media to learn how to use a firearm.

“According to witness interviews, the perpetrator had begun showing interest in studying the use of firearms for some time, about one to two years,” Atthapol Anusit, deputy commissioner of the Provincial Police Region 1, told reporters.

The boy’s mother, however, said she’d seen no signs of trouble.

“He was a bright, cheerful person,” she told Reuters, asking that her name not be used. “He behaved normally.”

She said she had asked him if he’d ever been bullied. “He always said no, there was nothing unusual.”

A forensic police expert works at the site of the residence of the Debsirin Nonthaburi School teen shooter on the outskirts of Bangkok, Thailand, on August 7. Tananchai Keawsowattana/Reuters

BB gun confiscated last year

Atthapol, who said police had so far interviewed 17 witnesses, said a knife had also been found in the boy’s bag and other evidence found at the crime scenes included a firearm, spent cartridge cases, and a personal computer.

“After examining the PC, it was found that the child had watched social media content involving violence,” the deputy commissioner said, but added there was no evidence yet that he had practiced shooting.

He said that last year a teacher had confiscated a BB gun, a type of air gun, that the boy took to school. The boy had lived with his grandparents for 12 years after his parents had separated, Atthapol said.

The Ministry of Education said it would develop new safety protocols over the next three months, including mental health screenings and a system to refer at-risk people to specialists, drills for emergency response plans, a drive to stamp out bullying and better detection to stop items from being taken into schools.

Along with those who died, more than 20 people were injured in Thailand’s worst mass shooting since 2022, which has reignited debate over firearms control in Southeast Asia’s largest gun-owning nation.

The boy lived with his grandparents, and his mother said she last saw him during a recent school holiday.

“On the day it happened, I didn’t know he was the one who did it,” she said, adding that she sent him messages and tried to call when she heard there had been a shooting. “I just told him, if anything’s wrong, contact me, I’m worried, that’s all it was.”

She apologized for his actions.

“We are truly devastated, because no one thought this would happen.”

World.title: AI agents fake identities, target real people in new security incident
World.content:
Anthropic’s most advanced artificial intelligence model used fake identities to deceive real people and try to plant malicious code during testing by Britain’s AI Security Institute (AISI) –– the latest example of an AI model going rogue.

Anthropic and OpenAI models were tested with lowered security guardrails in lab environments, but, in a first, were found to engage in “social engineering” to pressure a human approver while carrying out an unsanctioned task, the government research lab said.

“This is the first time AISI has seen deception of this severity that was targeted at a real person, unprompted, in the real world,” the institute said Tuesday. There has been no evidence of real-world harm, it added.

The security incident is the latest in a string of examples of advanced AI models engaging in unauthorized actions, events that have prompted growing calls for more government action to regulate artificial intelligence and even to slow its pace of development.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic reported their models escaping testing environments and hacking into other systems in late July. But unlike these earlier reported security breaches, the British institute explicitly gave the models internet access during its testing.

Among the 122 cybersecurity challenges the institute ran, it found that in 10 of those runs, AI agents “took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organizations,” with most of them stemming from Anthropic’s Mythos 5 model and the rest from OpenAI’s GPT-5.6-Sol.

In the most serious incident, the agent attempted to get approval from human reviewers to “insert malicious code into a publicly used open-source project” by creating “multiple fake identities,” according to the institute.

The agent “tried to contact real people directly, sending messages and files through an online file-transfer service to persuade them, or their own AI coding tools, to run malicious code,” it said. After the agent’s actions were challenged, it then modified earlier records and considered using a new identity to continue.

The institute’s disclosure came on the same day representatives from the top AI companies met with the White House to discuss the new framework where the government will review the most advanced AI models before they’re released publicly.

In a statement on X, Anthropic said the models were tested under “deliberately permissive conditions” with the removal of safeguards and no specific restrictions on how the internet should be used.

“We’re working closely with them to gather more details of the incident as we conduct our own investigation,” it said, adding that there was no evidence of an escape from a secure environment.

OpenAI identified the two unsanctioned actions as crossing outside the test environment and engage in actions unrequired for the exercises.

“We are committed to working across the industry to strengthen shared practices for conducting high-risk evaluations safely,” it said in a Tuesday company blog post.

World.title: Syria agrees deal with Russia over future use of two key Mediterranean bases
World.content:
Damascus, Syria AP —

Syria and Russia have reached an agreement over the future of two strategic Mediterranean coastal bases that ultimately ends their use as military outposts for Moscow, Syria’s Foreign Ministry said Sunday.

Russia was the top political and military ally of ousted President Bashar Assad between 2011 and 2024 when Syria fought against an Islamist-led armed opposition of which current interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa was a prominent militant leader.

Throughout the conflict, the Hmeimem air base near Latakia and the Tartus naval base were key Russian outposts in the eastern Mediterranean.

Under the agreement, Syria will take control of the Hmeimem air base and the commercial berth at Tartus port as part of its civil administration. The military facilities at both sites will become “joint training and qualification centers,” the Foreign Ministry said.

The new arrangements represent a “reorganizing of the Russian presence” along Syria’s coast, the ministry said.

“This move marks the most significant development since negotiations began approximately a year and a half ago, paving the way for a new phase in Syrian-Russian relations,” a statement read.

Russia did not immediately comment on the agreement.

Moscow did not interfere during the lightning insurgency that led to the overthrow of Assad, but it did provide the longtime Syrian leader and his family asylum. After Assad’s ouster Russian troops remaining in Syria gradually left the country.

Syria’s new leadership has aimed to maintain strong bilateral ties with Moscow. Al-Sharaa has visited President Vladimir Putin in Moscow twice since taking power, with the two Mediterranean bases being key points of discussion.

Since Assad’s ouster, Syria has also bolstered its ties with the United States, Europe, and neighboring Arab countries that had cut ties with Damascus during Assad’s crackdown on protests. Washington has lifted most of its crippling sanctions on the country, and French President Emmanuel Macron made a visit to Syria in July during which he announced that the two countries would appoint respective ambassadors for the first time in 14 years.

World.title: Government following up entrepreneurship file closely
World.content:
Planning and Economic Development Minister Ahmed Rostom affirmed that Egypt’s hosting of the third edition of the “Global Entrepreneurship Festival” reflects its leading regional position in the Middle East and Africa in the entrepreneurship sector.

He noted that the government, through the Ministerial Group for Entrepreneurship headed by Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs Hussein Issa, is closely following this file to provide all forms of support to startups and enhance their ability to grow in order to contribute to the national economy.

Rostom made the remarks on Sunday, August 9, 2026, during an expanded meeting to follow up on preparations for Egypt’s hosting of the third edition of the festival, scheduled to be launched in November, in light of the government’s strong focus on this vital sector due to its key role in driving economic growth, providing innovative solutions to development challenges and attracting venture capital investments.

The minister pointed to the continuous follow-up by the prime minister on the entrepreneurship file and directives to ensure coordination and integration among various concerned bodies to support this important sector.

He explained that the meeting emphasized the importance of coordination among participating entities to ensure the festival is held in the best possible manner, reflecting Egypt’s significant potential in terms of promising youth talent and attractive investment opportunities.

Rostom highlighted that the festival will witness broad participation from thousands of attendees from Africa and around the world, creating a regional and international platform that underscores the pivotal role of startups in leading development.

For her part, Head of the Technical Secretariat of the National Alliance for Civil Development Work and Secretary-General of the festival Nabila Makram said the event has received unprecedented interest from entrepreneurs and startups across Africa.

She noted that the festival organizers are working in continuous coordination with the Egyptian government across various areas to ensure the success of this important international event.

The third edition of the Global Entrepreneurship Festival is scheduled to take place in Cairo from November 6 to 8. The event is considered one of the largest international gatherings specializing in entrepreneurship, with this edition aiming to attract more than 10,000 participants from over 70 countries, alongside more than 100 exhibitors and 60 international speakers, including government leaders and experts in economics and investment. The event is expected to further consolidate Cairo’s position as a key gateway for cross-border partnerships and investments.

World.title: FM affirms necessity of continuing efforts aimed to stabilize Gaza
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty on Sunday, Aug 9, 2026, stressed during a phone with High Representative for Gaza Nickolay Mladenov the importance of continuing efforts to stabilize the Gaza Strip and create conditions to transition to the peace plan’s next phase.

The phone call comes within the framework of ongoing contacts to follow up on Gaza developments and efforts to implement the US president’s peace plan. It addressed following up on the roadmap for Gaza peace plan commitments.

Abdelatty stressed committing to all agreed obligations, including ensuring full, safe, and sustainable humanitarian aid access and completing the Israeli withdrawal to pave the way for the second phase and support early recovery and reconstruction.

Both sides discussed arrangements for the next phase.

The Egyptian top diplomat emphasized enabling the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) to assume its temporary duties from within the Strip and advancing arrangements to deploy the International Stabilization Force to monitor the ceasefire, support security during the transitional phase, and preserve Palestinian territorial unity until the Palestinian National Authority assumes full responsibilities in Gaza and the West Bank.

Abdelatty stressed that all parties must fulfill their obligations and refrain from taking actions that obstruct implementation or undermine progress.

World.title: Foreign Minister reaffirms Egypt’s firm support for Sudan’s unity
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty reaffirmed Egypt’s firm and unwavering support for Sudan’s unity, sovereignty, territorial integrity and national institutions during a phone call with Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohieddin Salem.

During the call, which came as part of continued consultation and coordination between the two brotherly countries, Abdelatty stressed the importance of ensuring that the political process remains fully Sudanese-owned in a manner that preserves the country’s resources and fulfills the aspirations of the Sudanese people for security and stability.

The two ministers discussed bilateral relations and ways to further strengthen them across various fields.

Abdelatty underscored Egypt’s pride in the deep-rooted historical and fraternal ties between the Egyptian and Sudanese peoples and its keenness to continue developing cooperation in a manner that serves the common interests of the two countries.

The two ministers agreed to maintain close coordination and consultation in the coming period on various issues of common interest and to follow up on bilateral cooperation, in a manner that reflects the unique nature of Egyptian-Sudanese relations and serves the interests and aspirations of the two brotherly peoples.

World.title: PM opens renovated June 30 Corniche in Matrouh
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly on Sunday, August 9, 2026, inaugurated the renovated June 30 Corniche in Matrouh governorate.

Madbouli also toured the “Treasures of Egypt in Matrouh” exhibition during a visit to the Mediterranean coastal governorate.

The corniche renovation is part of a wider state project to upgrade infrastructure and roads, including the development of 100 km of roads across Matrouh city, Governor Mohamed El Zamlout said.

The project aims to keep pace with rapid development, accommodate population growth and meet rising tourist demand in Matrouh, he added.

The renovated corniche has been expanded to three traffic lanes in each direction, alongside a modern tourist promenade, landscaping and interlock paving.

The project also included the installation of 570 lighting poles and upgrades to traffic signs and U-turn areas to improve traffic flow and road safety.

The development also included 45 new cafes and retail outlets and expanded beach areas by adding a layer of sand along the corniche.

The upgrades are intended to enhance public recreational spaces and strengthen Matrouh’s position as a major tourist destination on the Mediterranean coast.

The project reflects cooperation between Matrouh Governorate and the Armed Forces Engineering Authority, which carried out the development works along the roughly 2-km stretch.

Madbouly also toured the “Treasures of Egypt in Matrouh” exhibition, held along the renovated corniche. The exhibition brings together products from 20 Egyptian governorates, showcasing the country’s diverse cultural and traditional heritage.

The exhibition also features about 22 shops operating along the corniche and offers a range of traditional, handicraft, environmental and food products associated with different Egyptian governorates.

During the tour, Madbouly praised the quality and diversity of the products and stressed the exhibition’s role in marketing them, supporting small-scale industries, creating jobs and preserving traditional crafts.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Appoints Ziankahn to Lead LDEA, Suspends Biago Over Ethics Concerns
World.content:
President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr. has dismissed Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA) Officer-in-Charge Fitzgerald T. M. Biago over allegations he received a vehicle from an individual linked to a drug-trafficking network, and appointed Major General (Retired) Daniel Dee Ziankahn, Jr. as the agency’s new Director General pending Senate confirmation — the latest in a string of leadership purges at an agency battling both a worsening drug crisis and its own credibility problems.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr. has appointed Major General (Retired) Daniel Dee Ziankahn, Jr. as Director General of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA), pending Senate confirmation, while indefinitely suspending former Officer-in-Charge Fitzgerald T. M. Biago from the Liberia National Police over ethical concerns raised in a Ministry of Justice probe — even as that same investigation cleared Biago of any involvement in illegal narcotics trafficking.

New Leadership

Ziankahn, who most recently served as Military Advisor to the President, previously led the Armed Forces of Liberia as Chief of Staff and later served as Minister of National Defense. He will report directly to the President in close consultation with the Minister of Justice.

Boakai also named Precious Rue as Deputy Director General for Operations and Prince Mulbah as Deputy Director General for Administration, both also pending Senate confirmation. All three are to assume their duties immediately in an acting capacity until the Senate returns later this year. Ernest Tarpeh, who had served as a deputy LDEA director general, returns to his prior post at the National Security Agency.

Chaotic 48 hours

The appointments follow the Ministry of Justice’s submission of its investigative report into Biago, ordered after he asked over the weekend to recuse himself from his duties amid allegations he had accepted a Toyota pickup from someone allegedly tied to a drug-trafficking organization. According to the Executive Mansion, the report did not establish that Biago was involved in narcotics trafficking, but it flagged unspecified ethical concerns warranting further scrutiny — prompting his suspension and a more detailed follow-up investigation.

The shakeup is the latest in a long run of upheaval atop Liberia’s anti-narcotics agency. Biago had been running the LDEA on an interim basis since August 2025, when Boakai dismissed then-Director General Anthony K. Souh and two deputies over what the government called administrative reasons, following weeks of public anger over the agency’s handling of enforcement. That reshuffle followed an earlier crisis in June 2024, when senior officials were suspended after a physical altercation at LDEA headquarters tied to a dispute over a synthetic street drug known locally as “kush” or “zombie” — a substance whose spread among Liberian youth Boakai has since called an existential threat to the country’s future.

Presidential Message

The changes were announced following what the Executive Mansion described as a marathon National Security Council meeting Monday evening. Boakai said his administration would continue to treat allegations of misconduct fairly and through due process, while holding officials accountable for questions of integrity.

He called on the LDEA’s new leadership to work with Joint Security, the Ministry of Justice, and international partners to dismantle trafficking networks, strengthen border security, and protect Liberia’s youth from illicit drugs.

“Our fight against drugs is a fight for the future of Liberia,” Boakai said. “We will continue to strengthen our institutions, hold public officials to the highest ethical standards, and pursue those who seek to poison our communities. There will be no safe haven for drug traffickers or those who aid and abet them.”

World.title: LIS, Guinean Soldiers Hold Peaceful Talks at Sorlumba After Sunday Standoff
World.content:
Foya District, Lofa County — Liberian and Guinean security forces stationed at the volatile Sorlumba border crossing held a peaceful dialogue Monday morning, easing fresh tension that flared a day earlier when Guinean soldiers ordered Liberia Immigration Service (LIS) officers to abandon their post.

By James Kollie

Local authorities from Foya District rushed to the border this morning after receiving reports that Guinean troops had demanded on Sunday that LIS personnel vacate their position. The Liberian officers refused to move, and the Guinean soldiers ultimately withdrew back to their own side.

Seeking to defuse the standoff before it could escalate, Foya officials traveled to Sorlumba to meet with both sides. Sorlumba Township Commissioner Hon. Harris Domah said the engagement produced a peaceful dialogue in which LIS officers and Guinean soldiers agreed to preserve calm and continue coexisting peacefully at the crossing.

During the meeting, it emerged that Guinea’s military had quietly rotated its command at Sorlumba, swapping out the previous unit for a new team of soldiers. Liberian officials used the encounter to brief the incoming Guinean commander on the border post’s long history of peaceful cooperation between security forces from both nations.

Following the talks, Guinean soldiers returned to their position and LIS officers remained at their assigned post. Authorities describe the border as calm for now, with both sides committing to avoid actions that could reignite tension.

A Border on Edge Since March

Monday’s brief standoff is the latest flashpoint in a border crisis that has simmered in Lofa County since early this year. Tensions first erupted on March 2, when armed Guinean soldiers confronted workers from BK Enterprise, a contractor hired to pave the Foya–Vahun road, at the Sorlumba crossing. Soldiers reportedly seized construction equipment and ordered the removal of a Liberian flag that had flown over the riverbank for decades.

The dispute escalated dramatically over the following days. Around March 9–10, Guinean troops allegedly pushed further into territory Liberians say lies roughly eight kilometers inside their border, tore down the Liberian flag and raised Guinea’s colors in its place — a move many Liberians called a direct violation of national sovereignty. Witnesses reported Guinean reinforcements arriving by helicopter and troops ordering Liberian security officers off their posts. In the ensuing unrest, a Liberian resident, Edward T. Lebbie, was struck by gunfire near the Makona River, the waterway long recognized as the natural boundary between the two countries. Local youths later erected a new Liberian flag at the site and briefly took control of the crossing, vowing to defend their homeland, before Liberia National Police officers deployed to restore order.

The unrest forced school closures in Foya District and sent thousands of residents fleeing deeper into Liberian territory. A subsequent fact-finding mission by Liberia’s rights commission found that at least 26 towns and villages were affected, with displaced families facing loss of shelter and food insecurity.

Diplomacy has run alongside the unrest. On March 17, Guinean President Mamadi Doumbouya hosted Liberian President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and Sierra Leonean President Julius Maada Bio in Conakry for an emergency summit, with Côte d’Ivoire attending as a witness. The three governments agreed to resolve border incidents through dialogue and announced joint technical commissions to tackle border delimitation and management — an arrangement regional analysts say reflects deeper, longstanding weaknesses in how Mano River Union states demarcate and jointly monitor their shared frontiers.

Monday’s peaceful exchange at Sorlumba — capped by the introduction of a new Guinean commander — suggests both sides are still working to hold that fragile truce, even as the underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved.

This is a developing story. FrontPageAfrica will provide updates as more information becomes available.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-LDEA Airport Commander Rearrested Allegedly Attempting to Leave Country in $19.2M Cocaine Case
World.content:
Monrovia — Moses Jallah, the former Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA) deputy commander at Roberts International Airport, has been rearrested after allegedly attempting to leave Liberia through the same airport where 237.6 kilograms of cocaine, valued at approximately US$19.2 million, were seized.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

Jallah was taken back into custody and brought before the Monrovia City Court on Monday, August 10, after authorities received information that he had attempted to board an outbound flight while already facing criminal charges stemming from the cocaine investigation.

His rearrest adds a new twist to a case that has already raised questions about how a massive cocaine shipment passed through Liberia’s main international gateway and who may have been positioned to facilitate its movement.

Jallah was previously charged by the Ministry of Justice’s Special Investigation Team with obstructing law enforcement, interfering with a government function and tampering with a criminal investigation.

Those charges do not accuse him of trafficking cocaine. However, investigators have linked his alleged conduct to efforts surrounding the attempted export of the 237.6 kilograms of suspected cocaine.

Prosecutors are now weighing whether the evidence supports additional allegations involving trafficking, facilitation or conspiracy. As of Monday, no such amended charge had been filed against him.

Such a development would substantially change Jallah’s position in the case—from an official accused of interfering with an investigation to a potential participant in the broader cocaine operation.

The Shipment That Triggered the Investigation

The case began with six cargo boxes presented at Roberts International Airport as general merchandise, including lappas and Maggi cubes, and destined for England.

Airport screeners reportedly detected discrepancies between the declared weight of the shipment and what appeared on X-ray images. A physical inspection subsequently uncovered a white powdery substance that was later confirmed as cocaine.

Investigators allege Jallah became involved after the discovery, particularly in efforts to have the shipment released.

The investigation identifies businessman George Harris, also known as Leroy Harris, a Paynesville bar operator, as one of the individuals allegedly involved in efforts to secure the release of the cargo.

According to the investigative report, Harris contacted senior security and law enforcement officials, including Jallah, and allegedly offered money in exchange for the release of the shipment.

Investigators further allege that Jallah later met Harris despite knowing of his alleged connection to the cargo.

The report also claims Jallah had prior knowledge of some individuals allegedly linked to the operation but failed to act on the information.

Jallah’s Defense

Jallah disputes the investigators’ account.

In a statement contained in the investigation report, he said he was acting on intelligence from his superiors and reported the approaches made to him to the appropriate authorities.

He said he was offered money to stop the inspection and prevent arrests, but instead passed the information up his chain of command.

Jallah also maintained that he had been gathering intelligence on some of the individuals who were later implicated in the cocaine case.

The Special Investigation Team, however, concluded that his explanation did not remove his potential criminal liability and recommended that he face prosecution.

How Did He Get to the Departure Gate?

Jallah’s alleged attempt to leave Liberia now presents investigators with another question: How did an official already charged in connection with the country’s largest cocaine case make it through the departure process at Roberts International Airport?

The question is particularly significant because the airport was itself the scene of the cocaine seizure and because Jallah previously served as an LDEA commander there.

Authorities will now have to determine whether he was subject to any travel restriction, whether immigration officials were aware of his pending case, and how far he had progressed in the departure process before being intercepted.

Beyond the airport incident, prosecutors face a broader task: determining exactly what Jallah knew, when he knew it and whether his actions after the cocaine was discovered were intended to facilitate the shipment or interfere with its seizure and investigation.

For now, Jallah has not been charged with cocaine trafficking, facilitation or conspiracy.

He remains presumed innocent unless proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.

World.title: Liberia: Inside the Deadline That Could Define President Boakai’s War on Drugs
World.content:
“A Detailed Report Within Forty-Eight Hours”

The presidency did not wait for the controversy to cool on its own. The Minister of Justice has been instructed to submit a detailed report to the President within forty-eight hours, a timeline that turns what had been an agency-level dispute into a matter the Executive Mansion is now personally supervising, on the record, with a deadline attached. President Boakai reaffirmed that his administration remains “unwavering in its fight against illegal drugs, organized crime, and corruption,” and emphasized that “no individual or institution is above the law.” He stressed that the investigation must be “thorough, objective, and guided solely by the facts,” and said that upon receiving the report, he would “carefully review its findings and determine the appropriate course of action.”

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

The move, according to the president’s own framing, comes directly in response to “emerging public allegations and social media reports linking a pickup truck — allegedly connected to a narcotics suspect or trafficker — to the LDEA OIC’s office.” That a matter first raised by an activist on social media has, within days, reached the president’s desk and produced a personal deadline is itself a measure of how seriously this allegation is being taken inside the Executive Mansion — whatever the eventual findings turn out to show.

Biago’s own letter, addressed to the Minister of Justice, frames his recusal in similar terms. He said he was stepping back from his “active duties and functions as head of the LDEA” to preserve “the utmost integrity, transparency, and public trust in the national anti-drug campaign,” and to ensure an “unhindered, credible administrative and security investigation.” Read together, the president’s 48-hour order and Biago’s own recusal letter tell a consistent story: both men, in their own words, are treating this as serious enough to require distance and speed rather than a quiet denial left to stand on its own. Whether the next 48 hours produce a report that matches that seriousness is now the only question that matters.

A Truck, a Wife, and a Bar Owner

The allegation at the center of this week’s storm is specific enough to be either easily disproven or genuinely damaging, which is exactly why it has not gone away. Activist Martin K. N. Kollie says Biago received a Toyota pickup from Leroy Harris, the private bar owner now facing prosecution over alleged cartel ties. Kollie has gone further, claiming a second vehicle was purchased for Biago’s wife, and that this purchase, too, traces back to Harris. He says he has photographs and vehicle-registration records to back the claim — the kind of documentary evidence that, if real, would move this from rumor to something considerably harder to wave away.

The allegation does not arrive in isolation. This newspaper has previously reported that Biago’s own driver maintains close personal ties to Harris — a detail that, if accurate, puts the alleged benefactor only one degree removed from the OIC’s daily orbit. This paper has also previously reported alleged ties between Biago and Michael Brown, a fugitive wanted in connection with drug trafficking. Neither claim has been independently verified by prosecutors or the courts, and Biago has not been charged with any offense connected to either one.

The Agency Pushes Back

The LDEA did not stay quiet. In a statement issued Friday, August 7, the agency called the vehicle allegation “false” and said it is “not supported by any verifiable evidence.” Biago, through the agency, said he “neither received nor accepted” the pickup described in the claim and did not authorize anyone to accept it on his behalf.

The statement struck a dual tone — categorical denial paired with an invitation to scrutiny. “Public officials must remain open to legitimate scrutiny,” it read, urging anyone with credible evidence to bring it to investigators rather than “the court of public opinion.” It closed with a pledge of “zero tolerance for corruption, misconduct, or collusion with criminal networks,” and a warning that unverified claims risk undermining ongoing operations and public confidence in the security services. Kollie was not persuaded. He has argued that the LDEA’s denial sidesteps the specific documentary evidence he says he holds, and has continued pressing the agency to explain, in his words, under what circumstances the vehicle came into Biago’s possession or use.

A Scandal with a Body Count of Its Own

The allegations land at a combustible moment. In June, the LDEA intercepted roughly 237.6 kilograms of cocaine, valued at close to $19.2 million, hidden in cargo boxes at Roberts International Airport — a bust Biago himself hailed at the time as proof that “intelligence-driven operations” and “strengthened interagency cooperation” were paying off. A month later, in July, security forces seized nearly 3,971 kilograms of cocaine in Duazon, one of the largest hauls in the country’s history. Those seizures were meant to be the LDEA’s vindication. Instead, they have become the backdrop against which every question about the agency’s own leadership now gets asked. If the state can find nearly four tons of cocaine in Duazon, critics ask, why can it not resolve a straightforward question about a truck?

The scrutiny of Biago is also inseparable from how he got the job. Montserrado County lawmaker Thomas Fallah — writing through Representative Yekeh Kolubah’s rival, Cllr. Mulbah Morlu Koijee — alleged that the 2024 removal of former LDEA head Abe Kromah was engineered to install a more pliable leadership, and that Biago, then a deputy commissioner working under police official Coleman, was elevated as part of that arrangement. Koijee has petitioned the U.S. Embassy to back an international probe, alleging that a cartel gave vehicles not only to LDEA leadership but to figures closer to the presidency itself. None of those broader claims have been substantiated in court, and Biago has publicly rejected suggestions that he was ever on the verge of resigning over the pressure — a separate rumor the LDEA also moved quickly to knock down earlier this summer.

Konneh: “There Is No Free Lunch”

The political temperature rose further this week when Senator Amara Konneh weighed in with some of the sharpest language yet directed at the presidency over the affair. “An expensive gift, supposedly from the cartel to the chief drug enforcer — who leads the commandant-in-chief’s declared war on the cartel — represents a transaction that clearly undermines the war effort,” Konneh said. “There is no free lunch.”

Konneh called for the arrest and prosecution of “all current and former senior officials who protected the cartel,” and for an independent counsel to work alongside foreign investigators. He framed the moment in stark terms for President Joseph Nyuma Boakai: “President JNB, this Cocainegate is your LD$15 billion Containergate scandal — an issue that could define your presidency and Liberia’s future.” The comparison to Containergate — the LD$15 billion scandal that has already shadowed the administration’s fight against graft — was pointed. It signals that, fairly or not, Cocainegate is being read by some of the president’s critics less as a personnel problem and more as a test of whether the Boakai government can police its own security sector at all.

Who Is Actually Being Chased?

The Biago affair broke into public view the same weekend Senator Nathaniel McGill of Margibi County held a news conference to address what he described as circulating reports that the government was preparing to investigate or arrest him and other former officials of the Coalition for Democratic Change, the party of former President George Weah, in connection with the drug probe. Freshly back from a trip that took him through Europe and Ghana, McGill opened by rejecting the reports outright, telling reporters he had received no call, notice, or contact whatsoever from any government investigative agency. “I don’t associate with drugs,” he said, dismissing the speculation circulating on social media as “stupid” news and “foolish” talk.

McGill argued the reports made little sense set against his own standing inside the current government, pointing to his relationship with Vice President Jeremiah Koung, whom he described as a close friend, and suggesting the entire government and security apparatus around him would be implicated by the same logic if the rumors were true. He invited scrutiny rather than shying from it, telling reporters they were welcome to examine his house and his associates, and pushed back on the idea that a sitting senator should have to answer for online chatter with no formal notice behind it. He pivoted repeatedly back to his work in Margibi County — a hospital project he said he is hoping to see resourced and turned over this year, an ongoing school project in local communities, and a scholarship program supporting students in the county — framing himself as a public servant being distracted from real work by rumor rather than by any actual investigation. This newspaper cannot independently confirm or deny whether any government agency is examining McGill or other former CDC officials; no formal notice, charge, or confirmed investigation involving him has been made public.

Placed next to the Biago allegations, McGill’s press conference sharpens an uncomfortable comparison. An opposition senator felt compelled to publicly deny an investigation that has not been formally confirmed, while the government’s own drug agency chief faces a specific, documented allegation — a truck, a second vehicle, a name Kollie says he can prove — that has so far been met with denial rather than an independent review of the evidence either side claims to hold. Mark Kuiah remains uncharged more than two weeks after his own dismissal. Inspector General Coleman’s claim that trafficking was “sanctioned at very, very senior level” has never been followed by a name. Now the LDEA’s own leadership is the one asking the public to simply trust its denial.

What Happens Next

For now, the facts in dispute remain exactly that — disputed. Kollie says he has documentary proof. The LDEA says none exists. Biago says he neither received nor sanctioned receipt of the vehicle. No independent body has yet examined the registration records, photographs, or other evidence either side claims to have. That is precisely the gap Konneh, and others want an independent counsel to close.

Until then, Liberia is left with competing narratives about a truck — and a straightforward test of the president’s own words. Boakai did not say there would be no sacred cows except inside his own drug agency, or that the promise applied only to the political opposition and not to the man leading his government’s own war on narcotics. He said no one would be permitted to hide behind “public office… political influence… or any other position of authority.” An opposition senator has already had to answer, publicly and at length, for rumors that have not produced a single formal charge. Liberia’s actual drug chief, facing a specific, documented allegation involving two vehicles and a name Kollie says he can prove, has so far had to answer only with a denial. Whether that gap closes — or simply becomes the latest example of a sacred cow standing exactly where the president said none would be allowed to stand — is now his to decide.

World.title: After Three Weeks, Three Countries and One Broken Chain of Command, the IB Atlantic IV Is No Longer Liberia’s Alone to Find
World.content:
MONROVIA — For the better part of three weeks, the IB Atlantic IV existed mostly as a rumor with coordinates attached. It was a ship the government said it was watching, a ship whose engine trouble nobody could quite verify, a ship that drifted at 0.3 knots toward a port it wasn’t supposed to be near, flying a flag that asks almost nothing of the vessels that fly it. Liberians read about it in fragments — an anonymous government source here, a rejected letter there, a pursuit off Rivercess that didn’t end so much as move somewhere else.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

That fragment collecting is over. The IB Atlantic IV has been arrested in Ivory Coast, and for the first time since this saga began, the ship everyone was chasing is not the one deciding where it goes next.

It is Ivorian security forces who now decide that. Liberia is left to ask for it back.

A quieter ending than the chase deserved

There is something almost anticlimactic about how it ended. After Armed Forces troops pursued the vessel off Rivercess, after the Coast Guard admitted its boats simply weren’t built for a chase that went this far, after Nigerian partners were brought in to help track a ship Liberia couldn’t catch on its own — the capture came not from a Liberian deck but from a neighboring country’s port authority, acting on a warning Liberia itself had sent to Abidjan and Conakry.

That is not nothing. Liberia’s outreach to Ivory Coast and Guinea worked exactly as regional cooperation is supposed to work. But it also means the country’s own maritime enforcement — the Coast Guard, the National Security Agency, the Armed Forces chief of staff who was, by his own agency’s account, “personally monitoring” the situation for a week — never once had the ship in hand. Now the Liberia Maritime Authority is scrambling to arrange a Sea Shepherd Global escort just to bring the vessel home, the same partnership that has helped Liberian authorities make roughly twenty fishing-vessel arrests since 2017. It is a solution built for a different problem, repurposed now because Liberia has no faster one.

Whether narcotics were aboard the ship remains, as of this writing, unconfirmed. That single unanswered question is the hinge the entire story turns on — and Monrovia will not rest easy until it is answered.

The paper trail that came before the pursuit

To understand why this ship earned three weeks of national anxiety, it helps to go back to July 13, to a letter that, read today, sounds like a rehearsal for everything that followed.

That was the day Mark Egon Kuiah — then a deputy at Roberts International Airport, a man with no formal role in maritime affairs — wrote to the Liberia Maritime Authority not as a government official but as “registered agent” for a company called Madris Group of Companies Incorporated. The vessel he was writing about, he said, was in distress at sea, its engine performance compromised by “external obstruction affecting the vessel’s propeller.” It needed a berth. It needed a dive team.

LiMA said no. The agency’s reasoning, delivered plainly to this newspaper, was that the story didn’t add up: the ship hadn’t docked anywhere, was still sitting in Sierra Leonean waters, and yet was already being arranged for a Liberian welcome, as if the paperwork had gotten ahead of the emergency.

Weeks later, Kuiah was swept up in the same dismissal wave that has since widened into Liberia’s broader cocaine purge — a purge that has also ensnared the former commander of the Liberia Immigration Service post at Bo-Waterside and his deputy, both allegedly caught in March carrying suspected narcotics while trying to cross back from Sierra Leone.

The ship in Kuiah’s letter was the IB Atlantic IV.

A ship that told two different stories about itself

What makes the IB Atlantic IV genuinely strange is not that it was suspicious — plenty of vessels off West Africa’s coast are. It’s that the ship told two irreconcilable stories about itself at the same time, and neither matched what its own transponder was broadcasting.

One account, from an anonymous government source, placed it in distress off Sierra Leone, drifting toward Guinea-Bissau. Kuiah’s letter, filed a week earlier, told a third version entirely. And the ship’s Automatic Identification System — the transponder every large vessel must broadcast, showing position, speed, and declared destination — placed it in open West African waters, moving at a crawl, declaring a destination of Lomé, Togo. Not Sierra Leone. Not Guinea-Bissau.

A 41-year-old cargo ship, flagged in Comoros — a registry international shipping analysts describe as asking few questions of anyone — moving at less than a third of a knot is not a ship in transit. It is a ship waiting. And in the days after it first appeared, intelligence sources told FrontPageAfrica that a smaller, unidentified vessel approached it and appeared to attempt passing something aboard. Officials have never said what, or whether the attempt succeeded. But the detail reframes everything that came before it: not a disabled ship asking for mercy, but a ship parked at a fixed position, waiting for a delivery that Liberia’s institutions were too slow, or too divided, to intercept.

The week nobody was in charge

Ask three Liberian security institutions who was responsible for the IB Atlantic IV in its first days in Liberian waters, and — as this newspaper found when it tried — you get three different answers that all point somewhere else. LiMA said it had “information relative to the vessel” and had passed it along to the National Security Agency. The NSA said the Coast Guard was aware. The Coast Guard’s own chief of staff was, according to the NSA, personally monitoring the situation.

Everyone was watching. No one was catching.

That is the sentence this episode leaves behind, and it is the sentence Liberia’s Legislature should sit with before it advances a bill to break the National Port Authority into four separate regional operators.
