World.title: Australia to give bird flu vaccines to native species most at risk
World.content:
Australia’s most vulnerable native birds will be vaccinated against the H5N1 flu sweeping the nation, but challenges remain in protecting the poultry industry to prevent egg shortages. Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said on Tuesday the government had acquired $2 million worth of vaccines to inoculate about 1500 native animals in captivity that are most at risk from the disease. Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Julie Collins speaking at Parliament House, Canberra, on Tuesday morning. Alex Ellinghausen “We’ve been very clear that we cannot stop the H5 bird flu from spreading amongst wild birds, but we can take action to protect the species most at risk, and the vaccination is now part of that response,” Collins said. The escalation of the national response follows confirmation of the first mass casualty event last week and as deaths exceed 200. As the outbreak spreads, Collins said reporting would shift from counting dead birds to confirming major events and newly affected locations.



Collins said species would be prioritised for vaccination based on the needs of state and territory governments, which would announce which populations they would target in coming days. Environment Minister Murray Watt said wild birds may be vaccinated where possible, but doing so was difficult. “It does take two vaccination doses to vaccinate birds, and it is difficult enough to catch wild birds once, let alone twice,” Watt said. “The priority here is to vaccinate birds that are ... in our zoos and various other institutions.” Watt added that Australia had increased its populations of captive birds while bracing for the virus to hit as it spread around the globe.



Collins added the risk of the H5N1 strain to human health remained low and there was no evidence it had infected Australia’s poultry industry. “Overseas we have seen it spill over into agriculture, so we’re doing everything we can do to keep it out,” she said. Related Article Live

National News Live Australia news LIVE: Albanese tells Labor caucus he expects gambling bill to pass with Coalition support; Ministers back PM as scrutiny over ‘melons’ remark grows The government is examining whether vaccinating poultry is feasible, but a rollout would be complicated. Biosecurity measures, such as keeping poultry away from wild birds, will remain the first line of defence for farms, which are bracing for stock infections. “The vaccine itself is not 100 per cent protective,” Australia’s chief vet Beth Cookson said. “So even in flocks that are vaccinated, they can still have the virus introduced if their biosecurity is not keeping the infection out.”



She said infected birds would need to be killed even if vaccinated, and some countries had imposed restrictions on the export of vaccinated poultry. Cookson said the vaccine had been developed for poultry, and had been tested for efficacy and safety in different sizes and species of birds over 18 months. On the weekend, the first case of H5N1 bird flu in inland Australia was detected in western NSW, at the junction of the Murray and Darling rivers on the Victorian border. Experts say it is a sign the virus will spread rapidly across the continent. This strain has devastated wildlife populations overseas, leading to the deaths of millions of birds and mammals and first arrived in Australia in June from Antarctic seabirds. A jury has been discharged in a trial of a doctor accused of manslaughter after a woman gave birth at home and died of heavy blood loss.

Robyn Mary James, 67, had pleaded not guilty to the charge after Vicki Butler died the day she gave birth at her Ipswich home west of Brisbane.

Butler, 41, died as a result of a postpartum haemorrhage which she suffered between James’ arrival at 5am and when the doctor called an ambulance at 6.42am on December 27, 2017, the prosecution said.

Dr Robyn Mary James outside Brisbane Supreme Court. AAP

Photos retrieved from Butler’s phone showed she had given birth between 3.22am and 4.07am.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Brother of complainant ‘J’ gives evidence in former 2GB broadcaster’s alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day six of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Jacqueline Maley will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

Last week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Sam Mooy

Our live coverage was paused on Wednesday after Local Court Judge Glenn Walsh temporarily imposed a non-publication order on the cross-examination of the complainant, known as “J”, by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC. That order was lifted on Thursday afternoon.

“J”, now in his early 40s, denied under questioning by Bashir that he had a financial motive for making the allegations against Jones, and denied that they were a fabrication.

He has given evidence that Jones groped him as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls farm. “J” has also told the court that Jones had indecently assaulted him at the property after telling him to wear “a robe and nothing else”.

The complainant said he came forward to police after seeing reports about Jones’ arrest in November 2024 because he wanted justice.

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box for a sixth day. He will be re-examined by prosecutor Georgina Wright, SC, after his cross-examination concluded on Friday.

A man known as “C” will be the next complainant to give evidence.

Bashir asked “J” a series of questions about whether he read media reports containing similar allegations about Jones in 2023 before he spoke to police the following year. He said he did not.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing, and Bashir said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to the court.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: ‘First-world problem’: Why Wallabies star says Suaalii shouldn’t be pigeonholed
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies ‘First-world problem’: Why Wallabies star says Suaalii shouldn’t be pigeonholed Nick Wright Updated August 11, 2026 — 12:41pm ,first published August 10, 2026 — 9:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wallabies fullback Tom Wright believes versatility will prove both Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Australia’s greatest weapon, dismissing the notion the game’s $5 million man needed to be cemented in one position. Every pundit in rugby circles has had an opinion on where the former NRL star’s future must lie in the build-up to the 2027 Rugby World Cup, having been largely used in the centres but deployed at fullback for the Waratahs this year. In the latter stages of the Wallabies’ 35-32 triumph of Japan to launch a new era under coach Les Kiss, Suaalii was shifted from outside centre to the wing – the same position he began his rugby league career in, where his near two-metre tall physique made him a lethal aerial threat. Les Kiss speaks to Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii during a Wallabies training session. Getty Images Wright was asked in Brisbane if the 23-year-old’s long-term future rested in the flank or in the midfield, getting his hands on the ball more frequently.



“I think it depends what lens you want to put on it; if we leave it ambiguous they [our opposition] won’t know what we’re going to do, so that’s awesome. Being that talented is a first-world problem, for there to be so many opinions on it means he’s almost too good,” Wright said. Related Article Wallabies ‘Is this the end?’: Contract call twists fate for plagued Wallaby “Everyone has an opinion on someone who’s that talented and has brought so much good coverage to our game. I think the versatility we’ve got pretty much across the entire backline is something that potentially is a weapon for us, being able to change the point of attack. “I think ‘Su’ could jump in anywhere; you could mould him into an inside centre if you wanted, you could give him enough time to play five-eighth I think he’d jump at the opportunity to do that. “He’s going to be brilliant wherever we put him. There are so many opinions on it, so you can run with how you will, but he’s such a good player for us, and such a team-first guy – there’s no mention from him that he wants to do this, or doesn’t want to do this.”



While Wright conceded the victory against the Brave Blossoms was far from the polished performance the Wallabies had sought to put in place, he said there were signs Kiss’ philosophies would reap rewards between now and the World Cup. Since arriving at the Queensland Reds three years ago, Kiss has encouraged his players to trust their instincts and skill sets – pushing them to freely express themselves with the ball and backing their judgement. Loading That mentality led to five tries in sweltering Osaka conditions – the first three to outside backs Wright, Harry Potter and Max Jorgensen – but also yielded four unforced dropped balls between Wright, Aukuso-Suaalii and five-eighth Declan Meredith. However, Wright – speaking ahead of Saturday’s return bout with Japan in Townsville – remained undeterred, adamant the group would continue chancing their arm under Kiss’ tutelage, while continuing to develop an understanding of when to pull the trigger depending on the conditions.



“You want to be able to trust your instincts, you love having a coach and coaching staff from top to bottom who push that style of play as well. We speak about bringing the game back to how you grew up playing in the backyard, and that was all systems go,” Wright said. Related Article City life Rugby star on the family ties that bind him to Brisbane “You want to trust the first thing that comes into your mind, but understand we’re versing the best of the best in the world. To be able to think in the next five or 10 minutes what’s going to give us the best chance … finding that balance is probably what every team in world rugby is trying to chase. “The way the coaching staff here, directed by Les, give you that confidence to play what comes to mind, and then everyone getting on the same page and backing that first call, has been awesome.” Wallabies assistant coach Tom Donnelly also confirmed forward Tom Hooper would be available for selection, having overcome a shoulder injury suffered in last month’s loss to Ireland.



“He trained with his club team down in Canberra during the week and ticked off everything he needed to do to become available,” Donnelly said of the 25-year-old, who will join the Reds from Exeter in mid-2028 ahead of the 2029 Super Rugby campaign. “He’ll train with us fully this week.” The Hooper revelation came before lock Miles Amatosero was issued a three-match suspension, after the Foul Play Review Committee found him “guilty of dangerous play for a contrary charge into a ruck or maul” during the Japan clash. Loading The 24-year-old’s yellow card was later upgraded to red for his contact on Japan captain Warner Dearns, and the FPRC determined the act of foul play merited a mid-range entry point of six weeks. Amatosero’s foul play admission, his disciplinary history, experience and remorse led to a reduction in his suspension.



He was given permission to apply to take part in World Rugby’s Coaching Intervention Programme as a substitute for the final match of the sanction, which would make him available to take on Argentina on August 29. That has opened the door for Reds star Lukhan Salakaia-Loto to replace him, having been recalled into Kiss’ squad following his surprise omission from the group that took on Ireland, France and Italy under Joe Schmidt. World.title: Broadcasting Standards Authority upholds complaints about The Platform host Sean Plunket
World.content:
The Broadcasting Standards Authority has upheld two complaints about broadcasts on The Platform.

The first complaint was about morning talk show host Sean Plunket comparing tikanga Māori to "mumbo jumbo" while discussing Fire and Emergency New Zealand's Kaupapa Māori strategy on July 22 2025.

The second complaint was around comments made by Plunket on 15 October 2025 that ridiculed the complainant, shared his private information with listeners and led to abuse, harassment and threats.

Both complaints were upheld because they breached the Broadcasting Act's good taste and decency, privacy and law and order standards.

"The 'mumbo jumbo' comment, in itself, was unlikely to threaten standards of taste and decency. However, this was never just about calling tikanga mumbo jumbo. This remark was made amid comments throughout the broadcast that denigrated Māori, including the use of te reo Māori and consideration of tikanga by public sector organisations," the authority said.

During the October broadcast, Plunket disclosed the complainant's full name repeatedly during a series of disparaging remarks about him. Later that day, the BSA's correspondence was posted online by The Platform, including the complainant's name and email address.

"This was despite explicit notice that the information was not for publication, which should have been a signal that it contained private information. As a direct result of the broadcaster's actions, the complainant said he received a threatening email almost immediately and subsequently received many more abusive messages. The complainant is still the target of mocking and abusive comments online, even on unrelated matters," the authority said.

In March, the authority confirmed it had jurisdiction under the Broadcasting Act to consider a complaint about The Platform, the first formal complaint referral it has received about an online broadcaster since publishing its policy on online broadcasters in 2020.

The authority noted freedom of expression was a vitally important human right and the starting point of every decision it issued but said it always came with limits.

"Media entities, particularly those who reach a large audience, have the power to influence public opinion and behaviour. The complainant was singled out by name for ridicule and belittlement, and the broadcaster could reasonably be expected to foresee the threats and abuse that followed," the BSA said.

World.title: Remote Tokelauan atoll becomes temporary global comms hub
World.content:
For two weeks in November the remote Tokelauan atoll of Fakaofo will become a global communications hub.

The remote Tokelau atoll of Fakaofo is 3,380 to 3,790 kilometres northeast of New Zealand - the number of people who live on Fakaofo is just over 470. However, this tiny dot in the Pacific is one of amateur radio's most sought-after locations, and for two weeks in November will become a global communications hub.

In amateur radio, "DX" comes from telegraph shorthand: "D" for distance and "X" for the unknown or distant.

For about two weeks in November, DX enthusiasts from the Perseverance DX Group and the Western Washington DX Club will set up temporary stations on Fakaofo, giving radio operators around the world a rare chance to make contact with Tokelau.

Tokelau's project coordinator, Aleki Silao, said the idea for the project came about following a request in 2024 from a group who were keen to travel to Tokelau, in particular Nukunonu, to link up with colleagues around the world through shortwave radio. However, Fakaofo was selected because of its greater remoteness and the challenge that connecting it to the world would pose.

"And that's why this group expressed a special interest to bring their know-how and technology to Fakaofo for two weeks," Sialo explained.

Knowledge sharing

The Fakaofo team plans to operate several stations from the 160-to-6-metre amateur bands using voice, Morse code and digital modes.

When asked how the atoll will benefit from this project, Silao said it would be on numerous fronts.

"They have agreed to a number of things, training to pass on their knowledge in terms of this technology, furthermore they have offered to give twenty laptops through which Fakaofo may set up some internet cafes or even how the locals can communicate with the outside world."

For operators around the world, a confirmed contact with Tokelau is a prized achievement.

For Fakaofo, that global interest creates an unusual opportunity to exchange access and welcome for equipment, learning and enduring relationships.

Shortwave offers new possibilities

The group of 12 travelling to Fakaofo are mostly Americans and Europeans including retirees, doctors, pilots and computer experts.

This is not the first time a group of shortwave enthusiasts have visited Fakaofo - the last group visited in 2019.

"There are some reasons why the other two atolls (Nukunonu and Atafu) could not accommodate this visit, mainly because this year is the 100th year celebrating Tokelau under New Zealand, and of course the general fono, the parliamentary sessions, so Fakaofo was the most available island for them to go to," Silao said.

RNZI

The great benefit of the project is during times of disaster on the atolls, silao said.

"For example, in a cyclone or tsunami, when Teletok (Telecommunication Tokelau Corporation) or Starlink is out, this is the way to communicate with the rest of the world."

He said they hope to explore further opportunities in the future and share any knowledge with the other two atolls.

World.title: Tragic accident: Toddler who choked on drawing pin reminder about home safety
World.content:
The death of a toddler who choked on a drawing pin is a timely reminder to parents about safety around the home, a coroner says.

In his findings made public on Tuesday, coroner Ian Telford said Siuta Laulaupea'alu Uhi was aged a year and nine months on 21 November, 2025 when he was playing with his siblings in the loungeroom of the family home in the west Auckland suburb of Henderson.

Siuta's mother, Lisita Laulaupea'alu, then noticed her boy was choking.

He had a bag of lollies in his hand, so she turned him on his front and banged him on his back in an effort to clear his airway, the coroner said.

When that didn't work, his family put him in the car and drove towards the hospital in thick traffic.

They called emergency services and were instructed to return home, where paramedics would meet them.

Paramedics worked on Siuta and took him to hospital, but he could not be revived.

Coroner Telford referred to a post-mortem examination carried out by pathologist Dr Simon Stables, who found a drawing pin in the back of Siuta's throat.

The coroner said Siuta's death was a tragic accident.

"This death nevertheless serves as a reminder to us all of the serious and often unpredictable risk that small household objects can pose to young children," Telford said. "Everyday items such as drawing pins, coins, lollies, button batteries, magnets and other small objects can present a fatal choking hazard, if they are accessed by infants or toddlers.

"This may also be an opportunity for parents, caregivers and anyone responsible for the care of infants and young children to review current first aid guidance for responding to choking incidents.

"St John provides information and training resources on choking first aid - available online at Choking | Hato Hone St John.

World.title: Climate change adaptation not keeping pace with fast-growing risks - report
World.content:
Communities are being "left in limbo" by the government's unwillingness to decide how the country will pay for climate change adaptation, the Climate Change Commission's boss says.

In a report published on Tuesday, the commission said New Zealand's progress on adaptation was "patchy" and was not keeping pace with how fast the risks were growing.

While there had been some progress since its last update in 2024, delays on crucial issues such as funding were leaving communities exposed to greater damage, disruption and costs.

"The pace and scale of the action required is growing year by year," the report said.

"Sharp efforts to reduce future climate-related risk are needed to avoid an intensifying spiral of urgent response to extreme events without time between to fully recover."

It made six urgent recommendations, saying they were not "pick and mix" but must be put in place together.

Commission chief executive Jo Hendy said the government's next national adaptation plan was not due until 2028, but the commission was looking for progress on its recommendations earlier than that.

"There is a lot that people can do to reduce their risk to changing climate - the problem is, that lack of clarity around these fundamental areas is standing in the way."

Flooding in Cobden, in the north of Greymouth, July 2026 Supplied

Investing in proactive adaptation would help to reduce future costs and protect communities, but there were not enough resources available at the moment to do that, the report found.

Central government must first decide what it would and would not pay for itself, to make it clear what the funding gap would be.

Then it needed to work with local councils and the private sector to find new ways to fund and finance the remaining costs.

Some councils and communities had already developed plans, but were "being left in limbo because these building blocks have not been put in place", Hendy said.

"Some of these are hard decisions that need to be made, but delaying the hard decisions - kicking them down the road - doesn't actually make them go away. It increases the future cost and harm that we face."

The government currently contributed about 60 percent of disaster recovery costs after an event, Hendy said.

"But there's nothing comparable for proactive adaptation, even though we know acting proactively is much more cost-effective."

Last month, the government introduced legislation that would require councils to make adaptation plans for high-risk areas, at least 30 years into the future.

The commission said that was an important step, and partly addressed its second recommendation to require local adaptation planning.

However, without any decisions about who would pay, the proposed changes would "increase the gap between what is required and funds available to local government".

The government has repeatedly said it will defer any decisions about cost-sharing until the next parliamentary term.

Climate Change Minister Simon Watts. LDR / file

Climate Change Minister Simon Watts told RNZ last month that the government was not "head in the sand" about the potential costs, but it was the most complex and politically charged part of the adaptation challenge.

The commission said while the proposed requirements for local adpatation plans were positive, it was not clear how a high-priority location would be defined.

The report's other recommendations are that the government:

Embed climate change into laws governing the natural and built environment

Improve national climate change data and make it accessible and usable for all

Ensure iwi/Māori can plan for and carry out adaptation

Make the next national adaptation plan a stronger driver of action

This year's government Budget marked the end of funding for the Māori Climate Platform, which has helped to fund small-scale climate resilience projects at about 10 percent of the country's nearly 800 marae.

The final $1.4 million was allocated last month to four projects, in addition to $10.8m that had already been spent.

Hendy said there needed to be dedicated, ongoing funding for that work.

"After many of the flooding events, it's often the local marae that is providing support to the wider community," she said.

"We all benefit from Māori-led action."

There was also still work to do on the government's resource management reforms, to ensure they did not work at cross-purposes with climate adaptation planning.

"What we really want is for all decisions that people are making about the future to be properly considering what is going to be happening to our climate and the risks we will face," Hendy said.

"In that way, we build communities that are more resilient, rather than building the next climate disaster."

In a written statement on Tuesday, Watts said recent severe weather events had highlighted the challehnges facing communities across the country.

The government recognised the importance of being better prepared for the future and would carefully consider the commission's recommendations, he said.

"Our focus remains on practical action to help communities prepare for the impacts of climate change while protecting taxpayers' money," he said.

That included $200 million from the Regional Infrastructure Fund that had been invested in flood resilience, and $400 million allocated in this year's Budget to make the road network more resilient.

The government was also funding New Zealand's first national flood hazard map, which is due in its first iteration mid-next year.

World.title: Precautionary boil notice for Ohakune when water returns after 'good progress' made
World.content:
Ohakune residents will have to boil their tap water when it returns.

The central North Island town's been without water since Sunday due to damage to the pipeline caused by an earthquake more than two weeks ago.

It was originally expected the water network would return to normal on Monday evening, but that was pushed out by 24 hours. The outage has caused schools and eateries in the town to close, and the Ruapehu District Council has provided a water tank, containers of water and portaloos for the town's 1400 residents.

An update released by the Ruapehu District Council just before 12pm on Tuesday said "good progress is being made on recharging the Ohakune water network".

It also said a precautionary boil water notice would be in place when water returned until testing confirmed the water was safe to drink.

Residents were advised to boil water for two minutes and then allow it to cool before drinking or using for food preparation.

Colin Young fills a water bottle. RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Ruapehu Civil Defence controller Vini Dutra thanked Ohakune residents for their patience during the outage.

"Please continue to use water sparingly over the coming days so the reservoir can fully recover and pressure can be restored to normal levels," he said.

The council has asked residents to turn on outside taps and let them flow to help clear air from the pipes, while their inside ones were kept off.

"Taps may splutter when first turned on. This is just trapped air being released and is nothing to worry about," the council said.

"Water may also look milky. This is caused by air bubbles and is not a health concern. Low pressure may continue to be noticed until the reservoir has refilled several times."

What happened

The council's water services are contracted to Veolia.

A company spokesperson said on Tuesday afternoon the network was being flushed to make sure drinking water would be available as quickly as possible.

"The crack in the pipe caused by the earthquake remained undetected because no system data indicated a major leak," the spokesperson said.

"The leak was only discovered in dense bushland by a passing bush walker.

"Veolia took this seriously and responded immediately, as soon as it became aware of the crack, as this critical piece of infrastructure supplies water to the Ohakune Reservoir and is the town's only water supply," they said.

"If there had been a complete break it would have been far worse, with longer impacts."

Veolia worked quickly to repair the pipeline, in what it said was a hard-to-access area, and brought in extra staff from throughout New Zealand.

"The pipe was repaired quickly, but it is much more complex restarting the flow in a 7 kilometre-long, gravity-fed pipeline than simply switching on a garden hose.

"Air can become trapped if the water is simply switched back on at full capacity, which could cause pressure to build up and potentially lead to multiple breakages along its length."

The spokesperson said that air had to be cleared and the pipeline reopened in sections.

They thanked the community and said once the outage was resolved it would do a review of what happened and its processes.

On Tuesday, the council said it was too soon to answer questions about whether it could seek to fine or take other action against Veolia because of the outage, or whether closed businesses could get financial assistance.

"Far too early to answer that - we are still in response mode," a spokesman said.

"When the water is safely back on there will be a review of what happened ... and those issues will be looked at then."

A water truck in Ohakune supplying drinking water. RNZ / Kate Pereyra

School stays shut, businesses scramble

Ruapehu College remained closed on Tuesday.

Principal Kris Vine said staff were staying in touch with the school's 250 students.

He was waiting on more information so he could plan the school's reopening, and communicate information to students' families.

"Most students are probably not too disappointed with not coming to school, to a certain extent, but I know that they'll be missing their mates and, obviously, there's the realisation of what water means to a community," he said.

"It's probably a nice little learning curve and a timely reminder about emergency planning and that kind of stuff for whānau that are dealing with it."

Students from places such as Waimarino or Raetihi weren't affected by the outage.

"I'm just here waiting for phone calls and checking in on any updates and things," Vine said.

"It's a nice little admin day, so to speak, but also a bit of a sit-and-wait kind of day, which is long."

At The Peaks Motor Inn, manager Remi Butler previously told RNZ the motel had taken a financial hit when a large group booking cancelled.

After the council confirmed the water would be out until Tuesday evening, she said she was disappointed and stressed by the news.

She said she and her husband were even contemplating buying a pump to get river water to flush toilets at the motel.

World.title: Various Vogel's bread recalled due to the possible presence of small pieces of metal
World.content:
Various Vogel's breads are being recalled due to the possible presence of small metal pieces.

New Zealand Food Safety (NZFS) said it was supporting Goodman Fielder New Zealand Ltd in its recall of various Vogel's brand breads in the South Island as the products could contain foreign matter.

"The concern with these products is that they may contain small metal pieces," NZFS deputy director-general Vincent Arbuckle said.

"If you have a Vogel's bread bought in the South Island with a best-before date of 15 August, please check it against the recalled products list. If it's one of the bread varieties listed, don't eat it. You can return it to the place of purchase for a refund. If that's not possible, throw it out."

The affected loaves were sold at stores across the South Island and included:

Vogel's Original Mixed Grain Very Thin (750g)

Vogel's Original Mixed Grain Sandwich (750g)

Vogel's Original Mixed Grain Toast (750g)

Vogel's Dark Rye Toast (720g)

Vogel's Sprouted Whole Grain Toast (720g)

Vogel's Fruit and Spice Extra Thick (720g)

World.title: Former inmate says Mt Eden Prison should become crime museum
World.content:
Former inmate calling for old Mount Eden Prison to be preserved Morning Report Download MP3 4m

When 23-year-old Greg Newbold shuffled under the imposing rocky archway, it felt like he was stepping into the past.

"I was really shocked when I first went in there," he said. "I mean, I was from Auckland and I'd driven past the prison many, many times, but it looked like a medieval dungeon.

"I said, 'What's this?', and [my co-offender] said, 'This is the remand wing'. I said, 'What? You mean, this is where we stay?'

"He said, 'Yep'."

The now-author and retired sociology professor was arrested for dealing heroin in 1975, and remanded at the old Mt Eden Prison for five months, before he was moved to Pāremoremo to serve his sentence.

He remembered the awful conditions.

A general view of the Mount Eden prison 1900. Auckland Libraries Heritage Collections/Auckland Weekly News

"It had high windows, which had no glass in them, because the glass had been smashed, and it just had bars," Newbold recalled.

"In the winter time, pigeon feathers would fly in, because the pigeons used to roost there, and you'd quite often get lice in your blankets.

"There was no plumbing in the prison either. You had to piss in a piss pot."

Constructed as a timber stockade in 1856, the prison's stony exterior was built up over the next 60 years, using volcanic rock mined by the prisoners from Mt Eden itself.

The damp and rugged cells held inmates until 2011, when the last prisoners were moved next door to the new Mt Eden Corrections Facility.

Since then, historian Mark Derby said it had fallen into disrepair.

"When I last saw the prison, it was in an obviously decaying state," Derby recalled from researching his 2020 book Rock College.

"It has been closed now for quite a few years. Nothing's been done to it, it's been sitting empty.

"Clearly, some decision has to be made as soon as possible about this."

Despite some bad memories, Newbold said it should become a museum.

"Oh, it's a museum, it's unbelievable," he said. "There's so much history in that institution and it's a relic of a past era.

"It should never, ever be pulled down."

Mt Eden Prison entry 1900. Auckland Libraries Heritage Collections/Auckland Weekly News

"They could do it relatively cheaply and they could make money out of it, because people would love to see inside that place."

The prison was a treasure trove of historical misadventures, Newbold said, including a rumoured explosive escape attempt.

"In 1931, the inmates at Mt Eden, who worked in the quarry, they used to get gelignite and bring it in underneath their fingernails, and then scrape the gelignite out," he recounted.

"Finally, they had enough gelignite to create a big blast and they blasted a hole right through the f**king prison wall - right through the wall - and two guys escaped."

Derby suspected that particular escapade had been exaggerated over the decades, but said prison breaks were common.

"It was very easy to escape, but not at all easy to remain at large once you're outside the walls," he said.

"Guys used to do it more or less for a break in routine, knowing that they'd be stuck in solitary for a few weeks on bread and water, once they got back."

The prison's colourful history also contained much darker shades.

Derby recalled the 'Lock Hospital', a short-lived wing of the prison that kept people with contagious diseases against their will in the late 19th century.

Mt Eden Prison corridor with celldoors. Auckland Libraries Heritage Collections/Auckland Weekly News

"Most of the patients at the Lock Hospital were sex workers," he said. "The youngest I found on record was 13.

"She would have been regarded as the one at fault - the malefactor - not the clients who were responsible for her medical condition."

Derby said many of the people held at Mt Eden Prison wouldn't be considered criminals today.

"Male homosexuals held for consensual sex as adults were in there," he said. "Alcoholics were held there for no other reason than they were a nuisance on the streets.

"We have a lot to learn about the past and it can give us plenty of pointers for the future, I think."

Derby said that uncomfortable history was precisely why the building should be preserved and opened for public viewing.

He said many former inmates he had interviewed felt the same way.

"Sometimes, I would ask them, 'What do you think should happen to it?' They all said that they didn't want to see it demolished, that even though they thought it was a terrible place where terrible things had happened, that wasn't a sufficient reason to see it knocked down.

"It would be a marvellous base to construct a museum from."

A Department of Corrections spokesperson shot down the idea.

"The old prison sits within the confines of the new, fully operational prison, which would pose challenges for use such as a public museum," they said.

World.title: Workers in University of Otago building exposed to asbestos for years
World.content:
This story has been updated to clarify that the University of Otago's asbestos coordinator is not a new role.

University of Otago has carried out remediation work at one of its buildings after workers complained they were unwittingly exposed to potentially hazardous asbestos for about eight years.

Electricians and maintenance staff working in the Adams Building learned about the "high material risk contamination" through a 2018 report, according to incident forms lodged in February and released under the Official Information Act.

The contaminated material was within the building's plant rooms and risers, or utility shafts, which is home to the Department of Public Health.

The university has since had the material removed and the area inspected by a registered consultant.

Workers told the university's health and safety office it should have restricted access and removed the material much earlier.

One said they had been in the plant rooms daily for three years without knowing it was potentially unsafe and another said they would stay out of the rooms until they saw a negative asbestos test.

A third person said they came across the hazard assessment while they were on shift one day.

"I would like it to be noted that I in the course of my duties have been in both these plant rooms hundreds of times and have most definitely disturbed the suspect lagging in the bottom plant room. At no time have I been informed of an asbestos risk in either of these rooms," the person said.

In a statement, a University of Otago spokesperson said the contaminated areas could only be accessed by a small number of authorised personnel, not students, the public or non-maintenance staff.

The 2018 report showed material in the rooms "had a high potential for fibres to be released if the material is disturbed," the spokesperson said.

"At the time, this was recorded in the asbestos register, which was available to be viewed by our trades services staff and external contractors with access to the plant rooms and risers," they said.

"While available, it was not readily accessible. To enable our trades services staff to be better informed about asbestos containing material, we invested in upgrading our digital systems earlier this year so that information was more easily obtainable. When trade services staff in the Adams Building saw this information, they followed protocol and logged concerns via our health and safety register."

The university responded immediately by temporarily closing the plant room and carrying out further testing with a consultant who determined it was "safe to continue regular activities", the spokesperson said.

"A clearance certificate was issued in May when the asbestos-containing material was removed."

Asbestos generally only presented a health risk through exposure to airborne fibres, the spokesperson said.

"There is no evidence that this has happened in the plant rooms, risers or elsewhere in the building. We have regularly monitored air quality in the Adams Building for the past eight years and no test has indicated that any airborne asbestos risk was present," they said.

An asbestos coordinator position, advertised by the university in March, has since been filled.

A job description showed the asbestos coordinator would be responsible for organising safety surveys, keeping the university's official asbestos register up to date and communicating any risk of exposure to workers and contractors before they entered campus buildings.

The position was not created in response to the Adams Building remediation work, the unviersity said.

"The University of Otago employs specialist staff with expertise in asbestos management, which has included a role responsible for asbestos health and safety, for several years."

World.title: 'Evidence is clear': Players association says brutal schedule behind injuries
World.content:
The Professional Tennis Players Association (PTPA) believes a string of withdrawals from the Canadian Open underscore concerns that professional tennis's lengthy calendar and expanded top-level events are increasing injury risks.

The players' advocacy group said it was saddened but not surprised by the absences from the tournament, arguing that reduced recovery time between tournaments was contributing to injuries occurring earlier in the season and becoming more serious.

The Canadian Open men's event in Montreal was hit by the withdrawals of world number one Jannik Sinner and 24-time grand slam champion Novak Djokovic, while Carlos Alcaraz was also sidelined with a wrist injury. Hometown favourite Felix Auger-Aliassime also pulled out due to a back injury before his opening match.

On the women's side, defending champion Victoria Mboko, Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova, Emma Raducanu and Jasmine Paolini are also missing the tournament with injuries.

The first quarterfinal matches of the tournament begin later on Tuesday AEST.

Tournament organisers said last month that recurring late withdrawals from Masters 1000 events had become a wider issue for the sport.

PTPA says 'evidence is clear'

The PTPA said it had collected and analysed injury data from more than 30,000 professional matches across all levels of the game over the past eight years in a project launched three years ago with its medical director, Dr Robby Sikka.

'Not ready to compete': Sinner pulls out of tournament ahead of US Open Men's tennis world number one Jannik Sinner pulls out of the Cincinnati Open with a right knee injury, handing the Italian a blow in his preparations for this month's US Open.

"The evidence is clear: the season is too long, recovery time is shrinking, and injuries are occurring earlier and becoming more severe," the PTPA said in a statement posted on social media.

The group said upper-body injuries were up 42 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, according to its analysis. Arm injuries were up 112 per cent this year compared with the 2025 average, it added.

The ATP expanded seven of its nine Masters 1000 tournaments to 12-day events under its OneVision strategic plan, with 2025 the first season in which the longer format was used across those events.

The PTPA said the change had cut into the time players have to rest, train and travel between tournaments, despite players having voiced concerns about the demands of the schedule for years.

"Short-term commercial interests cannot come at the expense of player health," the association said. "Protecting players isn't just about today's competitors, it is about protecting the future of tennis."

Schedule the players' choice

The ATP has previously said players retain choices over their schedules and that it is working to create incentives for an appropriate number of matches to be played during the season.

Spokespeople for the ATP and WTA Tours did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The PTPA called for the sport to take a player-health and data-driven approach to restructuring the calendar.

It said players should have a meaningful role in shaping the schedule, while mandatory tournament commitments should be reduced to allow adequate recovery.

It also urged the ATP to consider reversing the 12-day Masters 1000 format.

Reuters

World.title: Bird flu drives a 50 per cent cost increase for badminton players
World.content:
While bird flu has only landed on Australian shores in the last few months, a group of sportsmen and women have been feeling its impact for years.

The deadly strain of H5 avian influenza has riddled wild and domesticated avian species across the world, with the total number of dead birds in the hundreds of millions.

While the spread of the disease has Australians across science and agriculture increasingly concerned, the nation's badminton players have long counted its costs.

The mass culling of flocks of geese and poultry across east and central Asia in recent years has massively cut the global supply of feathers critical to making the shuttlecocks needed for any game of the racquet sport to go ahead.

Countries across the world have culled birds to manage H5N1 outbreaks. (Reuters: Luc Gnago)

Shuttlecock shock

The impact has seen equipment costs skyrocket for badminton clubs across the country.

A high-quality shuttlecock uses 16 feathers from the left wing of either a duck or a goose, though each bird can only supply two to three feathers that meet specifications.

China is home to most of the world's poultry farms where the specific feathers are harvested, leaving the product exposed to major price fluctuations pinned to the health of the birds.

Goose feathers are at a premium as healthy flocks become rarer. (ABC Great Southern: Eliza Kavanagh)

Badminton Australia chief executive Tjitte Weistra says even a mid-range shuttle, such as the Yonex AS-30, has become near-unaffordable for most players and clubs.

"A decade ago a tube of a dozen AS-30s would sit from $30 to $35. That's now well over $70," he said.

"This means the cost of hosting a tournament or even club play can get very, very expensive."

Tjitte Weistra said synthetic shuttles are not yet good enough for most players. (Supplied: Tjitte Weistra)

Great Southern Badminton Association chair Michelle Watson said her organisation spends $3,000 on shuttles every four to six months.

Nightly fees have had to rise to maintain quality equipment with synthetic alternatives not an option.

Michelle Watson (right) says increasing costs have been challenging for local players. (Supplied: Michelle Watson)

"Feathers are what the game should be played with and are far superior," she said.

"Players that understand the game and play more than at a social level expect quality shuttles.

" I believe synthetics will be the way of the future due to feathers being unsustainable [but] they are currently not close to where they need to be to be an appropriate option. "

WA players particularly hard-hit

Metamorph Shuttle director Ryan Zengyuan said WA's near-total reliance on imported equipment left local players even more exposed.

"An agricultural supply crash in Asia instantly triggers inventory shortages and doubles prices for local players," Mr Zengyuan said.

"[As a result] local sport retailers have been forced to increase retail prices by 30 to 50 per cent over the last few years to cover the skyrocketing cost of raw feathers and international freight."

Players say you cannot replicate the flight of natural feather shuttles. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

While bird flu has decimated the global feather market, freight costs, oil prices and competition for the cork used in the head of the shuttle are additional factors in the rising prices.

Seeking alternatives

Mr Weistra said local clubs are starting to look at alternative options to curb the price rise, including players making peace with synthetic shuttles.

"They're trying to get cheaper feather shuttles which don't have the same characteristics," he said.

" In the past, they just weren't open to it because the crisis wasn't big enough. But now the cost is becoming really prohibitive. "

"I guess they are inclined to look at alternative options and accept that maybe they're not perfect, but it will do for now."

World.title: Major football bodies pen letter seeking Infantino exit over 'deception'
World.content:
UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC believe FIFA President Gianni Infantino's recent plan to sell an interest in the World Cup was a "fundamental breach of trust" with the institutions world soccer's governing body serves.

In an "open letter to the football family", the governing bodies also said that "when trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned."

UEFA runs football in Europe, CONCACAF does the same for North, Central America and the Caribbean, while the AFC governs the sport in Asia.

FIFA pledges 'full support' for Infantino and apologises for sell-off plan FIFA has reiterated its support for embattled president Gianni Infantino, while apologising to its member associations for the aborted bid to sell off stakes in the World Cup.

The letter was co-signed by UEFA President Aleksander Čeferin, AFC President Salman Bin Ibrahim Al-Khalifa, CONCACAF President Victor Montagliani and three general secretaries.

"Football is the world's greatest shared passion. It belongs to no individual and no institution. It belongs to the players, the fans, the clubs, the member associations and every institution entrusted with safeguarding its future," the open letter said.

"It is in that spirit, as confederations representing its members, that we speak collectively today."

Infantino is facing a revolt after his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private equity investors.

"It is not the conduct of a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him," the letter said.

"These are not the qualities football deserves in its leadership. That is why we have taken this stance: not lightly and not alone, but together, and out of duty to the game we serve."

Australia's Socceroos also fall under the AFC, which has spoken out against Infantino. (Getty Images: Xinhua/Ziyu Julian Zhu)

UEFA previously issued a threat to boycott the World Cup and other FIFA competitions despite the governing body abandoning and apologising for its failed plan.

Norway's football federation called for Infantino to step down, while the English Football Association has also withdrawn its support for his re-election next March.

"Football's strength has always been its unity. We call for that unity to be honoured now," the letter said. "For leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it."

Last Wednesday, FIFA said it had apologised for errors made over the failed plan but that senior staff at a crisis meeting in Morocco "reaffirmed their full support" for his presidency.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

However, the nature of the meeting was also met with criticism.

"FIFA's own letter also confirms that only one elected official was present at the leadership meeting in Morocco," the open letter said.

"No FIFA Council members or Member Associations were invited to participate. Only the management committee, composed of FIFA-employed senior staff, was present."

FIFA was also urged to go further than just acknowledging mistakes were made.

"It treats this as a failure of communication, when what football witnessed was a failure of judgement," the letter said.

"There remains no recognition that attempting to sell an interest in the FIFA World Cup was a profound failure of judgement — not just a procedural misstep, but a fundamental breach of trust with the very institutions FIFA exists to serve."

In a statement Saturday, FIFA defended Infantino against what it called a "concerted and ongoing effort" to undermine his leadership of the organisation.

That statement followed a report by British newspaper The Daily Telegraph raising questions about an exit package paid by UEFA to a female staffer who worked with Infantino when he was general secretary of European soccer's ruling body.

UEFA confirmed a "departure payment" was made to the employee and said it was "in line" with regulations at the time.

Infantino worked at UEFA for 16 years before being elected FIFA president.

AP

World.title: Big Tex leaves big impact on and off the field
World.content:
Taylor Walker's legacy is littered with athletic greatness and career-defining goals but his impact off the field and in the community makes him a true champion.

Nineteen years ago, a boy from Broken Hill with tips in his hair and a room littered with Crows posters crossed the border to pursue a dream.

The man affectionately known as Tex, after Chuck Norris' iconic character, was a 75-kilogram prospect who'd only ever wanted to be a footballer.

"When I arrived here as a skinny kid from Broken Hill, I never imagined where this journey would take me," Walker said on Monday.

"Football has given me so much but more than anything it's given me people."

Walker — who yesterday announced he would be retiring at season's end — was the final pick in the 2007 draft, but had to wait as Melbourne and Fremantle passed their final selections before the Adelaide Crows took a punt on an injured prospect who had been injured riding his motocross bike shortly after making the NSW Under-16 squad.

Walker joined the Crows as a "skinny kid from Broken Hill". (Supplied: Gavin Schmidt)

What followed was a rollercoaster journey of growth, leadership and legacy.

"His stats tell a story … but that is just part of his story," Crows CEO Tim Silvers said on Monday.

"He's been a great person, a wonderful leader, and he's led through the ups and downs of our footy club. He's led with strength, resilience, passion and determination.

" We're really proud of what he's done, the human he's become and the family man he is. "

Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks echoed those sentiments, saying Walker's legacy at West Lakes is the greatest of any Crow in club history.

"I don't think there's been anyone bigger, when you talk about the impact he's had — not just on football, but on this state and our supporter base," Nicks said.

An emerging talent

It was a perfect storm that landed Walker at West Lakes. The AFL was eager to expand its growth areas in New South Wales and launched a scholarship program requiring clubs to take two players from the state.

Junior scout Mark Ross was sent to the region and caught a glimpse of a young man who would become Adelaide's all-time leading goalkicker.

Thankfully for recruiting boss Hamish Ogilvie, his injury meant no-one else got to see his potential ahead the draft.

Walker takes a mark in front of Port Adelaide's Paul Stewart during a 2011 Showdown. (AAP Image: Ben Macmahon)

It wasn't all smooth sailing for the soon-to-be seven-time leading goalkicker. After kicking over 50 goals in the SANFL for Norwood, Walker was given a debut against Collingwood in the first round of 2009, recording five touches and a goal in a thrilling four-point win.

But his 14-game debut season ended in the reserves and numerous omissions in 2010 as the young forward clashed with coach Neil Craig over his defensive pressure.

Premiership Crow and former Adelaide board member Rod Jameson remembers his treatment being unique for key forwards at the time.

"Neil Craig made it hard for him. They sent him back to work on his defensive game which was rarely heard of then," Jameson said.

" He'd go back and still kick numerous goals. We all knew there was talent there but it was the timing and consistency. "

There were rumours of a move to expansion club GWS and an omission after being caught on live TV drinking a beer at the SANFL — but the appointment of Brenton Sanderson as Adelaide's head coach in 2012 proved a turning point.

Walker watches from the player's bench after injuring his knee in 2013. (Joe Castro: AAP Image)

A 63-goal season led to a runner-up finish in the Coleman Medal and it felt like South Australia's next big thing had arrived, but an ACL injury early in 2013 was a devastating blow.

"I always tried to look at it glass half full … you've always got a choice to make. You can sit and sulk and look at the negatives or get on with life and do something about it," Walker said.

"You go through challenges in your career that make you want to get better."

Securing the captaincy

Walker's optimism and determination saw him return early in the 2014 season and inspired his teammates to appoint him captain the following year.

His first season at the helm was one of the most difficult any leader could have faced, with the tragic death of senior coach Phil Walsh.

But Walker was able to unite a shattered playing group and guide them into three consecutive finals series that culminated in the club's first grand final in 20 years and back-to-back AFLPA best captain awards.

The Crows got close to a premiership in 2017, but Richmond proved too good on the day. (AAP: Julian Smith)

Jameson recalls Walker's maturity and guidance in the club's darkest period being an inspiration to a devastated community.

"At heart he's a larrikin … [but] he says and does things that the group is able to follow, and it's a special trait," he said.

"The passing of Walshy and the grand final hardship … it wasn't easy but that's how you learn.

"He's just a ripping bloke. It's what good clubs are made of — they're the building blocks you want in the club. To build connections and catchers, he's gone about it his way and it's been an incredible career."

Walker himself believed the experience gave him perspective and pride.

"One of Walshy's favourite sayings was just get the job done," Walker said.

"If he was looking down he would've been incredibly proud of what we were able to do in that time.

" Life is hard, it's challenging. Things happen that you can't control. Don't take it too seriously. Have fun along the way because it's so short. "

Challenges on and off the field

Entering 2020, the winds of change had struck West Lakes, with coach Don Pyke stepping aside for Matthew Nicks, and Walker handing over the captaincy to Rory Sloane.

Walker faced concerns over his own future, battling a knee injury and engulfed in a racism scandal that saw him suspended for six matches for delivering a slur to North Adelaide's Robbie Young.

"That was an incredibly difficult time for my family and … I learned that words don't just hurt one person, they can hurt so many different people," he said on Monday.

"I'm a better person for that mistake I made. I wish it never happened but also I feel like I'm better for it."

Walker shakes hands with North Adelaide's Robbie Young in the aftermath of the 2021 incident. (Adelaide Football Club)

A refreshed strength and conditioning program not only wound back the clock but saw Walker soar to career highs, with a 76-goal season in 2023 and his first All-Australian blazer.

Firmly in the premiership window after a minor premiership in 2025, Walker was hell-bent on helping the club break its near three-decade long drought but as the injuries rose and the weekly recovery got harder, the decision arrived at 3am last Tuesday.

"The closer I've gotten to the end it's probably become more evident it might be this year but I've treated it like my last year for the past six years," Walker said.

"I knew it was the right time for me and the football club to retire at the end of the year, hopefully with a premiership medallion around my neck.

"I might go out with a bang."

Walker celebrates a Showdown victory in 2018. (Getty Images: AFL Media/James Elsby)

Leaving a legacy

Walker's influence and impact will forever be etched into South Australian footy folklore, with a club record 706 goals and counting, and over 300 games that will see him finish third all-time.

"He's up there with the greats of the club. His impact, his longevity and his leadership," Jameson said.

"When you reflect on the stats and what he's been able to accomplish — he puts himself up in the elite category."

"Everyone sees the goals and big moments but those who have worked closely with Tex know the care he has for his teammates, our coaches and staff, and the club," Nicks said.

"He's someone who led through actions as much as words. He was prepared to stand up when things were going well and, importantly, he stood tall when they weren't."

Taylor Walker and Crows coach Matthew Nicks in 2020. (AAP: David Mariuz)

A clash with the ladder-leading Fremantle Dockers awaits Friday night as the Crows fight for a top-four finish, but when it's all said and done Walker will finish thankful for the opportunity to represent his childhood club.

"I've had three loves in my life — my family, my friends and footy," he said.

"I want to go back [to Broken Hill] and win a premiership there. Coaching is on the radar but I want to take a deep breath.

World.title: Dog hurt in race marketed as opposing Tasmania's racing ban
World.content:
A greyhound has suffered a fall and injury at a regional New South Wales race named in solidarity with Tasmania's racing industry, which faces a possible statewide ban.

WARNING: This story contains images that may cause distress for some readers.

It was race two on Sunday night in the town of Temora.

The race, named "We Stand With Tasmania Pathways", was a 330-metre dash to the finish for seven greyhounds.

Five-year-old greyhound Manila Shelby bolted from the box and collided with another dog at the first turn.

She was flung into the side metal barrier and struggled to get back up.

A stewards' report from the night said it was likely she broke her shoulder blade and injured her "tricep".

A Greyhound Racing NSW spokesperson later said the trainer took his dog to the vet the following day and an examination and x-rays showed no fractures.

Manila Shelby was given oral medication and will not be able to race for several weeks, vet notes shared by Greyhound Racing NSW showed.

The race replay video has been deleted from the state's racing website.

On a prominent betting site, the race replay has also been edited to exclude the fall.

It is one of several races called "We Stand With Tasmania" that have resulted in falls and injuries.

Loading...

On December 22, 2025, during race three at Maitland in NSW, Hey Pat fell and sustained a serious foreleg fracture.

The greyhound is now listed as deceased.

Two greyhounds fell on October 20 last year during race one in Nowra, NSW.

And during race five in Warragul, Victoria, on October 23, Collinda Blinder fell and tumbled after the first turn.

Printed caps in support of Tasmania's greyhound industry have been spotted track-side. (Supplied)

The race where Manila Shelby was injured has been uploaded to Greyhound Racing SA's website.

In Tasmania, when a dog is injured on the track, a video of the race is never uploaded.

The Tasmanian industry's peak body Tasracing said this decision is made out of respect to the industry, as well as the greyhound trainer and animal involved.

Tasmanian Greens animal rights spokesperson Cassy O'Connor said the race was "horrible viewing" and "characteristic of the dangerous conditions greyhounds are forced to race in".

"This is happening in our name as Tasmanians," Ms O'Connor said.

"Manila Shelby isn't the first greyhound to be injured in mainland races under the 'Stand With Tasmania' banner, and sadly, she won't be the last.

"But we have the power to stop greyhounds being put in harm's way in this state."

Five-year-old greyhound Manila Shelby sustained injuries during a race in Temora, New South Wales, on August 9, 2026. (Supplied)

The greyhound races authorities don't want you to see If you watched greyhound race videos on Tasracing's website, you would likely never know that dozens of dogs were injured or killed during events last year.

The state government has committed to cutting funding to the industry from 2029, which coincides with the end of the current funding deal for the code.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said in August last year "it was time to make a call on the future of the sport", and he "continues to be concerned about animal welfare".

"It's time to draw a line in the sand and ensure an orderly exit from greyhound racing in Tasmania," Mr Rockliff said at the time.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff with a greyhound (Facebook: Jeremy Rockliff)

Legislation to phase out the industry passed the Tasmanian parliament's lower house in December 2025, but was pulled from the upper house after the state government feared it didn't have the numbers to pass.

"Greyhound racing is out of step with community expectations. It does not prioritise animal welfare," Tasmanian Liberal MP Marcus Vermey said.

Tasmanian Labor continues to support the industry.

Editor's note 11/8/26: A previous version of this story said the greyhound Manila Shelby was 'badly injured' based on a stewards report that mentioned suspected fractures. Greyhound Racing NSW later provided a statement and vet notes and the story was updated to reflect that a fracture was not found.

World.title: Former championship winning team cut from A-Leagues
World.content:
Western United has had its A-Leagues participation agreement terminated, effectively ending any flicker of hope of the troubled club making a return.

United has essentially been an A-Leagues club in name only for more than a year amid varied financial woes, which included not paying players and staff.

The club was placed into hibernation by the Australian Professional Leagues (APL) in September 2025, with A-League Men and Women players having to scramble to continue their careers elsewhere.

Ownership West Melbourne Group avoided a wind-up order from the Australian Tax Office in January by settling a $15.5 million tax debt.

Football Australia declined to reinstate the Tarneit-based club's licence in May and United again won't participate in either the ALM or ALW.

West Melbourne Group have another wind-up hearing in the Federal Court on Tuesday and on Monday the APL officially terminated their participation agreement in the A-League competitions.

Western United won the A-League Men's grand final in 2022. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

"Since the club was placed into conditional hibernation in September 2025, the APL has been in close consultation with Western United as they've worked through financial, governance and legal matters to try and rebuild the club," APL chair Stephen Conroy said in a statement.

"The APL board has since taken the decision to terminate Western United's club participation agreement.

"The club was in breach of a number of its obligations under that agreement, including its obligation to comply with the Football Australia National Club Licensing Regulations.

"It's been a difficult period for everyone connected to Western United — and we want to acknowledge the management, staff, players and especially the fans — who have given so much to the club and will no doubt be hurt by this news."

Sadness after Western United licence removal Western United fans have expressed their disappointment and sadness after the team was stripped of its A-League licence late last week.

AAP understands United still owes some of its former players and staff money.

United was granted a licence in 2018, off the back of grand promises to build its own stadium, entered the A-League Men ahead of the 2019-20 season and won the ALM championship in 2021-22.

A women's team followed in 2022-23 and reached the grand final in their first season.

United has consistently been defiant and adamant it will return to the A-Leagues.

When put into hibernation, the club claimed it wasn't a "step back".

Western United finally opened their small Ironbark Fields ground in 2024. It saw just one season of A-League football. (Getty Images: MB Media/Santanu Banik)

After the tax debt was paid in January, the club declared its ambition to seal a "strong return to the A-Leagues".

Despite the latest development, the club on Monday broadcast plans to return in a year's time under new ownership.

"Over recent months, we have worked closely with the APL on a pathway that gives the club the best opportunity to survive, rebuild and return to the A-League under new ownership," United said in a statement on Monday.

"This creates an opportunity for new custodians, new investment and a fresh start.

"The objective must now be to preserve Western United's identity in Melbourne's west and work towards a return to the A-League for the 2027-28 season.

"This should not be the end of Western United. It should be the reset that allows the club to rebuild and return stronger."

AAP

World.title: Injury could rule Socceroos defender out of Asian Cup
World.content:
Socceroos defender Cameron Burgess's Asian Cup hopes appear in jeopardy following a possible Achilles injury while playing for Swansea City.

The towering central defender played every minute of the gruelling English Championship campaign last season.

That made for 4,140 minutes, plus stoppage time, across all 46 league matches.

But there are fears Burgess's season is over after he limped off late in Swansea's 1-0 League Cup loss to Birmingham City.

In the 87th minute he challenged for a header, landed awkwardly and grabbed at his right lower leg, prompting his Birmingham opponents to check on him.

The 30-year-old, who has 29 Socceroos caps, headed to hospital for scans.

Cameron Burgess played against Türkiye and the USA for the Socceroos at the World Cup. (Getty Images: Richard Heathcote)

"It doesn't look good, but I prefer to wait for the assessment we will do," Swansea head coach Vítor Matos said.

"It could be related to the Achilles, but let's see."

If Burgess has ruptured his Achilles, he faces a significant stint on the sidelines, ending his Asian Cup hopes.

Losing Burgess ahead of tournament, to be held in Saudi Arabia early next year, is a significant blow to Australia's defensive stocks.

Burgess lost his starting spot to teen sensation Lucas Herrington during the World Cup, with coach Tony Popovic preferring a back three involving the teenager, Harry Souttar and Alessandro Circati.

But as a left-footer, Burgess is always a valuable part of Popovic's squad.

Souttar spent more than a year on the sidelines after his own Achilles tear, while wing-back Lewis Miller is on the comeback trail from the same injury, which ruled him out of World Cup contention.

Star wing-back Jordan Bos is sidelined until about October after having surgery on the left knee injured in Australia's round-of-32 loss to Egypt.

The Socceroos are next in action for friendlies against Brazil in Townsville on September 25 and Brisbane four days later.

AAP

World.title: Head aims to maintain opening spot ahead of busy 12 months
World.content:
Travis Head can envisage himself continuing to open the batting for Australia at the end of next year's Ashes.

The positive mindset of the back-to-back Allan Border Medal winner is no surprise.

Head was a revelation in home conditions in last year's Ashes series with three centuries after moving up from the middle order.

Ahead of the opening Test against Bangladesh in Darwin, the 32-year-old was asked if his order switch was short-term or whether it could work across the 20 or more Tests Australia will play in the next 12 months.

There was a sense that Head's move up the order against England was intended to counter their ultra-aggressive "Bazball".

It worked so well that the term "Travball" was coined.

Prior to the home Ashes, his stints as an opener had been short-lived.

Travis Head scored three centuries as an opener in the last Ashes series. (Getty Images: Eurasia Sport Images/Ayush Kumar)

Head was unstoppable on home tracks in the Ashes series, but he will face a variety of surfaces in Australia, South Africa, England and India in the next 12 months.

He says he is not worried about playing in different conditions.

"I feel like I have been adaptable in the places that I have played," Head said.

"In India and England I have opened the batting, which is a slightly different to Australia.

"Everything is going to be different, but what I have been able to do over my career is problem solve the best that I can and work through challenges — whether they are green wickets or flat wickets.

"It will look different in every Test match or every series. I am trying to be as calm and consistent as I can."

Whether Head stays an opener will depend largely on how he performs and also on the displays of the middle order.

Tweaks may be made but right now Head plans to be opening in the final Test of next year's away Ashes series.

"I think it will work," he said.

"If I have done it for [another] 20 Tests and I am sitting there in a few years and I have opened the batting the whole time … I would have done an OK job and been consistent, contributed and had a good partnership with Jake [Weatherald].

"It is a new challenge coming here and a new challenge in South Africa in a month's time and I am looking forward to the challenge."

International cricket coach Joe Gatting has posted videos of how Head plans for a variety of scenarios and surfaces and he is expected to continue to find the best approach in all conditions.

"We have a lot of footage and we couldn't be more resourced in that space. I'll continue to do that," Head said.

AAP

Tech.title: Mark Zuckerberg doesn’t understand how to live
Tech.content:
Recently, a man I was rock climbing with told me about how he’d used AI to make a motivational poster for himself, which he’d hung on his bedroom wall: a bear, walking a slackline over a canyon, holding a sign that said, “Do cool shit.” I made what I hoped was a polite noise. What reaction was this man looking for? He probably hoped someone, maybe me, would say it was cool or inspiring. It seemed I was not the first person he’d told about this poster. “You know, it’s funny,” he said to me. “No one ever says anything about it.”

I have been thinking about this now for several days. There’s a sort of turducken of things that I find off-putting all rolled into this anecdote: hippie shit, motivational posters, AI “art.” Still, the sum total of reactions to this poster appears to be polite noises.

But what is the correct answer to someone showing you their slop? No one made it. Even bad art — for instance, a version of that motivational poster drawn by a person — requires effort on the part of the artist, and expresses the artist’s mind, both in the content and in the motor skills required to draw lines on a page. It requires a person’s time and attention. AI “art” requires typing a prompt into a box, and maybe refining the results a couple times. There’s nothing to react to.

Zuckerberg is trying to be the soothing tech guru

I bring this up because Mark Zuckerberg has posted a manifesto that he — or his communications team, or possibly an AI — wrote. The point of this 6,500-word essay is to define a positive future for AI. It strikes me as an inauspicious sign for AI that a new, supposedly world-changing and value-creating technology should need such a defense, but AI has been getting bad press these days. People hate data centers, and the higher electricity bills that come with them. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said the technology may cause “unusually painful” job losses across multiple industries. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s house was the target of, first, a Molotov cocktail, and then gunfire.

“It is surprising that the discourse from many developing AI is so filled with doom,” the essay says. “I do not understand why anyone who believes that AI will eliminate most jobs and much of humanity’s relevance would rush to build that future.”

I find it difficult to believe that Zuckerberg doesn’t have Amodei’s phone number. Or Altman’s. I know he has Elon Musk’s — I’ve seen their texts in court. Perhaps he should have texted them to ask!

Anyway, Zuckerberg is trying to be the soothing tech guru, here to tell us that things are going to be okay. He’s addressing, however belatedly, the rage that many people feel about AI. There are sections on data centers (Meta is building power sources for some data centers in the future, but don’t ask for renewable energy) and “preventing government tyranny.” This essay exists to try to quiet the AI backlash — even if it never quite says that directly.

Love is not just a feeling; it is a way of paying attention

We will leave aside the question of “superintelligence,” which is Zuckerberg’s preferred term for what the rest of the industry calls “artificial general intelligence”; let’s stipulate, for the purposes of this essay, that it is indeed possible to create. I am also going to ignore the risible defense of the pervert glasses contained in this piece; they are indefensible. As for the risks, I think they are best addressed elsewhere. What I am interested in is what Zuckerberg — or whoever is writing for him — believes will improve all our lives.

Here is his first pitch: “Everyone will have an exceptionally capable personal agent that understands you, your goals, and everything you care about. Your agent will work 24/7 on your behalf to improve your relationships, health, career, finances, home management, hobbies, and more.” I am struck, here, by the inclusion of “relationships” and “hobbies.”

What strengthens a relationship? Almost always, it is personal investment. Perhaps an AI agent might be better at predicting what my father will want for his birthday than I am, but it definitionally cannot give him my time and consideration. Love is not just a feeling; it is a way of paying attention.

Zuckerberg’s vision of maximizing productivity comes at the cost of my experience

Zuckerberg uses an example that is telling, in a grim kind of way: He asked an AI to pick out a “personalized” recipe to bake with his daughter. He could have considered what kind of baking his daughter enjoys, what her skill set is and what he might be able to teach her, then picked a recipe. Maybe he would have picked a bad recipe, and they would have bungled it — but that might have been a fun experience and a good story. Or maybe he would have picked a family recipe, and it would have given him the opportunity to tell her about when he was a child, or what his grandmother was like. Certainly he’s a busy man, but wouldn’t that make the gift of his attention to her hobby even more precious? Perhaps he might have come to understand her better by spending more time thinking about what she likes. Without that attention, the baking they do together seems more focused on accomplishment than quality time.

Relatedly, the point of a hobby is that you do it. Granted, many of my hobbies are physical activities — hiking, running, yoga, rock climbing (with guys who make bad AI art, apparently).
